items.title: Mutual Linearity in Nonlinear Population Dynamics
items.summary: Mutual Linearity in Nonlinear Population DynamicsMutual linearity, the persistence of affine relations among stationary observables under arbitrarily strong changes of one transition rate, is known for Markov jump processes and chemical reaction networks. We show that generalized Lotka--Volterra dynamics form a new class of mutually linear systems, even though species can go extinct and attractors can be chaotic. Any change to one species' equation acts on the others as one effective press and keeps all abundances affinely related: piecewise across extinctions, and as time averages on chaotic attractors.

items.title: Spatial patterns of transportation choice in Niterói
items.summary: Characterizing how people move through a city requires spatially and temporally fine-grained data that are often costly and difficult to obtain. Here, we introduce a computational framework that uses macroscopic, aggregated, and static urban data to construct a microscopic, dynamic, and spatially detailed representation of urban mobility. Building on an existing activity simulator, the framework combines a synthetic population, the built environment, and transport networks to generate daily trips and assign walking, car, or public transit. Applied to approximately 475,000 synthetic residents of Niterói, Brazil, simulated neighborhood-level transit patterns show a strong association with an empirical activity proxy (Pearson r=0.885). Walking is more prevalent in compact central areas, car use increases toward the periphery, and public-transit use remains comparatively high along bus corridors. Reducing walking times to and from bus stops by 30% increases the modeled public-transit-to-car ratio by 11.3%, with larger transit-share gains in several peripheral areas. These results reveal spatial differences in transportation choice and identify where improved transit access may have the greatest modeled effect.

items.title: Agentic Symbolic Search: Approximating Solutions of PDEs Beyond Hand-crafted Expressions, Meshes, and Neural Networks
items.summary: Numerical methods and neural networks have transformed our understanding of nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs), yet discovering mathematical representations that explain their dynamics remains largely an expert task. We introduce Agentic Symbolic Search (ASYS), in which coding agents construct and refine explicit approximations from a known PDE and supplied mathematical knowledge. ASYS couples evolutionary search over differentiable symbolic programs with gradient-based fitting, using the governing equation to evaluate candidates and guide their revision. For a singular generalized Constantin-Lax-Majda profile, ASYS infers a missing decay term that sets how fast the field approaches its singular-time limit, and builds a basis that fits the profile to a median error of $3.90\times10^{-5}\%$. For Fujita blow-up, separating diffusion from reaction and deriving a local response lowers the supplied formula's error from 55.5% to 0.0879%. For Allen-Cahn interfaces, a 14-parameter construction yields a mode-coupling law confirmed by independent simulations. These studies show how agentic search develops mathematical starting points into accurate, analyzable approximations.

items.title: Thin-film lithium niobate integrated photonics at 493 nm
items.summary: Visible and near-ultraviolet light underpins applications from biophotonics to quantum computing, which demand fast control of optical amplitude and phase. Integrated photonics offers scalable control, yet most visible-wavelength platforms lack gigahertz-scale modulation. We demonstrate a thin-film lithium niobate platform at 493 nm integrating grating couplers, beamsplitters, ring resonators, and modulators. Segmented traveling-wave modulators achieve a half-wave voltage--length product of 450 mV$\cdot$cm, $>$20 dB extinction, and bandwidth beyond 50 GHz. Ring resonators show $2.9 \pm 0.2$ dB/cm propagation loss and quantify the platform's photorefractive response. This enables agile visible beam delivery for trapped-ion systems, although photorefraction and substrate uniformity remain key challenges to scaling.

items.title: Before the First Bond: Depletion-Assisted Stochastic Capture at the Onset of Endocytosis
items.summary: The first barrier to receptor-mediated endocytosis is not binding but arrival within a few nanometers of the membrane. In a crowded extracellular environment, this pre-contact approach is driven by thermal fluctuations and entropic depletion, yet continuum models usually start from established contact or treat the approach deterministically. We formulate a thermodynamically consistent stochastic theory for this stage. The sphere--plane depletion geometry uses the exact Asakura--Oosawa spherical-cap overlap, not a fitted cap, with either ideal van~'t~Hoff or pressure-only Carnahan--Starling (CS) pressure. Near-wall mobility enters with its essential and often omitted noise-induced drift. The first specific reaction is a Robin radiation boundary; the outer boundary is reflecting or absorbing. Three first-passage quantities are obtained analytically by quadrature: the mean reaction time, the reaction-before-escape probability, and the conditional success time, the last encoded by a Doob transform that exposes the selection bias of conditioning on capture. The local Damköhler number diagnoses the boundary reaction-to-diffusion ratio, while the mean-time crossover follows from the exact reaction and diffusion terms. At baseline, ideal and CS contact depths are \(2.33\) and \(5.95\,k_{\rm B}T\), and the reflecting-outer mean reaction time is approximately \(0.20\,{\rm ms}\); with an absorbing outer boundary the conditional success time is shorter, but the two observables use different boundary protocols. Numerical checks reproduce the analytic results and the radiation-boundary mass balance. This provides a quantitative theoretical framework for crowding-assisted capture before membrane wrapping.

items.title: Silicon and silicon nitride photonic ring resonator arrays for photonic trimming metrology
items.summary: Proposed silicon on silicon oxide 4x4 matrix multiplier for use in refractive index measurements, based on the Advanced Micro Foundry deep ultraviolet process. Agreement between simulated spectra and analytic design spectra demonstrate the intended performance of the components given a 1550 nm wavelength spectrum analysis. Intended purpose of the design includes optical damage analysis of the cladding, and photonic chip refractive index analysis following sub-threshold laser ablation. Femtosecond multi-shot tuning of refractive index is not a recommended application, due to round trip-losses causing quality factor and transfer function degradation.

items.title: Gravitational radiation from a particle in circular orbit around a wormhole: the nonrotating case
items.summary: In this paper, we have generalized Poisson's(1993) calculation for the case of gravitational radiation from a particle in a circular orbit around a black hole to the case of the wormhole. Considering the motion of a test particle around a Schwarzschild like wormhole and using Teukolsky formalism, we have obtained an analytical result of flux at infinity under the assumption of small velocities. Focusing on the 22-mode, we have found a novel 0.5PN order term beyond the quadrupole order, which vanishes in the black hole limit. On the other hand, all higher order terms are getting modified in such a way that they give correct correspondence in the black hole limit. We have further corroborated our results with the numerical investigations, which show that the two waveforms match well when the particle lies far from ISCO. Thus, our work provides one of the first attempts toward the study of the post-Newtonian waveforms involving wormholes (ECOs).

items.title: Angle-Resolved Reflectance Measurements in the Vacuum Ultraviolet for Metallic Samples
items.summary: The light yield of noble-element scintillation detectors depends strongly on the reflective properties of detector materials in the vacuum ultraviolet (VUV), where optical measurements are scarce. For this reason, we built a custom rotary setup at IFIC, equipped with a monochromator and operated in a gaseous argon atmosphere, to perform angle-resolved reflectance measurements in the specular reflection plane. We describe the setup and its extensive characterization, together with the procedure used to measure the bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) of materials at various angles of incidence, for wavelengths from 128 to 500 nm, covering both the argon (128 nm) and xenon (175 nm) scintillation wavelengths. To illustrate the capabilities of the setup, we present results for rough aluminum and stainless-steel surfaces as reference materials. Fitting the measured angular profiles with the analytical GGX microfacet model allows us to extract the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index and the surface roughness parameter of each sample. These parameters are then used to extrapolate the in-plane measurements to the full hemisphere and from gaseous argon to liquid media, enabling the inference of the hemispherical reflectance in gaseous argon, liquid argon and liquid xenon.

items.title: Nucleation of water ice under weak ionization via clustering on negative ions
items.summary: Water-ice grains are shown to form spontaneously in a cold, weakly-ionized laboratory plasma with trace water admixture when neutrals and ions are cooled below $\sim$200 K. These conditions serve as an analog of ice nucleation in cold astrophysical and atmospheric environments. The ice grains form without the presence of particulate impurities, and do not form in the absence of ionization, indicating that nucleation is induced by ions. Time-resolved ion mass spectrometry provides separate detection of clusters of water molecules on both positive and negative ions. Hydrated negative ions, mainly $\mathrm{OH^-(H_2O)_n}$, grow to $\sim$200 amu, while hydrated positive ions, mainly $\mathrm{H^+(H_2O)_n}$, remain small and short-lived. As the temperature is reduced from room temperature toward 200 K, negative ion clusters grow in size and then drop sharply in abundance, consistent with the onset of rapid growth into macroscopic ice grains below a critical temperature. This indicates that hydrated negative ions are key precursors to ice nucleation in cold, weakly ionized environments, such as the Earth's mesosphere and protoplanetary disks, providing a concrete pathway for ice formation in environments where the nucleation mechanism has remained unresolved. This negative ion pathway is estimated to dominate over ice deposition on pre-existing dust grains in protoplanetary disk locations where there is sufficient UV to partially dissociate water molecules, and in addition, where negative ions such as OH- can form readily through electron attachment at low temperature.

items.title: A first application of split conformal prediction for dose prediction in knowledge-based radiotherapy planning
items.summary: Radiation therapy treatment planning is a labour-intensive process prone to inter-expert variability. Deep learning (DL) dose prediction can accelerate this process, but most DL models do not quantify their reliability. In this study, we construct prediction intervals for DL-based radiotherapy dose prediction using split conformal prediction (CP), a model-agnostic and distribution-free method for uncertainty quantification that provides finite-sample coverage guarantees. We propose patient-level nonconformity scores obtained by aggregating voxelwise scores. Specifically, we formulate a maximum aggregation construction, which guarantees simultaneous coverage of the true dose in all voxels of a future patient with at least a user-defined probability, and a quantile-based construction, which guarantees, with the same probability lower bound, that a future patient attains a prescribed minimum level of voxel coverage. We also investigate groupwise calibration for region-specific guarantees and predictive uncertainty scaling for locally adaptive prediction intervals. The methods are evaluated on head-and-neck cases using a deep ensemble model. The proposed constructions achieved empirical coverage consistent with the nominal levels. Maximum aggregation led to conservative prediction intervals, whereas quantile aggregation produced narrower intervals. Groupwise calibration and uncertainty scaling reduced interval widths in some anatomical regions, while providing region-specific guarantees and local adaptivity. This is the first application of split CP to radiotherapy dose prediction. The explicit patient-level coverage guarantees offer a more interpretable characterisation of prediction reliability than raw uncertainty estimates. Split CP could help clinicians assess the reliability of model predictions and identify cases requiring further review.

items.title: Plasmascopy of ultrafast hot charge carriers
items.summary: We demonstrate an electric-field-resolved approach for probing ultrafast dynamics of photoinjected charge carriers in solids. Direct access to the electric field of few cycle pulses enables us to measure a broadband response of a medium with associated plasma frequency. We prepare an ensemble of hot charge carriers with energies sufficient to trigger impact ionization and establish a framework to measure its dynamics. Our time-resolved study reveals the short-lived ultrafast dynamics consistent with impact ionization and carrier trapping. This approach provides a promising route for studying ultrafast many-body physics in photoexcited solids, with predictions from advanced theoretical models.

items.title: Intensity limits for phase-only holographic optical-tweezer arrays
items.summary: Optical tweezers use tightly focused laser beams to trap and manipulate individual particles, enabling advances in quantum computing, drug discovery, and biological research. Scaling these technologies to large arrays requires delivering sufficient light to every trapping site while minimizing the total laser power required. Here, we investigate the fundamental limits of how efficiently a phase-only hologram can distribute light across an array of optical traps. We derive upper bounds on the minimum intensity across trapping sites, accounting for illumination, target geometry, and diffraction from spatial light modulator pixels. For arrays arranged in a single plane or across two axial planes, we show how these limits scale with the number of traps and SLM pixels, and establish conditions for focusing light in three dimensions. Numerical experiments demonstrate that optimized holograms can closely approach these theoretical limits, suggesting that further improvements in phase optimization alone offer limited power savings. Instead, our results reveal how the choice of illumination and trap geometry can improve light efficiency, providing practical guidelines for designing larger, more power-efficient optical-tweezer arrays.

items.title: Cotangent-lift inference of stochastic microbial dynamics
items.summary: We study the parameter estimation for the stochastic logistic and Lotka--Volterra diffusions from discrete, irregularly spaced observations corrupted by measurement noise, a setting typical of microbiome time series. For the logistic equation, the growth rate acts as a time change and does not enter the stationary law, so it can be identified only from the temporal structure of the data. We prove that the maximum-likelihood estimator of the Euler scheme, with the observations taken as the states, coincides with the regression of log-increments on abundances used in the literature, and we characterise what this estimator cannot see under measurement noise: for the linearised dynamics, the law of consecutive pairs of observations is invariant along an explicit one-parameter family of relaxation rates and noise levels, and the regression converges to a limit set by the noise. Treating the true abundances as latent, we compute the likelihood with a Gaussian moment filter and show that measurement noise is precisely what couples the filter states across samples. The exact gradient is then the backward recursion of the discrete cotangent lift, whose cost, two to three likelihood evaluations, does not depend on the number of parameters, and we give the covector map of each filter step in closed form. In simulations, the latent estimator recovers the relaxation times, noise levels and interaction strengths that the regression biases, while larger communities require prior information on the interactions. In gut microbiome time series it attributes most of the variability of a dominant genus to measurement noise and estimates its relaxation time at about $64$ hours, with a large standard error.

items.title: When can buoyancy be neglected in simulations of crystallization fouling? Evidence from a confluence flow cell
items.summary: Predicting crystallization fouling remains difficult because it couples supersaturation, nucleation, crystal growth, transport, and adhesion. Separating these processes requires model systems in which they can be independently controlled. One such system is the confluence flow cell, where two incompatible brines mix and generate supersaturation at their interface. The mixing pattern is often predicted using constant-density simulations because density differences between the brines are typically only a few percent or less. We investigate whether this assumption holds when calcium chloride and sodium sulfate react to form gypsum. A constant-density simulation predicts deposition on the channel floor along the centreline. Experimentally, however, gypsum forms bands on both side walls, with deposition moving upstream as flow rate decreases. Dye experiments spanning density differences of 0.14 to 2.1 %, three channel heights, and 32 flow rates show that the distance required for the dyed stream to reach the opposite wall is governed by the bulk Richardson number, $Ri=g'H/U^2$, following $L/H = 3.31\,Ri^{-0.66}$ over four decades in Ri ($R^2=0.89$). When the stream densities are matched, the dyed stream typically no longer reaches the opposite wall, and a reacting experiment shows gypsum deposition on the floor, consistent with the constant-density simulation. A small density difference alone is therefore insufficient to neglect buoyancy; the Richardson number must also be small. At the low flow rates typical of confluence flow cells, this condition is often not met. Because Ri depends only on density difference, channel height, and flow velocity, we recommend evaluating it before applying constant-density models of mixing, reaction, or fouling.

items.title: Heat as gauge
items.summary: We show that thermodynamics can be viewed as a gauge theory. In particular, it is a principal R-bundle over a space of observable work configurations, with gauge transformations representing changes in the 'hidden' contributions to energy not captured by work. Heat defines a connection, and its curvature measures deviation from local equilibrium. Summed negative curvature on a disc is shown to give an expression of the Clausius inequality on the oriented loop bounding that disc. This allows one to derive a geometric expression of the Second Law. The framework further allows one to exhibit a thermal analogue of the Aharonov-Bohm effect. Instead of producing geometric phase shifts, this effect produces geometric entropy shifts.

items.title: Discovering Equations for the Thermodynamics of South Asian Monsoon Precipitation
items.summary: South Asian monsoon precipitation depends on the thermodynamic structure of the lower troposphere, but how its ingredients combine to shape precipitation remains unclear, partly because this dependence is nonlocal in the vertical. We use symbolic distillation, which combines neural networks and symbolic regression, to discover interpretable precipitation equations from 21 years of June-August reanalysis data. Neural networks first learn the vertical thermodynamic structure most relevant to precipitation, condensing each variable into a single interpretable feature not tied to a particular vertical grid. Then, symbolic regression derives closed-form equations from these features and the surface state. Our best equation explains 1.5 times as much precipitation variance as a widely used buoyancy-based diagnostic and recovers about 85% of neural network skill while using about a thousand times fewer parameters. Unlike the buoyancy diagnostic, which adds moisture and instability, the equations treat them as competing controls, with the heaviest precipitation occurring when the lower free troposphere is humid. Over ocean, sensible heating is associated with additional precipitation mainly when near-surface air is warm and moist, improving predicted precipitation and its diurnal cycle. Although the learned features were optimized only for precipitation prediction, the equations largely respond to each feature as expected from convective physics, consistent with the reanalysis. These responses reduce the dependence of monsoon precipitation on the entire vertical column to a few simple, testable constraints that could guide data-driven precipitation models to make them more physically consistent.

items.title: Improved Myelin Water Fraction Estimation and Uncertainty Mapping in Multicomponent T2 Relaxometry via NNLS Bootstrap Aggregation
items.summary: Estimating the myelin water fraction (MWF) from multicomponent T2 relaxometry requires solving an ill-conditioned inverse problem, making estimates sensitive to noise. Regularization can improve stability but may introduce bias. Conventional NNLS-based methods also provide point estimates without directly quantifying voxelwise variability. To address these limitations, we propose the non-negative least squares Bootstrap Barycenter (NNLS-BB), combining residual resampling with repeated NNLS reconstruction. We average spectra and derived parameters across bootstrap replicates and use their standard deviations to characterize sensitivity to signal perturbations. The method requires neither an explicit spectral regularization penalty nor a training dataset. NNLS-BB was evaluated on 40,000 simulated voxels with signal-to-noise ratios of 50-1000, against conventional NNLS, two regularized NNLS methods, and a model-informed machine-learning (MIML) method. Scan-rescan repeatability was assessed across 20 white-matter regions in two independent cohorts comprising 13 healthy participants. NNLS-BB achieved the lowest MWF mean absolute error and root mean squared error in all simulated noise regimes. Mean absolute error decreased by 36-41% relative to conventional NNLS, alongside lower error dispersion. Compared with Bayes-Reg-$D^{-1}$ and MIML, NNLS-BB achieved comparable dispersion but substantially lower bias, although MIML reconstructed the full spectrum more accurately. In vivo, NNLS-BB yielded the lowest regional scan-rescan dispersion and highest mean correlation in both cohorts. Bootstrap standard-deviation maps provided complementary information about parameter variability. These results support residual-bootstrap aggregation for improving MWF estimation while providing voxelwise variability maps from a single acquisition.

items.title: Is the Kaniadakis deformation of holographic dark energy detectable? A non-flat analysis with DESI DR2, cosmic chronometers and Pantheon+SH0ES
items.summary: Kaniadakis entropy deforms the horizon entropy through one parameter $κ$, and holographic dark energy built on it (KHDE) reduces to standard holographic dark energy (HDE) when $κ\to0$. The deformation enters the equations through the dimensionless combination $β=KM_p^2/H_0^2$, where $K$ is the effective KHDE parameter. We test whether current data detect it in a curved universe without CMB information. We combine Pantheon+SH0ES supernovae calibrated with Cepheids, 32 cosmic-chronometer measurements of $H(z)$ with their correlated systematic errors, and DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations with a free sound horizon. Non-flat KHDE fits the data as well as flat $Λ$CDM ($Δχ^2=-3.0$), but $β$ is not detected: the profile $χ^2$ changes by only 0.44 between $β=0$ and its best value, and by 0.46 in the flat case. The upper limit $β<0.65$ (95%) comes from the condition that the model has a real solution, not from the data; where the truncated expansion is reliable, the limit is $β<0.57$. $β$ of order one corresponds to $κ$ of order $10^{-122}$. Comparing flat and non-flat HDE and KHDE with $Λ$CDM shows that neither curvature nor the deformation improves the fit enough to justify the extra parameters. The joint fit gives $Ω_{k0}=0.007\pm0.046$, $H_0=72.85\pm0.94$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ and $r_d=137.41\pm1.88$ Mpc. The expansion starts to accelerate at $z_t=0.66\pm0.03$, and a neural-network reconstruction of $H(z)$ from the chronometers agrees with the model.

items.title: Signs of Possible High-Temperature Superconductivity in Graphite Intercalated with Lithium-Based Alloys
items.summary: We report experimental results indicating possible high-temperature superconductivity in graphite intercalation compounds synthesized with lithium-based alloys. Temperature-dependent measurements of magnetic moment, trapped magnetic flux, and electrical resistance reveal transitions with critical temperatures (Tc) in the range of 240-350 K at ambient pressure, depending on the intercalation metals and synthesis conditions. The highest Tc values and largest high-Tc volume fractions (< 0.1 %) were observed in graphite samples intercalated with ternary Sr-Ca-Li alloy. Our results and analyses suggest that the observed transitions originate from local superconductivity rather than intrinsic magnetic properties of the intercalated graphite, which may be an alternative explanation. Accordingly, we propose and intend to pursue further investigations to test and confirm the nature of the observed high-Tc transitions, and to obtain larger high-Tc fractions by optimizing the intercalation materials and synthesis methods.

items.title: The two-component picture of soft hadron production: Regge exchange, duality, and resonance cascades
items.summary: The fragmentation regions of soft hadronic collisions approach energy-independent limits. Benecke, Chou, Yang, and Yen stated this hypothesis of limiting fragmentation in 1969. Feynman gave it a parton-model formulation the same year. Measurements from the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings (ISR) to the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) still show this approach. Fischer and co-workers interpret the NA49 spectra from the CERN Super Proton Synchrotron (SPS) as the sum of a target and a projectile component, each the decay of an excited hadronic system. This review traces the theory behind that two-component picture. It examines the hypothesis that the hadronic tools that predate quantum chromodynamics (QCD) suffice for the soft, non-perturbative domain of QCD. Regge exchange organizes the fragmentation region in triple-Regge form. It supplies the diffractive mass law of the excited systems, with the shrinkage of the Pomeron in its transfer dependence. Finite-energy sum rules and the two-component duality of Harari and Freund equate averaged towers of resonances with that exchange. Duality therefore motivates describing the excited systems in hadronic degrees of freedom. The review follows the cascade description through its predecessors, namely the fireballs of Niu, the novas of Jacob and Slansky, the clusters of Hwa, Good-Walker diffraction, and the two-stage dissociation of Hama. HEART (Hadronic Excitations And Resonance Transitions) assembles these pieces into an event-level cascade of two-body hadronic transitions. A companion paper (arXiv:2611.11570) defines it and tests it against the NA49 data. The review closes with the fragmentation-region measurements that would separate a resonance cascade from a string, namely the isospin of forward baryons, the local balance of strangeness in associated production, and forward resonance signals with their mass tails.

items.title: Optimization principles, revisited
items.summary: The brain solves a wide range of problems, and some of these solutions are very good indeed. It is an old idea that, in some cases, these solutions may be as good as possible given the relevant constraints. If this is true we can promote this notion of optimization to a principle from which aspects of function and mechanism can be derived, ideally with no free parameters. Optimization principles are powerful and have had many successes, but they remain controversial. We start with a reminder of a classic example---diffraction limited optics in insect eyes---and then a summary of why you should worry about optimization as a more general principle. Next we turn to recent progress on the theory of optimal motion estimation in fly vision, and finally summarize recent results on the landscape for optimization, arguing that (contrary to widely held intuitions) optimal performance need not require the underlying mechanisms to have finely tuned parameters. I hope to convince you that this is a moment to take optimization seriously as the basis for theories of neural coding and computation. This is based on a rather informal lecture at the summer school LASCON X in Sao Paulo, and I have tried to preserve that tone here; pointers are given to more detailed and technical discussions.

items.title: Mechanism-Aware Ensemble Conditioning for Data-Limited Emulation of Extreme Events
items.summary: Extreme events in chaotic systems are difficult to learn from short trajectories because they are controlled by finite-time instabilities rather than by frequently observed bulk dynamics. We propose a mechanism-aware conditioning plug-in framework that turns a nudged ensemble of an imperfect model into a non-intrusive sensor of the local instability geometry. In the small-noise regime, the ensemble covariance has the same finite-time deformation kernels that govern local instability, providing a Jacobian-free proxy for local amplifications around a trajectory. A small Feature-Wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) network injects the ensemble geometry into an otherwise unchanged backbone without modifying the low-fidelity model simulator. We demonstrate this interface in two settings: a Transformer-style residual-attention corrector for a controlled low-dimensional chaotic system and a probabilistic recurrent STORN corrector for topographic two-layer quasi-geostrophic (QG) flow. In the low-dimensional benchmark, leading ensemble-covariance directions identify transient instabilities that are also detected by Optimally Time-Dependent (OTD) modes. FiLM conditioning improves 99th-percentile exceedance-frequency errors over an otherwise identical unconditioned Transformer. In QG, an ensemble-conditioned FiLM-STORN model substantially improves long-horizon rare-event statistics in the data-limited regime, including density-tail errors, exceedance frequencies, and spatial exceedance-area distributions relative to an unconditioned STORN trained on the same data. On averaged high-threshold exceedance diagnostics, it also outperforms the unconditioned baseline STORN trained with 20 times more expensive trajectory data. These results show that local instability geometry is not merely interpretable post hoc, but an actionable conditioning signal for data-efficient rare-event emulation.

items.title: Stochastic Discrete Variable Representation: Tensor Network Eigenstates on General Potential Energy Surfaces
items.summary: Tensor network states such as tree tensor network states (TTNS) or matrix product states (MPS) allow very compact representations of high-dimensional wave functions. Using them efficiently relies on a compact representation of the Hamiltonian, and many methods are limited to the sum-of-products (SOP) form. General potential energy surfaces (PESs) do not have this form. To overcome this issue, a stochastic discrete variable representation (SDVR) is presented. The matrix elements of the potential operator in the node-local basis are estimated stochastically by importance sampling of grid configurations. The estimator of the matrix elements is unbiased, and the PES is only evaluated pointwise. The variance is reduced by representing parts of the potential with a 2-mode representation and only sampling the remainder. Sampling noise biases the eigenvalues. A noise-control scheme mitigates this bias. Final energies are obtained from an unbiased variational Monte Carlo estimator. The method is demonstrated by calculating vibrational states of CH3 (6D) and acetonitrile (12D), as well as the zero-point vibrational energy of uracil (30D). For all three systems, the energies agree with the exact references to sub-wavenumber accuracy.

items.title: A fast two-phase model for PEM fuel cell impedance
items.summary: We report a physics-based matrix model for PEM fuel cell impedance that takes into account liquid water transients in the cathode catalyst layer (CCL). This model is an extension of our previous single-phase matrix model for functionally graded CCLs. The solution to the boundary-value problem for the perturbation amplitudes is constructed from basic solutions to the respective Cauchy problem with constant coefficients on numerical cells. The single-phase model employed analytical solutions to this problem. Here, for a larger system of ODEs, the analytical solution does not exist and we used spectral decomposition of the ODE system matrix to obtain the basic solutions numerically. Our impedance model is two orders of magnitude faster than a model based on a standard, general-purpose boundary-value solver. Fitting the matrix model to an experimental spectrum takes about a minute on a laptop. The developed matrix method can be used to numerically solve high-order linear boundary-value problems with variable coefficients.

items.title: A Conservative Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes Formulation for Digital Rock Flow Simulation with Embedded Second-Brinkman Effects
items.summary: Accurate pore-scale direct numerical simulation (DNS) typically requires boundary-conforming meshes on fully resolved geometries, which is memory-intensive and often becomes impractical when modelling complex rock geometries. In contrast, the Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes (DBS) framework enables simulations to be performed directly on voxelized micro-CT images. However, the commonly used simplified DBS formulation (DBS1) neglects the second Brinkman term (SBT) and the porosity-gradient viscous-diffusion term, leading to errors in flow-field characterisation and permeability prediction. Although it is well established that the SBT is essential for capturing viscous boundary effects, it is often assumed that its inclusion requires separate discretisation. In this work, we show that no separate discretisation of the SBT is necessary: writing the DBS equation in its conservative form and applying a standard central differencing scheme in a finite-volume discretisation naturally retains the full DBS formulation. We refer to this formulation as DBS2, and validate its implementation in the GeoChemFoam framework (our open-source computational fluid dynamics simulator based on OpenFOAM) using three benchmark cases: (i) microchannel flow, (ii) a 2D heterogeneous micromodel, and (iii) a 3D micro-CT image of Bentheimer sandstone. Simulation results show that the DBS2 formulation reproduces the DNS velocity field exactly in the microchannel and matches DNS permeability to within 1.5-3.8% in the micromodel and Bentheimer cases at matched spatial resolution. In contrast, DBS1 systematically overpredicts permeability (14.1 to 37.9% in our cases) under the same discretization. Notably, the conservative treatment of the viscous stress preserves the computational efficiency of DBS1 while achieving DNS-level accuracy.

items.title: Constraining electron heat flux from reduced measurements
items.summary: Coronal heating estimates depend partly on electron heat transport. Different electron velocity distributions can match the same observations yet carry different heat fluxes. We ask which measurements are enough to determine heat flux without finding how electrons are distributed across all speeds and directions. The solar wind carries electrons outward from the corona and allows their velocities to be measured directly. Using one Wind measurement, we keep density, mean flow, temperature and angular summaries for each energy channel. In the fixed-bin model, electron distributions that match these quantities have heat fluxes from 3.58 to 19.85 $μ$W m$^{-2}$. Keeping the correlation between electron motion along and across the magnetic field fixes the heat flux at 11.73 $μ$W m$^{-2}$, matching the original bin calculation. This recovers heat flux without reconstructing the full shape of the electron velocity distribution. When the measured counts vary, retaining the required correlations leaves the same heat-flux range as direct calculation from those counts. We propose testing coronal observations in the same way to find which features of electron motion they constrain well enough to determine heat transport. Those constraints could help establish the heating requirements used to assess coronal heating mechanisms.

items.title: Deflating the Spacetime-Matter Dichotomy
items.summary: In this paper we analyse scalar-tensor theories-specific instances of which include mainstream inflation and dark energy models-in light of the spacetime-matter dichotomy. We argue that it is difficult to categorise the scalar fields as either a pure aspect of the spacetime structure or a pure form of matter, by focusing on the Jordan vs Einstein frames of these theories. We present and evaluate various interpretational options available, concluding that the spacetime-matter dichotomy becomes untenable in this context. At the same time, the ontological and conceptual category of spacetime can be decoupled from that of gravity, with the latter remaining viable in the context of scalar-tensor theories.

items.title: Below-shot-noise capacity in phase estimation using nonlinear interferometers
items.summary: Over the past decade, several schemes for imaging and sensing based on nonlinear interferometers have been proposed and demonstrated experimentally. These interferometers exhibit two main advantages. First, they enable probing a sample at a chosen wavelength while detecting light at a different wavelength with high efficiency (bicolor quantum imaging and sensing with undetected light). Second, they can show quantum-enhanced sensitivities below the shot-noise limit, potentially reaching Heisenberg-limited precision in parameter estimation. Here, we compare three quantum-imaging configurations using only easily accessible intensity-based measurements for phase estimation: a Yurke-type SU(1,1) interferometer, a Mandel-type induced-coherence interferometer, and a hybrid scheme that continuously interpolates between them. While an ideal Yurke interferometer can exhibit Heisenberg scaling, this advantage is known to be fragile under realistic detection constraints and in the presence of loss. We demonstrate that differential intensity detection in the Mandel interferometer provides the highest and most robust phase sensitivity among the considered schemes, reaching but not surpassing the shot-noise limit, even in the presence of loss. Intensity measurements in a Yurke-type configuration can achieve genuine sub-shot-noise sensitivity under balanced losses and moderate gain; however, their performance degrades in realistic high-gain regimes. Consequently, in this regime, the Mandel configuration with differential detection outperforms the Yurke-type setup and constitutes the most robust approach for phase estimation.

items.title: A New Computational Model for the Spin-Free Sum-of-Squares Energy Bounds of Electronic Hamiltonian
items.summary: Optimizing spin-free sum-of-squares (SOS) energy bounds for electronic Hamiltonians leads to semidefinite programs whose expanded size grows rapidly with the orbital dimension. We derive an exact reformulation of an established spin-free SOS model as a convex quadratic problem over a single symmetric matrix constrained between zero and the identity. Explicit recovery maps connect feasible quadratic-program iterates to certificates in the original SOS formulation, and identify the Frank--Wolfe gap with the separation between recovered primal and dual objectives. We implement the quadratic action through GPU-accelerated Coulomb contractions and solve the reformulated problem using a cached implementation of fully corrective Frank--Wolfe, referred to here as the dimension-reduced simplicial method (DRSM) that caches operator products and optimizes convex-combination weights in a small corrective quadratic program. Numerical experiments cover 65 FCIDUMP models, molecular geometries, and regular hydrogen rings, including original-coordinate recovery checks on nine instances and comparisons with FISTA and a boundary-point SDP solver. On eight H100 GPUs, a cold-start calculation for C$_{720}$ with 10,080 spatial orbitals reaches a freshly recomputed Frank--Wolfe gap of $8.82\times10^{-9}$ hartree in 5.02 hours. Full-space hydrogen-ring calculations reach 10,000 orbitals, with cyclic reduction providing further computational savings. These results show how exact reformulation, data structure exploitation and reuse of Coulomb actions make optimization of the selected large-scale SOS relaxation practical.

items.title: Cavitation near the oscillating piezoelectric plate in water
items.summary: Gas and vapor bubbles at a wall can reduce the skin friction of a liquid flow. We estimate whether an oscillating piezoelectric plate mounted flush with the wall can create such a near-wall bubble layer by acoustic cavitation. Once the cavitation threshold is reached, the liquid can no longer follow the receding plate, and the excess plate displacement is accommodated by cavitation bubbles forming at the wall; this kinematic argument gives the bubble volume generated per stroke and its energy cost. Homogeneous cavitation in pure water (about -30 MPa) requires pressure amplitudes far beyond those of flat piezoelectric plates and produces submicron bubbles that collapse within nanoseconds. Heterogeneous cavitation on wall and gas nuclei (-0.1 to -1 MPa) is within reach of piezoceramics and concentrates the void on fewer, larger wal-attached bubbles, which survive between strokes if they exceed a few micrometres at 5 MHz. The acoustic power needed to sustain a bubble layer in a turbulent boundary layer at 10 m/s is about 20 kW/m2 for heterogeneous and about 0.4 MW/m2 for homogeneous cavitation.

items.title: Experimental Investigation of Heat Transfer in Axisymmetric Open Cavities at Hypersonic Speeds
items.summary: An experimental investigation was conducted to characterize the heat-transfer behavior of an axisymmetric cavity mounted on a cone with a semi-apex angle of $(48^ \circ)$ under Mach 6 freestream conditions in a Ludwieg tunnel. The effects of cavity geometry, represented by the length-to-depth ratio $(L/D = 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0,$ and $6.0)$, rear-wall height-to-depth ratio $(h/D = -0.25, 0,$ and $0.5)$, and Reynolds number ($Re_D = 23000 - 74000$) were systematically investigated. Flow-field characteristics and surface heat-transfer behavior were examined using schlieren and planar laser Rayleigh scattering visualization techniques, together with surface pressure and heat-transfer measurements. The results indicate that increasing the cavity length-to-depth ratio leads to a reduction in the downstream Stanton number $(St_d)$. For the longest cavity $L/D = 6$, however, the downstream Stanton number was found to exceed the upstream value $(St_u)$ indicating enhanced heat transfer in the region downstream of the cavity.

items.title: Turbophoresis of inertial particles in inhomogeneous turbulence generated by oscillating grids
items.summary: Turbophoresis in inhomogeneous turbulent flows leads to the formation of large-scale nonuniform particle number density distributions of inertial particles. This effect is associated with an effective drift velocity directed toward regions of lower turbulence intensity. It depends on the Stokes and Reynolds numbers, as well as on the gradient of the turbulence intensity. In the present study, turbophoretic transport is experimentally investigated in air turbulent flows generated by one-grid and two-grid oscillating systems. The flow velocity field is measured using Particle Image Velocimetry, and the particle spatial distribution is obtained by applying image processing techniques. To isolate the effect of particle accumulation due to turbophoresis from that associated with mean fluid flow, the measured particle number density of inertial particles is normalized by the corresponding distribution obtained for noninertial tracer particles under identical flow conditions. The measurements show preferential accumulation of inertial particles in regions of minimum mean-square turbulent velocity, consistent with the expected behavior of turbophoretic transport.

items.title: Reconstructing High-Fidelity Light Yield Maps for Surface LArTPCs Using Crossing Cosmic Muons
items.summary: Photon detection systems in liquid argon time projection chambers provide prompt scintillation light information that can improve triggering, timing, calorimetry, and interaction reconstruction. These applications require an understanding of the spatial dependence of the detected light yield (LY), which is not adequately described by a single detector-wide average. We present a method for reconstructing voxelized 3D light yield maps in surface LArTPCs using crossing cosmic muons. For each selected muon, the path length through every crossed voxel is converted to deposited energy using a minimum ionizing particle approximation, producing a linear system relating the unknown voxel light yields to the total detected photon signal. The resulting inverse problem is solved using nonnegative least squares, with an additional $L_2$ smoothness penalty used to stabilize weakly constrained voxel values. The method is studied in simulation using the ProtoDUNE-VD detector geometry and photon detection system. Reconstructed maps recover the dominant spatial structure of a visibility-based truth reference and respond as expected to changes in the photon detector configuration. Smoothness regularization reduces zero-valued voxels and localized fluctuations while leaving the detector-average light yield approximately unchanged at the selected regularization strengths. The voxel-wise RMSE relative to the truth reference is reduced by approximately 44% for the regularized reconstruction.

items.title: Tidal potential measured with distant optical clocks
items.summary: Fibre-linked optical clocks sense tidal changes of the gravitational potential, but separating overlapping tidal components and quantifying their precision remain challenging. Using strontium and ytterbium clocks 692 km apart, we measure over 353 days a response of 0.95 (0.11) to the combined solid-Earth and ocean-loading tide and 1.01 (0.13) for the lunar semidiurnal group, and separate the lunar and solar-frequency semidiurnal contributions. A signal-to-noise model based on the actual sampling accounts for the lunar precision and guides future clock-network observations.

items.title: Nanostructuring Semiconductor Surfaces Using Self-Assembled Metal Nanoparticles for Optoelectronic Applications
items.summary: Semiconductor nanostructures are key light-management elements because their geometry can strengthen light-matter interaction, suppress reflection, and enhance optical coupling. Yet their adoption across material platforms is constrained by lithography, multistep pattern transfer, persistent masks, and material-specific etching. Here, we introduce a lithography-free two-step strategy in which thermally evaporated self-assembled Ga nanoparticles act as self-consuming masks during Ar inductively coupled plasma reactive-ion etching. Correlated transmission electron microscopy on GaAs reveals the formation mechanism. Comparable erosion of the Ga nanoparticles and exposed substrate progressively converts Ga-capped pedestals into pure semiconductor nanocones while preserving crystalline order. Nanocone dimensions extend from tens to hundreds of nanometres, and surface coverage is tunable through Ga deposition and plasma power. The same process produces nanocones on GaP and Si and dense nanostructures on polycrystalline hybrid metal-halide perovskite without detectable PbI2 formation. During nanostructuring, the sun-weighted reflectance reaches minima of 11-15% on the monocrystalline substrates, whereas the perovskite achieves 0.5% after complete mask consumption. The approach therefore combines a self-assembled mask, its consumption, and pattern transfer in a single physical etching step, providing a simple route to light-coupling surfaces for III-V, Si, and perovskite optoelectronics.

items.title: Nonreciprocal Josephson Dynamics of a $\mathcal{PT}$-Symmetric Atomtronic SQUID
items.summary: We investigate non-Hermitian Josephson dynamics in an atomtronic quantum interference device (AQUID), formed by a ring Bose Einstein condensate with balanced atomic gain and loss regions and two moving optical barriers. The balanced gain and loss profile establishes a parity time symmetric potential while breaking spatial inversion symmetry, providing the essential ingredients for nonreciprocal Josephson transport. The dynamics are monitored nondestructively through the phase quadrature spectrum of an optomechanical cavity driven by Laguerre Gaussian beams coupled to the condensate. We demonstrate that increasing the local gain and loss strength softens the parity time symmetric collective mode towards an exceptional point, as verified by Bogoliubov de Gennes analysis. The associated coherent population exchange produces an additional characteristic splitting in the cavity output spectrum. For linearly translating barriers, non-Hermiticity provides an additional control parameter for tuning the critical current. When the barriers undergo simultaneous translation and rotation, the rotation induced phase modifies the interference between counter propagating currents, offering further control over the nonreciprocal response. Under periodic barrier modulation, we find more pronounced Shapiro steps in the current voltage characteristics due to the intrinsic parity time symmetric collective mode. Finally, we propose an alternative Hermitian realization using a tilted optical lattice, providing an experimentally accessible route to engineering biased transport and population transfer. Our results establish parity time symmetric atomtronic SQUIDs as a versatile platform for controlling nonreciprocal Josephson transport and collective excitations in driven quantum fluids.

items.title: Bare and stretched string tyre models with distributed FrBD dynamics
items.summary: This paper presents a novel class of string tyre models with FrBD friction dynamics. By modelling the distributed carcass and tread deformations with string-like equations, the resulting formulation leads to a system of semilinear parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs) that describe the evolution of the tyre states without explicitly distinguishing between stick and slip regimes. Rigorous stability and passivity analyses are also conducted using a Lyapunov-based approach, establishing boundedness of the distributed states and energy dissipation during rolling contact. The proposed Lyapunov function admits a clear physical interpretation as the total elastic energy stored in the tyre, enabling a direct link between mechanical energy storage and frictional dissipation due to slip losses. The steady-state and transient behaviours of the model are investigated both numerically and experimentally, revealing that the new formulation can satisfactorily reproduce nonlinear relaxation phenomena excited by step slip inputs. The resulting model provides a physically interpretable, mathematically well-posed, and computationally efficient basis for advanced vehicle dynamics simulations and control-oriented applications.

items.title: ANTIOCH-VS: From Sequence to Hits with Modular, Open-Source Ensemble Virtual Screening
items.summary: Structure-based virtual screening needs a receptor conformation that fits the ligand class, but for most targets no ligand-bound crystal is available -- and a single predicted model or an apo structure often misses the binding-competent state. We present ANTIOCH-VS, an open-source framework that runs an entire in silico screening campaign, from a protein sequence to a ranked shortlist of candidate binders, as one plug-and-play workflow. It first builds a conformational ensemble by reduced-MSA subsampling with ColabFold, then uses AlphaFold2-RAVE (AF2RAVE) -- short molecular-dynamics simulations with State Predictive Information Bottleneck analysis -- to pick out docking-ready, Boltzmann-weighted metastable states. It then detects the binding pocket, prepares receptors and ligands, docks the library across the ensemble with DOCK6 or AutoDock Vina, builds a consensus ranking, and triages the top hits by physics-based metadynamics (CTMD). We benchmark it on two very different targets, JAK2 kinase and ADRB2 GPCR, using their DUD-E benchmark sets of known binders and property-matched decoys. Starting from sequence alone -- no ligand-bound crystal, no manual intervention -- the AF2RAVE ensembles gave top-20 shortlists strongly enriched for true binders: a 20% hit rate for JAK2 and 60% for ADRB2 (random ~1-2%), on par with ligand-bound crystals and, for the kinase, above single AF2 models and an apo crystal. The full pipeline runs end to end on a workstation or HPC from a single command, or each module can be run on its own with user-supplied inputs. ANTIOCH-VS is freely available at https://github.com/tiwarylab/antioch-vs

items.title: Does quantum mechanics apply to macroscopic objects? How to define macro?
items.summary: According to Quantum Mechanics a narrow wave-packet of the center of mass of any macroscopic object should smear out after some time. The problem is usually waved out by assuming that due to their heavy masses this occurs over astronomical times. Without a clear definition of macroscopic objects this remains ambiguous. On the other hand, Quantum Mechanics allows and energetically even prefers largely smeared out c.m. states that never been seen. Why is this the real state of the world we know? Does it suggest a micro-macro threshold with different theoretical descriptions? Does offer micro-miniaturization a hope for answering these questions?

items.title: Direct numerical simulation of turbulent heat transfer in water with temperature-dependent viscosity and conductivity
items.summary: We study turbulent forced convection of liquid water in a plane channel by direct numerical simulation (DNS), with temperature-dependent viscosity and thermal conductivity. The simulations cover wall heating and cooling, mean-to-wall temperature ratios from 0.83 to 1.3, wall temperatures from 277 to 360\,K and wall Prandtl numbers from 2 to 12. Compared with constant-property flow at the same bulk Reynolds number, the friction coefficient changes by $-39\,\%$ to $+32\,\%$, the heat transfer coefficient referred to the wall Prandtl number changes by up to a factor of $2.3$, and empirical correlations deviate from the DNS by up to $26\,\%$. Instantaneous fields and spectra show that the wall friction Reynolds number misrepresents the range of turbulent scales, whereas near-wall streaks of velocity and temperature have a common spacing when scaled with the local viscous length. The density is constant, so the mean velocity and temperature defects in the core follow those of constant-property flow. To predict friction and heat transfer, we map the mean profiles onto those of constant-property flow through integral transformations derived from the mean momentum and energy balances, with empirical corrections of the eddy viscosity and diffusivity calibrated on the DNS. This approach, developed for air, is extended to liquids, whose conductivity is not proportional to the viscosity and whose Prandtl number varies across the channel. The inverse transformations predict friction and heat transfer within $2\,\%$ of the DNS, except at the lowest Reynolds numbers. The same corrections, introduced in the Spalart--Allmaras model, halve its friction error.

items.title: Memory-gated transient anomalous transport of quasiparticles out of equilibrium
items.summary: Anomalous transport is ubiquitous across condensed matter, materials science, and biophysics. Yet, in far-from-equilibrium settings, what determines when, how much, and in which direction transport departs from diffusion remains a fundamental open question. By adopting the dispersive Holstein model of small polarons as representative of a wide class of dissipative systems, we show that a signed bath memory time governs the direction and the strength of the transient departure, and that when it vanishes, diffusion emerges without an asymptotic delay. Tuning the dissipative environment from resonant to off-resonant with the carrier density of states, transport turns from subdiffusion to superdiffusion as the memory time changes sign. Microscopically, we trace this memory effect to a competition between polaron formation and coherent polaron motion. These findings establish a unified memory-based description of transient anomalous transport, offering a path to control nonequilibrium quasiparticle flow through environmental tuning.

items.title: Optimal Calibration of Qubit Detuning and Crosstalk
items.summary: Characterizing and calibrating physical qubits is essential for maintaining the performance of quantum processors. A key challenge in this process is the presence of crosstalk that complicates the estimation of individual qubit detunings. In this work, we derive optimal strategies for estimating detuning and crosstalk parameters by optimizing Ramsey interference experiments using Fisher information and the Cramer-Rao bound. We compare several calibration protocols, including measurements of a single quadrature at multiple times and of two quadratures at a single time, for a fixed number of total measurements. Our results predict that the latter approach yields the highest precision and robustness in both cases of isolated and coupled qubits. We validate experimentally our approach using a single NV center as well as superconducting transmons. Our approach enables accurate parameter extraction with significantly fewer measurements, resulting in up to a 50% reduction in calibration time while maintaining estimation accuracy.

items.title: Banding instabilities in poroelastic media under flow-driven compaction
items.summary: When cross-linked poroelastic media are subjected to a hydrostatic pressure difference, they compact, remaining fully swollen on their uppermost surface and becoming increasingly compressed with depth. A critical unexplored effect of cross-linking and resistance to shear deformation is investigated, which is not seen in classical models of poroelastic media treated as free elastic spheres, and resists the kind of compressive compaction that characterises these systems. Eventually, a steady-state profile dependent on osmotic, shear and transport properties is reached, supporting a uniform interstitial flow wherein the medium acts like a passive filter. In this paper, we show how these steady-state profiles are not necessarily stable, and propose a mechanism for the formation of instabilities, wherein some regions of the medium swell and others compact, forming distinctive horizontal or vertical banding patterns. In the latter case, these bands appear qualitatively to be higher-permeability conduits or channels, similar to wormholes or tunnels seen in granular media. It is possible to quantify the effect of changing the pressure head on the growth rate of instabilities and the separation lengthscale in this channelisation case, and how material properties like shear stiffness and dependence of permeability on porosity affect the dynamics of instability. Critically, it is shown that these instabilities are a fluid-mechanical effect, with an entirely new mechanism based on the porosity--permeability relationship and not on elastic effects. With an understanding of these mechanisms, we can derive insight into channelisation in poroelastic systems in geophysics, human biology and industry.

items.title: Comparative evaluation of future collider options
items.summary: In anticipation of the completion of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) programme by the end of 2041, CERN is preparing to launch a new major facility in the mid-2040s. According to the 2020 update of the European Strategy for Particle Physics (ESPP), the highest-priority next collider is an electron-positron Higgs factory, followed in the longer term by a hadron-hadron collider at the highest achievable energy. The CERN directorate established a Future Colliders Comparative Evaluation working group in June 2023. This group brings together project leaders and domain experts to conduct a consistent evaluation of the Future Circular Collider (FCC) and alternative scenarios based on shared assumptions and standardized criteria. This report presents a comparative evaluation of proposed future collider projects submitted as input for the Update of the European Strategy for Particle Physics. These proposals are compared considering main performance parameters, environmental impact and sustainability, technical maturity, cost of construction and operation, required human resources, and realistic implementation timelines. An overview of the international collider projects within a similar timeframe, notably the CEPC in China and the ILC in Japan is also presented, as well as a short review of the status and prospects of new accelerator techniques.

items.title: Some analytical solutions for the evaporative flux and the flow inside a sessile droplet in cylindrical-cap geometry
items.summary: We investigate the evaporation of sessile droplets in a two-dimensional (cylindrical-cap) geometry. To circumvent the singularity in the fundamental solution of the Laplace problem for the vapour diffusion in two dimensions, previous works have imposed a far-field boundary condition at an arbitrary distance from the droplet. To remove this arbitrary distance, we extend the approach of Yariv [Physical Review E, 107(6), p. L063101, 2023] for slender droplets (zero contact angles) to droplets with arbitrary contact angles. Using conformal mapping, we obtain an explicit expression for the evaporative flux for arbitrary contact angles, and verify the result via numerical simulation. We couple the evaporative flux to the Stokes flow inside the droplet and use a local analysis to characterize the flow near the triple point. For contact angles below $90^\circ$, the evaporative flux exhibits the same power-law divergence in the two-dimensional geometry as in the corresponding three-dimensional (spherical-cap) geometry. The flow near the triple point likewise has the same power-law dependence in the two geometries. Our expressions for the evaporative flux and flow inside the droplet are explicit and involve no special functions, and therefore provide a simple explanation of the mechanism which drives the contact-line flow in evaporating sessile droplets.

items.title: Sub-Ice: semi-automated mapping of basal channels from ice shelf surface elevation data
items.summary: Basal channels, troughs carved into ice shelf bases by buoyant plumes, modulate basal melt and can weaken ice shelves. Through hydrostatic adjustment they have a surface expression, yet their geometry is largely mapped manually, limiting the number of channels studied and the consistency between mappings. We present Sub-Ice, a semi-automated tool that maps basal channels from surface digital elevation models. From user-defined start and end points, Sub-Ice traces the channel centerline by iteratively locating elevation minima, extracts cross-sectional profiles and delineates channel edges using one of three methods (slope threshold, profile knee point or peak prominence), producing georeferenced centerlines and edges and along-channel width and depth. Applied to 34 channels on Roi Baudouin Ice Shelf, East Antarctica, Sub-Ice centerlines differ from manually digitized ones by a median of 132 m, at the upper end of the differences between manual records from different years (74-132 m), while following the channel trough more closely. Absolute channel widths depend on the edge method and the width of the edge search window, which we calibrate against a slope-based criterion. Rather than seeking a single "true" edge, Sub-Ice applies explicit, reproducible criteria, enabling consistent comparison of channel geometry across channels, ice shelves and time.

items.title: Classical phase unwrapping enables large-time-step unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization
items.summary: For computing molecular energies on early fault-tolerant hardware, unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization (UQKSD) avoids both the deep circuits of quantum phase estimation and the Pauli-term sampling of variational methods by extracting the energies from a projected real-time propagator. At a small time step $τ$, nearly linearly dependent Krylov vectors make the overlap matrix ill-conditioned. Our tests at fixed total evolution time show that additional Krylov vectors then add no accuracy, while the thresholded energy becomes increasingly sensitive to the choice of cutoff. A larger time step improves the conditioning and reduces the Krylov dimension $M$ needed for a target accuracy, but the energies are then known only modulo $2π/τ$. We present Classical Unwrapping for Resolving Eigenvalues (CURE-QKSD), a classical post-processing method that leaves the UQKSD circuits and generalized eigenvalue problem unchanged and recovers the missing multiples of $2π/τ$ from phase-consistency landscapes of one or, when needed, two UQKSD runs. In noiseless tests on six molecules with 12--20 qubits, all 28 targeted energies are recovered in their aliased regimes with final errors of at most $1.1\times10^{-7}$~Ha. Under Gaussian noise with $σ=10^{-4}$, the median error of the ground or first excited state reaches chemical accuracy at large aliased time steps with $M=20$--$65$, whereas uncorrected principal-branch energies are off by $0.7$--$115$~Ha. CURE-QKSD therefore makes aliased time steps usable for UQKSD calculations with smaller, better-conditioned Krylov bases.

items.title: Barriers to dequantization of near-term molecular electronic structure methods
items.summary: We prove classical simulation hardness, under the generalized $\mathsf{P}\neq\mathsf{NP}$ conjecture, for quantum circuit families with applications in near-term molecular electronic ground and excited state estimation. The proof exploits a connection to particle number conserving matchgate circuits with fermionic magic state inputs, which are shown to be universal for quantum computation under postselection, and are therefore not classically simulable in the worst case, in either the strong (multiplicative) or weak (sampling) sense. We apply these results to non-orthogonal quantum eigensolvers designed for near-term hardware by ruling out sample-based dequantization strategies to additively approximate the off-diagonal matrix elements between orbital-rotated correlated reference states that satisfy an irreducible fermionic magic property, which combines anticoncentration in any orbital basis with an average-case multiplicative approximation hardness conjecture for the associated matrix polynomials. We apply this complexity analysis to two choices of ansatz that incorporate both static and dynamic correlations to model the electronic eigenstates of molecular systems. These are linear combinations of orbital-rotated matrix product states, which are preparable in linear depth, and linear combinations of states prepared by generalized unitary coupled cluster with singles and doubles or unitary cluster Jastrow circuits of polynomial depth, for which computing the expectation values of local fermionic observables up to a constant additive error is $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete. We discuss the implications for achieving practical quantum advantage in resolving the electronic structure of catalytic systems composed from multivalent transition metal atoms using near-term quantum hardware.

items.title: Intracycle Interference in Strong-Field Photoemission from a Tungsten Needle Tip
items.summary: Electrons photoemitted by strong laser fields can rescatter, generating attosecond high harmonics. Spectral peaks arise from inter- and intracycle interference of coherent electron wave packets. While intercycle interference is well known, intracycle interference of plateau electrons has not been observed. We present carrier-envelope phase-resolved photoemission spectra from a nanometric tungsten needle tip driven at 1570 nm revealing such interference, supported by quantum orbit and TDSE simulations that elucidate attosecond-scale electron dynamics.

items.title: Phase transitions in the simplicial Ising model on hypergraphs
items.summary: Complex higher-order interactions can reshape higher-order dynamics in complex systems. Systematic understanding of the repertoire of phase transitions that higher-order interactions can trigger remains incomplete. Here we study the phase transitions in the simplicial Ising model on hypergraphs, in which the energy within each hyperedge is lowered only when all the member spins are unanimously aligned. We show that its Hamiltonian is equivalent to a weighted sum of lower-order interactions and use the Landau free energy to identify diverse phase transitions depending on the hyperedge sizes. For $q$-uniform hypergraphs, the nature of transitions shifts from continuous to discontinuous at the tricritical point $q = 4$. When both pairwise edges and hyperedges of size $q > 2$ coexist, diverse scenarios emerge, including mixed-order and double transitions, for $q > 8$. We further adopt the Bethe--Peierls method to investigate the interplay between pairwise and higher-order interactions in achieving global magnetization, illuminating the multiscale nature of double transitions.

items.title: Optical characterization of microcellular PET and crystallized PEN reflectors in liquid argon for LEGEND-1000
items.summary: Efficient collection of liquid argon (LAr) scintillation light is essential for background rejection in the LEGEND experiment. We investigate microcellular polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and crystallized polyethylene naphthalate (PEN) as candidate reflector materials for LEGEND-1000. Their optical responses to 450 nm light and 128 nm LAr scintillation are measured in LAr and complemented by room-temperature reflectance measurements in air. Under scintillation illumination, PET coupled to a PEN foil and crystallized PEN increase the detected photoelectron yield by factors of $2.36\pm0.11$ and $1.75\pm0.10$, respectively, relative to a black-metal-velvet reference. A Geant4-based optical model yields reflectivity estimates at $450~\mathrm{nm}$ in LAr of $(90\pm4)\%$ for PET and $(81\pm5)\%$ for crystallized PEN, compared with $(80\pm5)\%$ for the Tetratex reference. These results motivate further investigation of both materials for LAr instrumentation, including their radiopurity, long-term cryogenic stability, and performance under matched detector conditions.

items.title: SOPPA with the Complete Third-Order A Matrix: Singlet Excitation Energies
items.summary: We present the derivation and implementation of the complete third-order correction of the A matrix in the Møller-Plesset polarization propagator approximation. A new contribution to the third-order correction was discovered and we thus report the first results obtained with the complete third-order A matrix. The performance of the Second Order Polarization Propagator Approximation including the third order A matrix (SOPPA-A3) method in calculation of vertical excitation energies was assessed by comparing to the reference methods FCI or CCSDTQP. A substantial improvement over SOPPA was found with the inclusion of the complete third-order A matrix as the SOPPA-A3 method yields excitation energies of a quality comparable to CC2. The inclusion of the new contribution results in a change in the individual excitation energies of varying size and direction depending on the molecule and state and the contribution should therefore be included for a formally complete third-order treatment of the A matrix.

items.title: Filamentary dynamics in fan-like structures in high-altitude lightning discharges
items.summary: We present LOFAR radio telescope measurements revealing that high-altitude negative leaders (HANLs) exhibit behavior completely different from the current paradigm of negative leader propagation. Our data show that the fan at the tip of a propagating HANL is formed by filaments that behave like smoothly advancing negative leaders. These negative leader filaments appear to have moderate conductivity, remain thin (radius $\sim1$ m), grow continuously at $\sim10^5$ m/s over hundreds of meters, and emit VHF radiation persistently. The observations show that the filaments making up the fan in front of a propagating negative leader are not necessarily streamers, as commonly assumed. Previous work suggesting to observe streamers at the tips of negative leaders should be re-examined in light of these new findings

items.title: Revisiting Rotary Blade Aerodynamics and Wake Behavior of a Vertical-Axis Wind Turbine via a High-Order Actuator-Line Framework
items.summary: Vertical-axis wind turbines (VAWTs) experience highly unsteady blade loading and vortex shedding during operation, and the relationship between blade-wake interaction and useful power extraction remains unclear. The present study addresses this gap by relating phase-dependent blade loading and instantaneous wake activity to the mean velocity deficit and net power extraction across distinct operating regimes. Specifically, we show that deep dynamic stall produces large-scale vortex shedding and an energetic instantaneous wake, yet yields only a shallow mean velocity deficit and little net power. Near-optimal operation, by contrast, produces a more organized wake and substantially greater momentum extraction. To study the VAWT dynamics in a cost-effective way, we extended our previously developed steady source term formulation to a time-accurate, high-order numerical framework that couples flux reconstruction and actuator line model on fixed Cartesian grids, incorporating Gaussian force projection, a modified Boeing--Vertol dynamic stall model, and a double multiple streamtube based induction closure. The framework reproduces experimental near-wake profiles and predicts power coefficients comparable to those obtained from a three-dimensional large eddy simulation based actuator line model, with a peak power coefficient approximately 6% lower than the reference value. An upwind-downwind force decomposition shows that dynamic stall acts predominantly during the upwind passage, temporarily increasing power under deep stall conditions while providing little net power overall. Light stall, by limiting large-scale flow separation and the subsequent loss of lift, maintains more consistent power-producing blade loading and therefore yields substantially greater mean power extraction.

items.title: Infrared light scattering and emission from epsilon near-zero hyperbolic phonon-polaritons in two-dimensional crystals
items.summary: This work presents the near-field super-scattering and the near-field thermal emission from 2D hyperbolic crystals as general optical phenomena that link near-field nanophotonics to far-field photonics.

items.title: Contact mechanics and friction of soft materials: an apparatus combining multi-axes dynamical actuation/measurement and in situ/in operando visualisation
items.summary: The mechanics and friction of contact interfaces involving soft materials like gel, rubber or human skin are of both fundamental and applied interest. Recent insights have been made into this field thanks to in situ observations of the contact interface. However, current soft-material--oriented tribometers enable only few degrees of freedom for the actuation of the contact, far from covering the richness of the loading conditions relevant to real tribological contacts. Here, we introduce an instrument dedicated to the study of the contact mechanics and friction of soft materials which, in addition to in situ / in operando optical monitoring of the interface, enables simultaneous actuation along five degrees of freedom: three translations and two rotations. While all three translations feature large velocity/large stroke motion, the one responsible for normal contact loading can also apply high frequency/small amplitude vibrations. The contact's dynamical response is monitored using both a 6-axes force/torque sensor and a 6-axes displacement/rotation sensor. We first describe the structure of the instrument, its implementation, alignment, calibration and resolutions. We then illustrate its capabilities through a series of experiments on elastomer contacts. Our instrument will be useful to investigate the mechanics of a wide range of soft interfaces submitted to rich, tribology-relevant kinematic or dynamic stimuli.

items.title: Fundamental Relation between Conductance of Biomolecules and the Fukui Function
items.summary: We derive the finite-temperature conductance of a molecule coupled to metallic leads using open-system time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT). Tracing out the phonon bath via Wick's theorem yields an exchange-symmetric collision integral that preserves Pauli exclusion. When internal thermalization is faster than lead escape, as holds in proteins with multifractal orbitals at the Anderson transition, the exchange-correlation kernel projects out of the slow Liouvillian mode, making conductance directly proportional to the finite-temperature Fukui function of conceptual DFT.

items.title: Geometric regulation of stress-limited growth on surfaces
items.summary: We analyze a model for microbial communities growing on surfaces in which individual growth is inhibited by collective growth-induced pressure. Asymptotic and numerical solutions on the sphere and homogenization of periodic surfaces show surface geometry can be tuned to either slow or accelerate growth. We use these insights to identify classes of surfaces for which the growth rate can be made arbitrarily small or arbitrarily close to the stress-free growth rate. These results show stress-sensing is coupled to surface curvature and topography at scales much larger than the individual, and provide design principles for controlling the growth of stress-sensitive microbial communities.

items.title: Neural network scaling and generalization for 3D strain fields in heterogeneous materials
