Via high resolution single cell tracking at sea, we map a highly diverse repertoire of microbial motility, including rapid switching between motile and non-motile states. We identify a chemotactic horizon from measured reorientation towards chemical gradients, defining a spatial region around an aggregate within which chemotactic alignment overcomes flow-induced rotation due to sedimentation. This interplay produces a non-monotonic dependence of encounter rates on aggregate sinking speed, with a peak at 14.4 m/day followed by a sharp decline beyond 78.1 m/day, with a tracer-like regime at high effective sinking speeds. We incorporate the measured encounter rates into a kinetic transport equation in position-velocity phase space, with an effective nonlinear damping arising from velocity-dependent remineralization. The resulting particle dynamics reveal a threshold-induced separatrix dividing overdamped and ballistic microbial populations, leading to velocity segregation. Our study connects direct measurements of microbial motility and sedimentation-induced flow to the emergent phase-space for fate of marine snow in the biological pump, establishing a quantitative multiscale framework for investigating ocean carbon export.

items.title: Equation Recast for Canonical Operator Learning Across Parametric PDEs
items.summary: Learning solution operators across broad parameter ranges can require substantial coverage of both input functions and physical parameters, particularly for purely data-driven parametric models. In addition, the resulting models may fail silently outside the training distribution. We introduce equation recast, which reformulates parametric operator learning as the learning of a single canonical operator. Parameter-induced operator variations are derived analytically from the governing equation and absorbed into effective sources, enabling zero-shot prediction across new parameter regimes. Across multi-parameter, nonlinear, and singular PDE settings, equation recast supports extrapolation, integrates sparse heterogeneous datasets in a shared canonical representation, and uses loss of convergence as an internal warning signal for failure of the recast iteration. In high-fidelity tokamak simulations for nuclear fusion, the framework unifies electron-temperature data across four device geometries through canonical-domain mapping within one jointly trained operator. Equation recast provides a route toward reusable neural PDE solvers combining equation-guided transfer, data efficiency, and monitorable inference.

items.title: Background-free and laser-ionization minimized single-shot fs-EFISH in luminous pulsed plasmas
items.summary: This work introduces spectrally tuned electric field induced second harmonic (t-EFISH) generation for substantially reducing or eliminating background plasma emission in single-shot, time-resolved, electric field measurements. The technique is demonstrated using a femtosecond 1240 nm pump and 620 nm signal detection to avoid spectral and temporal overlap with the early, intense onset of N2(C-B) emission in nanosecond atmospheric-pressure air spark discharges. This enhances signal-to-emission ratios pre- and post-breakdown, enables lower pump energies, suppresses detector saturation, and reduces the coefficient of variation in the electric field measurements by 8.5x. This strategy also provides a pathway for background-free measurements in other discharge environments with varying spectro-temporal emission characteristics. Moreover, the longer 1240 nm pump wavelength reduces multiphoton intrusiveness, directly improving measurement fidelity.

items.title: Energy Dissipation Modulates Sensitivity to Corner Advantage in Weighted Dice
items.summary: Weighted dice have pedagogical value and a range of broader implications. The physics of such dice provides an entry point for understanding state probabilities, center-of-mass calculations, and inertia tensors. Related considerations arise in the physics of grains, seed dispersal, erosion, and materials science, all of which involve components that can be compared with the stochastic tumbling and settling of dice. Previous empirical results are consistent with a Boltzmann-like distribution. We reproduce this result at scale using 23 classes of corner-loaded dice and more than 500,000 physical dice rolls collected with an automated rolling and imaging system. Briefly, landing probability increases exponentially with corner advantage (lower center-of-mass). We test the additional hypothesis that landing statistics depend on the combined effects of corner advantage, inertia tensor, and energy dissipation. Corner advantage defines the direction of the gravitational preference, but the rate of energy dissipation determines how strongly that preference is expressed in the final landing distribution. Simulations suggest that the inertia tensor and its orientation affect roll statistics; indeed, we find a small but statistically detectable departure from uniform landing probabilities under our experimental conditions. Our approach has pedagogical value as an entry-level engineering and data science project. The dice are 3D-printed and automatically rolled at scale using affordable parts and open-source tools. Results are compared to rigid-body simulations and a six-state model of energy dissipation.

items.title: Everything in its right place: attention is a radio head
items.summary: Attention, the core of language models, is a digital calculation over tokens: an exponential selects them, a division normalizes and a positional code sets the order. We show that attention can instead emerge from the synchronization of a receiver with its context tokens. Each past token is an oscillator whose state carries its content and whose frequency drifts with its age. The present token selects them by content, aligning an antenna with its query, and by position, setting the frequency of a receiver with its dial. Solving Kuramoto's problem for this receiver yields an attention layer in closed form with two phases: above a critical coupling set by the context, the receiver locks and its weights normalize; below it, it stays silent and its weights sum to less than one. Trained networks use both phases to select, abstain and count, fail where the theory predicts and keep reading far beyond the training length. Each part of attention finds its place in one device, a radio head: it tunes in to what to hear and when, and stays silent when nothing relevant is on air.

items.title: Autonomous Optimization of Numerical Algorithms by an AI Agent: Application to Atomistic Simulation
items.summary: Coding agents built on large language models, run in automated improvement loops, can discover more efficient algorithms. We present AIOA, a framework that brings this approach to the numerical algorithms of atomistic simulation: an agent improves an algorithm against a pre-specified metric in a loop guarded by verifiers it cannot alter. Applied to ASE, a widely used atomistic simulation library, AIOA targets two facets of an algorithm: its implementation, rewritten to run faster with unchanged results, and the method itself, redesigned to converge with fewer force evaluations. Agents made six kernels 22-24 times faster on average in Python with NumPy and SciPy. On unseen problems, optimizers from the best configuration needed 3.1-3.4 times fewer force evaluations than L-BFGS for structure relaxation and 4.6-17 times fewer than standard climbing-image nudged elastic band calculations for reaction paths. The agents' optimizers also contain two algorithmic components we did not find in the literature.

items.title: Disentangling Forced and Internal Climate Variability in Single Realizations using Dynamic Mode Decomposition with Control
items.summary: Separating externally forced trends from internal climate variability is a fundamental challenge in climate science, particularly when analyzing observational records that exist only as a single realization. We show that a single climate realization can be decomposed into forced and internal components by treating external forcing as a dynamical driver within a linear stochastic system, an idea grounded in pullback attractor theory. This addresses a central challenge for climate projection and for detecting and attributing the forced response. Existing single-realization methods rely on linear inverse models (LIMs), which ignore forcing, or linear regression, which omits dynamics. Here we introduce PullbackDMDc, a method grounded in non-autonomous dynamical systems theory and dynamic mode decomposition with control (DMDc), incorporating pullback attractor estimation to decompose a single climate realization into spatial modes and their associated forced and internal components, yielding a physically interpretable picture of the underlying dynamics. After testing on a synthetic system with a known forced response, we illustrate the utility of PullbackDMDc for Earth System Model (ESM) evaluation by applying it to near-surface air temperature and sea-level pressure from reanalysis and four ESM large ensembles. PullbackDMDc estimates the forced response with skill matching or exceeding established baselines and helps select forcing predictors against model-based ground truth. Its internal-variability components reveal that ESMs qualitatively capture interannual and decadal modes while exhibiting systematic differences relative to each other and to observations. Skillful forced-response estimation and a novel decomposition position PullbackDMDc as a practical tool for single-realization climate analysis and ESM evaluation.

items.title: Electric Propulsion Database Development and Integrated Modelling Analysis
items.summary: Electric propulsion (EP) systems require significant subsystem integration and data driven mod- elling for accurate sizing. This paper is an overview of a high-fidelity database development and analysis aiming to fill the gap in electric propulsion sizing. This is a preliminary study to develop a tool that considers all thruster technologies that exist within Electric Propulsion. Since thrust is set by the product of efficiency and available electrical power, this paper showcases that thruster selection directly constrains the spacecraft power bus. We showcase and hypothesize within the database analysis and in the future work that the correct way to choose electric propulsion systems is through budgeting the EP system through Mission constraints. Comparing technologies for propulsion parameters is important for spacecraft optimisation and no such dataset exists. The literature offers either deep surveys of one thruster type, which cannot be compared across technologies, or broad catalogues that quote manufacturer figures at a single operating condition without checking whether those figures agree with one another. This paper reports the development, performance levels and preliminary analysis of a unified Electric Propulsion technology database. Every device is reduced to a common set of parameters including power, thrust, specific impulse, exhaust velocity and total efficiency linked by governing analytical equations and state space models. The database holds 390 distinct models from 22 countries across twelve thruster types, from 0.4 W to 1 MW, with first flights from 1964 to 2025.

items.title: A regularization-independent Information Criterion for correlated data
items.summary: We generalize the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) to allow model and data subset selection when regularized fits are performed on correlated data. While the standard generalization to regularized fits is inherently dependent on the type of regularization applied to the data covariance matrix, our definition, the RIAIC, is, on average, regularization-independent. The regularization-independence is achieved by defining the new Information Criterion as an estimator of the model-dependent contribution to the correlated Kullback--Leibler divergence. The Bayesian extension is derived as well. We test the new criterion on lattice QCD data by performing regularized fits and show that it reproduces the selection properties of the standard correlated AIC, with fluctuations which are compatible with the expected statistical uncertainties. These results enable the application of subset and model selection techniques to cases where regularizations are applied to the covariance matrix of the fitted dataset.

items.title: Quantitative global regularity for Navier--Stokes equations with odd viscosity on the cubic three-torus
items.summary: We study the three-dimensional incompressible Navier--Stokes equation on the cubic torus with a constant odd-viscosity operator given by the vertical derivative of the curl. Arbitrary real, mean-zero, divergence-free initial data and an independent steady force, both in the second-order Sobolev space, admit a unique global strong solution when the magnitude of one fixed odd-viscosity coefficient is at least a norm-uniform sufficient threshold. In the unforced case the solution is smooth at positive times. The qualitative argument adapts the resonant-averaging framework for rapidly rotating fluids to the different odd-viscous dispersion. Weighted lattice counts and signed corrected-energy estimates yield a sufficient bound for the odd-to-ordinary viscosity ratio that is polynomial in the normalized initial-data radius at each fixed normalized force radius, together with a separate bound in a specified force-dominated regime. No optimality is claimed for the polynomial exponents or prefactors; determining the sharp viscosity threshold for the original equation remains open. Direct kinetic and weighted enstrophy barriers also give regularity for every coefficient on explicit bounded data and force regions, including the closed unforced ball of homogeneous second-order Fourier Sobolev radius ninety-seven fortieths times the viscosity and seven closed forced rectangles. We specify how finite certificates enter the analytic argument and distinguish minimization of a sufficient formula from sharpness for the original equation. All three main theorems are formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib.

items.title: QRecoupling.jl: numerical and exact computation of classical and quantum recoupling coefficients
items.summary: The Julia package QRecoupling evaluates classical and quantum recoupling coefficients, such as Clebsch-Gordan coefficients and $3j$ and $6j$ symbols, and user-defined sums of factorial products, with numerical, exact and symbolic targets. One compact factorial rule covers classical and deformed evaluations, while its cyclotomic exponents reveal common factors and determine which terms contribute at unitary levels. Adaptive arithmetic resolves strongly cancelling sums, while exact tests in quantum integers distinguish algebraic zeros from small nonzero values without a computer-algebra system. At spin cutoff 500, classical $3j$ and $6j$ symbols are evaluated about 7 and 15 times faster than with WIGXJPF. For the tested quantum deformations, relative errors remain below $4\times10^{-14}$ through spin cutoff 400. Recurrences compute fusion matrices with 401 channels about 100 times faster than loops over their entries. The resulting coefficients support recoupling identities, changes of coupling basis and tensor-network calculations.

items.title: Real-time dynamics with bead-Fourier path integrals. II. Bead-Fourier RPMD
items.summary: Feynman path integrals (PIs) have found many uses in approximate quantum dynamics methods for efficiently calculating real-time quantum correlation functions. The PIs typically take the form of discrete imaginary-time slices along a closed path, where the slices form the ``beads'' of a ring polymer (RP) necklace. Some methods, such as centroid molecular dynamics (CMD), use the RP to generate an effective potential for the dynamics, while others, like RP molecular dynamics (RPMD), directly utilize the RP in real-time dynamics in order to incorporate approximate quantum effects. The standard, discretized bead forms of CMD and RPMD may require a large number of RP beads to obtain accurate results for systems with strong quantum effects and at low temperatures. In Paper I (J. Chem. Phys. 2025, 163, 144123), we introduced the bead-Fourier (BF)-CMD method, where we utilized the inclusion of a Fourier sine series to reduce the number of beads needed to converge the CMD effective potential up to eightfold. In this work, we extend RPMD to incorporate BF-PIs in the form of BF-RPMD. We study several implementations of the BF-RPMD method through the calculation of correlation functions for both linear and nonlinear operators. We found that the effectiveness of this method is sensitive to both the type of system and the form of the operators being studied. Our results show that this method is able to produce results on par with standard RPMD, with at worst a twofold and up to an eightfold reduction in the number of beads by including two to three Fourier components.

items.title: High Purity OAM Entangled Photons from SPDC with Reduced Spatial Spectral Correlations
items.summary: Entanglement generated by Spontaneous Parametric Down Conversion (SPDC) involves multiple, often mutually correlated degrees of freedom. These degrees of freedom are often treated independently, overlooking the intrinsic correlation between them. We focus on the spatial-spectral correlations that, if left uncontrolled, introduce distinguishability and reduce coherence, undermining applications such as high-dimensional OAM encoding. We analyze the spatio-spectral structure of the biphoton and identify conditions enabling a strong reduction of such correlations. We then quantify how spatial-spectral coupling degrades OAM spatial purity, mapping high-purity regions as functions of OAM order, crystal length, and pump/collection waists. The resulting design parameter regime enables engineering bright, high-purity OAM-entangled sources, reducing the need for additional loss-introducing filtering and therefore supporting scalable high-dimensional photonic quantum technologies.

items.title: Numerical-Relativity Particle-in-Cell Simulations: Self-Gravitating Collisionless Matter in Dynamical Spacetimes
items.summary: Gravitational collapse and instability, black-hole dynamics in systems with large scale separations, and questions surrounding extremal black hole formation require full nonlinear studies using accurate and adapted numerical tools. To this end, we present a new algorithm to study collisionless relativistic systems using a fully kinetic description of matter coupled to the evolving spacetime. In detail, we present a numerical-relativity particle-in-cell (NRPIC) framework for solving the Einstein--Vlasov system in three spatial dimensions. Implemented on top of the performance-portable \texttt{AthenaK} code, the method couples particle dynamics to Z4c spacetime evolution in moving puncture gauge through conservative stress-energy deposition on adaptively refined meshes. Our implementation makes use of advances in the computational modeling of relativistic plasmas using modern PIC models, now made available to general-relativistic gravity via an equivalent electrodynamic formulation. We introduce a Boris-type particle pusher that exploits the electrodynamic (Lorentz force) form of the geodesic force. We validate the coupled evolution against spherical dust collapse, follow prolate collapse through collisionless caustics into black-hole formation, and investigate the stability and nonlinear migration of relativistic clusters. Highlighting its potential to study gravitational instability in NR, we simulate the collapse of two overdensities within a common collisionless envelope, following black-hole formation, binary inspiral and merger, and subsequent mass accretion onto the remnant.

items.title: Validating direct solvers for Newton's gravitational N-body problem, and the systematic comparison between IEEE floating point and Posits
items.summary: We present a systematic comparison between arbitrary precise arithmetic and integration, IEEE-754 compliant floating point arithmetic (fp16, bfp16, fp32, double precision fp64, and quadruple precision fp128), and two implementations of Posits (type III unum) for solving Newton's chaotic N-body problem. Each implementation is benchmarked with arbitrary precise calculations to objectively evaluate their performance in precision as well as speed. We rely on hardware and compiler implementations for fp64, and software implementations for arbitrary-precision arithmetic and Posits. Half precision arithmetic (fp16, bfp16, and Posits$<16,1>$) are insufficiently precise for solving Newton's equations of motion. Single precision (fp32, and Posits$<32,2>$) could be used for statistical ensemble calculations, but lead to relatively large errors in any individual strong encounter. All 64-bit implementations fp64 as well as Posits (Posits$<64,3>$) experience difficulty in our tests. One of the implementations of Posits (Universal) gives precision comparable to fp64 but is slow (by at least an orders of magnitude compared to fp64 after correcting for the more efficient hardware support for the latter). The other (CPPPosits) has a speed comparable to fp64 but has systematically larger errors (by about an order of magnitude compared to fp64 with excesses exceeding two orders of magnitude). As a consequence, this implementation leads to a systematic drift in the result space and has difficulty resolving close encounters. Posits and fp64 have difficulty when integrating a dynamical system in a moving reference frame; testing Galileo invariancy. In their current implementation, Posits do not seem to be the ideal alternative for fp64 when integrating chaotic or stiff ordinary differential equations, such as Newton's equations of motion.

items.title: Experimental Evidence of Cellular Sparing under Single-Pulse Picosecond Irradiation at Extreme Dose Rates
items.summary: Understanding how biological cells respond to radiation delivered on extremely short timescales is central to resolving the fundamental mechanisms underlying radiotherapy and to defining new regimes of radiobiology. Experimentally accessing these earliest stages of physicochemical response is crucial to benchmark current numerical codes, whose predictions are known to vary substantially with under-constrained early-stage parameters. Using a laser-driven electron source, tunable doses up to 8Gy were delivered to normal and cancer human cell lines, in single pulses of picosecond-scale duration at mean dose rates above 10^10 Gy/s. Clonogenic survival assays and 53BP1 foci formation were compared with conventional X-ray irradiation at 2.4Gy/min. Surviving fractions are found to be comparable to conventional irradiation at doses up to 3Gy. At higher doses, however, all cell lines exhibited a consistent increase in surviving fraction, corresponding to an average RBE at 10% survival of 0.84+/-0.05. This sparing effect is associated with a statistically significant reduction in the beta parameter of the linear-quadratic model, indicating reduced cell killing from accumulated sub-lethal damage. Picosecond irradiation also produced a marked reduction in prompt 53BP1 foci, but no significant difference in residual foci at 24h and foci-size distributions. These results provide the first experimental evidence of cellular sparing following single-pulse picosecond-scale irradiation. Direct comparison with recent work at femtosecond timescales suggests the presence of a previously undetected sharp transition in biological response at the femtosecond/picosecond interface, giving critical insight on the possible mechanisms responsible for this differential response.

items.title: First demonstration of long-distance electron drift in liquid xenon with the Xenoscope time projection chamber
items.summary: Xenoscope is a dual-phase xenon time projection chamber operated at the University of Zurich to investigate electron transport over distances relevant to the next-generation XLZD (XENON-LUX-ZEPLIN-DARWIN) observatory. We demonstrate electron drift over $2.6$ m in liquid xenon using cosmic-muon-induced ionization signals. External muon tagging provides a timing reference for charge produced at known depths, while the endpoint of the average electroluminescence waveform probes transport over the full drift length. We measure electron drift velocities of $(1.320 \pm 0.006)$ mm/$μ$s at $(80.92 \pm 0.36)$ V/cm and $(1.436 \pm 0.001)$ mm/$μ$s at $(96.00 \pm 0.42)$ V/cm. These results establish detectable charge transport over meter-scale distances and provide an experimental benchmark for the development of future large liquid-xenon time projection chambers.

items.title: OCEAN: A Five-Phase Framework for Meaningful Change
items.summary: Managing meaningful change requires more than motivation, insight, or isolated techniques. This paper introduces OCEAN, a five-phase conceptual framework for structuring nonclinical developmental conversations and change-oriented work in coaching and in the practice of leaders and HR professionals. The five phases are Observe, Create, Expose, Awaken, and Nurture. In Observe, individuals develop a systemic, present-oriented understanding of the situation. In Create, they turn that understanding into goals that are meaningful and actionable. In Expose, they identify the attempted solutions that maintain the difficulty they are meant to remove, along with the resistances, biases, and self-deceptions that keep them in place. In Awaken, they activate new behaviors through planning, reframing, paradoxical movement, and emotionally significant experiences. In Nurture, they consolidate progress through repetition, habits, connection, and sustainable contexts. OCEAN integrates insights from systemic and interactional thinking, goal construction, emotional awareness, and habit consolidation into a structured process.

items.title: Dual-polarized, mid-infrared nonreciprocal absorption
items.summary: The emission and absorption of thermal radiation are usually coupled via reciprocity and Kirchhoff's law, stated as the equality of spectral directional emissivity and absorptivity. Magneto-optical materials have recently been identified as a promising route to lifting the constraint of reciprocity for thermal emission and absorption, with multiple experimental demonstrations using doped InAs, which is described by an antisymmetric, nonreciprocal dielectric tensor under an applied magnetic field. However, these demonstrations have been limited to p-polarized light in the Voigt configuration, whereas thermal radiation from a blackbody is unpolarized and thus comprised of both s- and p-polarized light. This means existing nonreciprocal emitter and absorber designs underutilize available power by 50%. Here, we report a photonic crystal slab-based structure that exhibits nonreciprocal absorption for both s- and p-polarizations in the mid-infrared spectral range. The structure operates from 11-20 $μ$m and consists of an a-Si photonic crystal slab on top of a doped InAs substrate. The photonic crystal slab supports eigenmodes that couple to both s- and p-polarized plane waves, resulting in absorption peaks that, because of the applied magnetic field, spectrally shift in opposite directions for forward- and backward-propagating light$\unicode{8212}$a signature of nonreciprocity in planar, subwavelength systems. We fabricate the designed structure, then experimentally demonstrate dual-polarized nonreciprocal absorption by measuring its room-temperature absorptance using magnetic-field-integrated absorptance spectroscopy. Our design is a step toward the complete control of light as heat, which could improve photonic energy conversion, thermal management, and mid-infrared optical isolation and circulation.

items.title: Scaling signatures of near-critical dynamics in large-scale human resting-state electrophysiology
items.summary: From 1/f noise to neuronal avalanches, evidence of scaling in brain activity has been increasingly linked to tuning to or near criticality. The concept of scaling is intimately related to the renormalization group (RG), in essence providing coarse-grained, simplified descriptions that generalize to classes of diverse physical systems. Following the RG idea, scaling laws have been reported in populations of spiking neurons at microscopic scales. Whether similar scaling principles govern large-scale neural activity in the human brain and how they relate to underlying neural physiology remains unresolved. Here, we analyze large-scale electrophysiological recordings (MEG) of human resting-state brain activity and apply a RG-inspired coarse-graining approach to track collective neural dynamics across spatial scales. We find that multiple observables exhibit robust scale-invariant behavior under coarse-graining: activity variance and correlations grow according to power laws, covariance eigenspectra follow a characteristic scaling relation, and neuronal avalanche statistics and scaling relationships are conserved. Using an analytically tractable neural network model with parameters inferred from data, we show that the observed scaling signatures arise close to, but slightly below, criticality, and that the scaling exponents can be modulated by network inhibitory drives. These findings demonstrate that RG-inspired scaling analysis can uncover signatures of critical dynamics in non-invasive human electrophysiology and suggest a principled route toward estimating excitation-inhibition balance from large-scale brain recordings.

items.title: Generalization of Rayleigh's high-frequency theory for the 2D Helmholtz equation in a half-space subject to a radiation condition at infinity and a Dirichlet condition on a 1D periodically-uneven boundary
items.summary: The 2D Helmholtz equation, radiation condition and Dirichlet boundary condition, are the translation, in mathematical terms, of (at least) three physical 2D problems for the prediction of the total scalar wavefield on one side of an impenetrable 1D periodically uneven boundary when: a) a plane TE electromagnetic wave propagating in the vacuum strikes the boundary the other side of which is occupied by a perfectly-conducting medium, b) a plane SH elastic elastic wave strikes a rigid boundary, c) a plane acoustic wave strikes a pressure-release boundary. The first attempt to solve such problems in a non-heuristic manner was made by Lord Rayleigh (in his book, 'The Theory of Sound' which appeared in 1896). My task will be to revisit Rayleigh's theory of diffraction by a sinusoidal-shaped, impenetrable boundary, and more specifically, his perturbation method for obtaining a mathematically-explicit solution to the diffraction problem in the high-frequency regime. In so doing, I shall correct and generalize Rayleigh's method to obtain solutions for arbitrary angles of incidence as well as for 1D periodic impenetrable boundaries of quite-general shape.

items.title: MarsNet: Learning the Martian Atmosphere from Observations Alone
items.summary: We present MarsNet, a machine-learned model of the Martian atmosphere trained only on observations. Existing reanalyses assimilate spacecraft retrievals into general circulation models (GCMs), so where observations are sparse their fields largely reflect the model. We therefore use extant reanalyses only for evaluation. MarsNet alternates a two-hour forecast with an update that assimilates the observations of each window, and both steps are learned jointly. Because the Martian record is too sparse for an unrestricted network, learning is confined within a fixed physical structure: the state is in physical units, the forecast uses physical tendencies of fixed form and learned strength, and the update is a bounded Kalman update. MarsNet is trained on Mars Years (MY) 24--31 and evaluated on independent observations. On three seasons of MGS radio-occultation temperatures assimilated by no dataset, MarsNet matches or improves on the three reanalyses in the lowest three scale heights, with a near-surface root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 4.2 K against 4.4--5.4 K, but is less accurate aloft. The model's surface pressures are the most accurate of the four products (RMSE 10 Pa against Curiosity in MY32, compared with 20--46 Pa). On withheld Mars Climate Sounder profiles of MY32, its temperatures beat an observed climatology and persistence, including in ten-sol forecasts without new observations, and its stated uncertainty is close to calibrated. Much of the temperature skill is present before training and appears to come from the structure and tables fitted to the observations, while training mainly improves the surface pressures, at some cost to dust. The model cycles stably through nine Mars years, and the influence of each observation can be traced. Its speed makes experiments on the observing record practical, and it offers an independent reference for GCMs and reanalyses.

items.title: Numerical Investigations on Bitumen Liberation from Oil Sands Lump
items.summary: The dynamic liberation and digestion of viscous oil-solid aggregates under turbulent flow is a critical transport phenomenon in multiphase chemical processes, including slurry transport, soil remediation, and industrial extraction. A primary industrial application of this phenomenon is oil sands hydrotransport, where pipelines are widely utilized to simultaneously transport and extract bitumen from lump ore. However, optimizing operating conditions requires a fundamental understanding of the localized hydrodynamic mechanisms governing detachment. To address this, a three-dimensional (3D) Eulerian-Eulerian (E-E) CFD approach coupled with k-omega SST turbulence model has been utilized to investigate bitumen detachment dynamics from complex solid matrices. Six numerical cases were analyzed across lump diameters (D) of 4 and 5 cm and particle Reynolds numbers (Re_p) between 2000 and 4000. The simulation results reveal that bitumen liberation is a shear-driven process, occurring only when the shear stresses exerted by the flow on the lump surface exceed a critical threshold value. The bitumen liberation rate increases with higher Re_p and smaller D, due to enhanced local shear forces and reduced particle shielding. Based on these mechanistic insights, a novel semi-empirical shear-driven model was formulated. The proposed model demonstrates excellent predictive accuracy when validated against experimental liberation data, with an error less than 8.3%. Overall, these findings clarify the fluid-particle interactions governing bitumen detachment and offer a robust, physics-based tool for predicting recovery efficiency in industrial hydrotransport operations.

items.title: Evaluation of the Ambipolar Diffusion Approximation in Partially Ionized Rarefied Hypersonic Flows
items.summary: Accurate numerical simulation of rarefied hypersonic plasmas is increasingly important for optimization of re-entry spacecraft design and the development of advanced aerospace technologies. For kinetic simulation methods, it is convention to enforce ions and electrons to diffuse at the same rate, known as the ambipolar diffusion approximation. This approach circumvents costly resolution of fast electron motion, but neglects the complex plasma dynamics of ions and electrons. Almost all studies that investigated the efficacy of the ambipolar diffusion approximation in hypersonics report noticeable differences in flowfield properties when electrostatic modeling is used, including increases in vehicle surface heat flux and decreases in electron temperature. However, studying the ambipolar diffusion approximation in multi-species hypersonic flows (such as air flows) makes it challenging to isolate the origin of these differences. Kinetic hypersonic flow simulations with electrostatic modeling are performed with argon to quantify the validity of the ambipolar diffusion approximation along a one-dimensional stagnation streamline. Three different plasma diffusion regimes are studied under two sets of rarefied freestream flow conditions. The approximation is evaluated in terms of predicting plasma density distributions, electron temperature, and stagnation point heat flux. New criteria are proposed for identification of plasma diffusion regimes in hypersonic flows and use of the ambipolar diffusion approximation.

items.title: Trapping of nanofabricated SiO$_2$ high-aspect-ratio discs in an optical lattice
items.summary: We describe the nanofabrication and loading of lithographically patterned, high aspect ratio $10$ $μ$m diameter silicon dioxide discs with thickness of $400$ nm into an optical standing wave trap in vacuum. We obtain motional spectra of the center of mass motion of the discs using a combination of interferometric and imaging methods. The method is capable of high-efficiency loading and optical trapping using small numbers of objects, of the order of a few particles, with customized geometries and sizes compatible with wafer scale nanofabrication methods. Disc-like particles in optical traps have been identified as promising candidates for detectors of high frequency gravitational waves or as sensitive accelerometers.

items.title: Metastable phase separation and information retrieval in multicomponent liquids
items.summary: Liquid mixtures can separate into phases with distinct composition. This phenomenon has recently come back to prominence due to its role in complex biological liquids, such as the cytoplasm, which contain thousands of components. For simple two-component mixtures phase-separated states are global free energy minima. However, local free energy minima, i.e., metastable states, are known to play a dominant role in complex systems with many components. For example, Hopfield neural networks can retrieve stored information from partial cues via relaxation to metastable states. Under what conditions can phase separated states be metastable, and what are the implications for information retrieval in multicomponent liquids? In this work we develop the general thermodynamic formalism of metastable phase separation. We then apply this formalism to an illustrative toy example inspired by recent experiments, binary mixtures with high-order interactions. Finally, as core application of the formalism, we study metastability in Hopfield liquids, a class of multicomponent mixtures capable of storing information on the composition of phases. We show that these phases can be nucleated from partial cues via metastable phase separation. Spatial simulations of liquids with a large number of components match our analytical solution. Our work suggests that complex biological mixtures can retrieve information through metastable phase separation.

items.title: Finite temperature and pressure structural relaxations including zero-point motion and anharmonicity
items.summary: At finite temperature and pressure, the equilibrium structure of a crystal minimizes the Gibbs free energy rather than the static Born-Oppenheimer energy. We present WARP (Wyckoff-constrained Anharmonic Relaxations at Pressure and temperature), a symmetry-constrained, variable-cell relaxation based on the stochastic temperature-dependent effective potential method, including anharmonicity and zero-point motion. Every position update is projected onto Wyckoff positions and every strain onto symmetric strains, so a relaxation can raise the symmetry but never lower it. For aluminum, the thermal expansion follows measurements at cryogenic temperatures, including the quantum plateau below 50 K. For lanthanum hydrides at megabar pressures, equations of state agree with phonon-based and path-integral calculations, and LaH$_{10}$ relaxes from its rhombohedral static minimum to the observed cubic phase, also with a machine-learned potential fine-tuned on 150 supercells. For brucite, Mg(OD)$_2$, lattice parameters, bond distances and thermal expansion agree with neutron diffraction, and the O-D isotope effect is captured.

items.title: Catalysis-induced phase separation of enzymes via diffusivity contrast
items.summary: Catalysis can drive phase separation by coupling local chemical composition to molecular transport, even in the absence of attractive interactions. Here, we demonstrate such catalysis-induced phase separation in a microscopic particle-based model of enzymes catalyzing the interconversion of substrate and product molecules with different diffusivities. We derive an analytical instability criterion in the dilute limit, showing that a homogeneous mixture becomes unstable when the nonequilibrium chemical drive and the diffusivity contrast are sufficiently large, and the substrate and product concentration exceeds a threshold set by the enzyme volume. Brownian-dynamics simulations confirm the predicted instability and reveal macroscopic coexistence of enzyme-rich and enzyme-poor phases, including in regimes where equilibrium depletion interactions cannot account for demixing. Finally, we show that, upon eliminating the fast chemical degrees of freedom, the reactive ternary mixture maps onto an effective binary mixture nonreciprocal interactions. Our results establish an explicit microscopic mechanism for catalysis-induced phase separation and connect chemically driven phase separation to the physics of motility-regulated and nonreciprocal matter.

items.title: On the Method of Projection onto Localized States for Describing Reactions and Clustering
items.summary: The method of projection onto localized states intended for describing reactions and clustering is examined. In particular, the method offers a simple extension of the no-core shell model to continuum- and clusterized bound states. A critical analysis of a previous realization of the method is provided. A way to minimize the number of basis functions required for convergence is given. An easy way to obtain exactly unitary and symmetric $S$ matrix from calculations is pointed out. The method is tested in one- and two-channel $np$ scattering problems with the Daejeon $NN$ interaction. It is shown that excellent convergence can be reached even when only oscillator states with low number of excitation quanta are retained.

items.title: The Weight Is in the Reading: Hidden States in Memristors, Memlumors, and Electrochemical Transistors
items.summary: Physical synapses are routinely described by a single number, the weight, that is identified with a conductance, a current, or a luminescence yield. This identification conflates two different objects: the internal state that the device stores, and the signal obtained when that state is read. Building on Chua's formulation of memristive systems, we separate the state variable, which evolves with the excitation history, from the observation map that converts it into a measured signal, and we define the weight as the outcome of a specified read protocol. Three platforms show the consequences: a memristor, in which the same voltage writes and reads; a memlumor, in which light both modifies the state and produces the photoluminescence that reports it; and an organic electrochemical transistor (OECT), in which the gate writes and the channel reads. In the transistor, two states prepared by different histories give the same channel current at a specific drain bias and become distinguishable again when the bias is changed, while the stored charge persists and the gate current continues to separate them. Published experiments provide precedents: a drain-bias-dependent cancellation of the OECT transient, and trapped charges in perovskite memlumors that are invisible to conventional time-resolved photoluminescence but revealed by a read-write-read sequence. A synaptic weight is therefore not a property of the material alone but of the material together with its readout, and reports of synaptic behavior should specify what is stored, what is measured, and how one is inferred from the other.

items.title: Renewal Bias in Parallel Simulations of Absorbing Processes
items.summary: Asynchronous parallel simulations of stochastic processes with absorbing states can exhibit systematic sampling bias when trajectory durations depend on their eventual absorbing outcomes. Workers that continuously restart upon absorption preferentially record rapidly terminating trajectories within a fixed computational budget, distorting the observed ensemble statistics. We investigate this effect using a minimal renewal model with two absorbing states and state-dependent exponential durations. Renewal theory yields exact expressions for the expected number and composition of completed trajectories, showing that the resulting bias decreases algebraically with execution time but persists as the number of parallel workers increases at fixed budget. We compare continuous sampling with First-Trajectory Filtering, which retains only the initial trajectory attempted by each worker. Although finite execution deadlines introduce residual censoring bias, this bias decreases exponentially with the computational budget. An analytical mean-squared error calculation reveals budget-dependent crossover worker allocations beyond which First-Trajectory Filtering becomes more accurate despite collecting fewer trajectories. We also examine the limitations of statistical inference under severe censoring when the absorbing-state probabilities and characteristic durations are unknown. Finally, simulations of the Axelrod model near its nonequilibrium transition demonstrate the preferential sampling of rapidly absorbing fragmented configurations, illustrating the relevance of the renewal mechanism in a spatially interacting system. Our results show that increasing computational throughput does not necessarily improve statistical accuracy and highlight the importance of accounting for trajectory-duration heterogeneity in parallel simulations of absorbing processes.

items.title: CoilStellaration: A Dataset and Benchmark for Engineering-Aware Stellarator Coilset Generation
items.summary: Stellarators are fusion devices that use externally generated, three-dimensional magnetic fields to confine hot plasma and offer a promising route to commercial fusion. Their electromagnetic coils pose a challenging design problem: they must reproduce the target magnetic field while satisfying engineering constraints and remaining practical and cost-effective to manufacture. Finding suitable geometries is a highly nonlinear inverse problem that generally has neither a closed-form nor a unique solution. This problem lies at the heart of stellarator design. We introduce CoilStellaration, a dataset and benchmark for learning the mapping between coil geometries from target plasma magnetic fields and engineering requirements. The dataset contains 177,000 optimized filamentary coilsets targeting plasma equilibria from ConStellaration, with sampled engineering requirements and achieved geometric and magnetic-field metrics. It spans multiple coil counts and field-period numbers, supporting studies of both specialized and shared models across configurations. The benchmark asks models to predict coils conditioned on a target equilibrium and requirements on coil-coil and coil-plasma spacing, curvature, and magnetic-field error. We show that magnetic-field accuracy remains the main challenge, with learned models rarely satisfying all requirements simultaneously. However, using learned predictions to initialize conventional coil optimization can accelerate early progress. We release baseline models and evaluation code to support reproducible research on both direct coil generation and learned optimization initializations. By lowering the barrier for machine learning and optimization researchers to engage with stellarator coil design, we aim to accelerate progress toward practical, cost-effective stellarator power plants.

items.title: Differentiable Inverse Rendering Recovers Intrinsic Properties from Intravascular Optical Coherence Tomography
items.summary: Medical images encode intrinsic tissue properties that indicate disease progression, yet these properties remain entangled with the system-dependent physics of image formation. Differentiable inverse rendering asks whether they are recoverable by inverting the imaging system's forward physics rather than through post-hoc correction. We address this in optical coherence tomography (OCT), focusing on the optical attenuation coefficient, a per-pixel marker of pathology and cellular composition. Conventional recovery relies on closed-form inversions limited to simplified light-tissue models, or learned methods coupled to specific imaging configurations. We instead recover per-pixel attenuation from a single OCT image by gradient descent through a differentiable physics-based forward model. We verified the method against analytical solutions, validated it on five in vitro phantoms, and applied it without modification to 29{,}269 clinical intravascular OCT images from 128 patients. The inversion needs no training data or segmentations and is portable across platforms and retrospective archives. Replacing the forward model or recovering another optical parameter leaves the optimization procedure unchanged. We demonstrate per-pixel recovery is tractable because gradient information scales to this high-dimensional problem, where gradient-free methods become intractable. Our work supports quantitative tissue characterization from OCT images and provides a framework for extension across imaging modalities and organ systems.

items.title: Damped polarizability and first hyperpolarizability of large systems with hybrid functionals: self-consistent and Lanczos solvers
items.summary: We present a damped coupled-perturbed Kohn-Sham method to compute the dynamical polarizability and first hyperpolarizability of finite systems, implemented in the CRYSTAL code for semi-local, global and range-separated hybrid functionals. The approach is based on the adiabatic time-dependent density functional theory for the complex-valued (hyper)polarizabilities, describing optical phenomena such as absorption, and the nonlinear second-harmonic generation, rectification and Pockels effect. These are obtained either at individual frequencies with a self-consistent solver based on Pulay extrapolation, or at an arbitrary grid of frequency and damping factors with a Lanczos solver, from which the first-order amplitudes required in the hyperpolarizability can be reconstructed. With hybrid functionals, the self-consistent solver tends to become impractical at some point beyond the absorption onset, where there are many excitations for which the external frequency lies between their energy and those of their contributing single-particle transitions, and its convergence eventually stalls for large systems. In contrast, the convergence of the Lanczos method is essentially independent of size, hence the cost of the dynamical response calculation scales with system size as the hybrid ground-state calculation. The implementation is validated in a small molecule and, as an application, we study the first and second-order optical response of a series of hexagonal boron nitride flakes of up to 324 atoms. The use of range-separated hybrid functionals allows to capture the strongly-bound first excitation of the monolayer, and evidences the failure of the self-consistent method to converge excitations with strong electron-hole attraction.

items.title: A stochastic agent-based extension of the GSM$^2$ model for particle therapy: cell-cycle dynamics, dose-rate dependence, and fractionation effects
items.summary: We present a stochastic agent-based extension of the Generalized Stochastic Microdosimetric Model (GSM$^2$) that links microscopic energy deposition by ionizing radiation to population-scale response. Each cell is represented as an agent whose DNA damage, cell-cycle phase, and fate evolve as a continuous-time Markov process. Particle arrivals, repair, misrepair, division, death, and migration are treated as competing stochastic events in an event-driven algorithm, enabling track-structure simulations of spheroids with up to $1.5\times10^5$ cells in minutes on a single workstation. For static populations, the model reproduces the Lea--Catcheside dose-rate dependence of survival for proton and carbon-ion irradiation over four orders of magnitude in dose rate. Dose-rate sparing decreases with increasing LET and disappears for low-energy carbon ions. After calibration to a single survival curve for aerobic X-ray irradiation of V79 spheroids, the model predicts without further fitting survival under anoxia and after carbon-ion irradiation in aerobic and anoxic conditions, reproducing measured oxygen enhancement ratios and relative biological effectiveness. Applied to three-dimensional tumor spheroids, the framework resolves responses to single, split, and fractionated irradiations, separates the effects of repair, reassortment, and repopulation, and quantifies stochastic variability between realizations. The model provides a mechanistic single-cell framework for studying time-dependent effects and uncertainty in particle irradiation.

items.title: A Hierarchy of Fast and Strong Signatures for Vertex Orbits
items.summary: The defining features of a physical system are its symmetries and its invariants. For a network, the symmetries are the automorphisms, and the invariants are the vertex orbits they define. Two vertices of a graph may appear structurally indistinguishable without being interchangeable under any graph automorphism. Distinguishing apparent similarity from genuine symmetry lies at the heart of the vertex-orbit partition problem. In this work, we develop a hierarchy of increasingly expressive, automorphism-invariant signatures that draw on the spectral properties of the graph Laplacian and the Dirac operator to reveal subtle structural differences. Guided by a sequence of counterexamples, we progressively strengthen these signatures, ultimately incorporating probing techniques, which are temporary structural perturbations, that expose the hidden distinctions in the original unperturbed graph. We evaluate our approach across diverse benchmark families, recovering exact orbit partitions in challenging instances, including graphs that resist low-dimensional Weisfeiler--Leman refinement. We also examine the computational and numerical limitations of our constructions, distinguishing empirical success from theoretical completeness. Our findings highlight the potential of spectral and probing-based methods for uncovering the structural distinctions that define vertex orbit.

items.title: Tuning Plasma Frequency of Nested Wire Media
items.summary: We study nested wire media possessing $C_6$ and $C_4$ rotational symmetries whose plasma frequencies can be controlled through breathing deformation. Numerical simulations reveal tunability exceeding $80\%$ and $60\%$ for the considered $C_6$ and $C_4$ breathing geometries, respectively. To describe these structures, we develop an analytical model based on the local field approach within the thin-wire approximation, which confirms the high tunability of the studied wire structures. We also propose an approximation for dense wire media. The developed framework is applicable to the general case of nested wire structures -- wire media with an arbitrary parallelogram lattice and multiple wires per unit cell.

items.title: Neutronic Field-Effect Transistor
items.summary: Field-effect electronic devices are in widespread use in communication, computing, data storage, and sensing applications. We demonstrate a neutronic field-effect transistor (NFET) that is analogous to the Datta-Das electron spin transistor and atomtronic devices. The NFET is based on a perfect-crystal Mach-Zehnder neutron interferometer with phase shifts applied to the spin and path degrees of freedom.

items.title: A Dual-Frequency-Constrained Structure-Function Kirchhoff Model for Near-Nadir Ocean Backscatter -- Part II: The Practical GMF, KuKa-Mod
items.summary: Near-nadir radars, from altimeters and rain radars to wave scatterometers, need a geophysical model function (GMF) relating backscatter to wind, yet most operational models are empirical and specific to one band. This paper delivers KuKa-Mod, an operational near-nadir GMF for wind retrieval at Ku and Ka band, built on one physical description of the sea surface, and evaluates it. Following the companion paper (Part I), the additive coefficient and log-slope of a logarithmic surface structure function are fitted jointly to the Ku-band incidence profile of the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) radar and to the same-footprint Ku-Ka shape difference. The model reproduces the Ku profile and reaches the azimuth-averaged Ka profile with no additional shape parameter and one fitted level, largely explained by the seawater dielectric and the clear-sky attenuation. Against scatterometer winds the Ka-Ku difference holds to within 0.3 dB up to 25 m/s, whereas the near-nadir Ka wind sensitivity is about 20% too weak. An empirical correction measured against the same winds sets the operational high-wind level of both bands, validated to 20 m/s. Without a sea-state coefficient, a long-wave tilt predicts where the response to significant wave height changes sign at Ku band, a tilt that CFOSAT/SWIM confirms, and the azimuth harmonics are reproduced once a sensor-dependent offset is removed. The operational model is released as parameters, an evaluator and look-up tables ready for retrieval processors.

items.title: Contrast-Enhanced Nonlinear Imaging with Moiré Flatband Superlattices
items.summary: Nonlinear metasurfaces offer a compact platform for infrared-to-visible conversion and imaging, yet resonant enhancement is often accompanied by restricted angular acceptance, limiting the range of transverse spatial frequencies that can interact efficiently with the nonlinear modes. Here, we address this challenge using a one-dimensional photonic moiré superlattice supporting multiple quasi-flat bands in the near-infrared. These moiré modes combine strong near-field enhancement with broad momentum-space accessibility, enabling efficient third-harmonic generation (THG) while maintaining stable excitation over a large angular range. Experimentally, we observe strong THG emission near $467~\mathrm{nm}$ under broadband excitation from $ 1180$ to $ 2000~\mathrm {nm} $. We further employ the nonlinear moiré superlattice for infrared imaging by converting an infrared target into visible through the THG process. By encoding image information into displacement-dependent THG signals and decoding their spatial variations, we experimentally resolve weak features and internal textures with improved contrast compared with THG imaging using nonlinear films or conventional nonlinear metasurfaces. These results establish photonic moiré superlattices as a versatile platform combining efficient frequency conversion, broad angular acceptance, and mode-sensitive spatial encoding for high-contrast, label-free nonlinear imaging with enhanced feature discrimination.

items.title: Frequency-selective membrane-based metamaterial filters for low-insertion-loss harmonic crosstalk suppression in sub-harmonic THz receivers
items.summary: Parasitic reflections and standing waves fundamentally limit amplitude stability and phase fidelity in coherent continuous-wave (CW) terahertz (THz) systems. We report a complementary metamaterial filter pair designed for frequency-selective isolation at 300 GHz and 600 GHz in sub-harmonic heterodyne architectures. Fabricated on ultra-thin polyimide membranes, the filters provide more than 30 dB stopband isolation while maintaining insertion losses below 1 dB in the passband. System-level coherent-imaging experiments demonstrate effective suppression of spurious-reflection-induced interference effects and improved spectral baseline stability. The filters mitigate wavefront distortions resulting from such interferences and enhance reconstruction robustness. These results establish membrane-based metamaterial filters as compact frequency-selective isolation elements for sub-harmonic heterodyne THz detection and highlight their potential for phase-engineered imaging and sensing applications.

items.title: Non-Equilibrium Ising-Bloch Transition in Polarization Cavity Solitons
items.summary: Polarization cavity solitons in coherently driven Kerr resonators undergo a sequence of dynamical bifurcations as the cavity detuning is increased. Here we show that a stationary localized state containing an Ising wall first becomes a fixed breather and then develops finite chirality and drift motion through a spontaneous non-equilibrium Ising-Bloch transition. Stability analyses identify the modes responsible for the breathing and the motion, revealing controllable dynamics of polarization cavity solitons.

items.title: Analytic $GW$-Bethe--Salpeter Gradients with Quasiparticle Response in the Resolution of the Identity
items.summary: Analytic nuclear gradients for excited states from the Bethe$-$Salpeter equation (BSE) in the static screening approximation are presented within this work. The response of the screened interaction to nuclear displacements is treated within the resolution-of-the-identity (RI) approximation, in close analogy to RI random phase approximation gradients, and is folded into the Lagrangian formalism of time-dependent density functional theory gradients. Quasiparticle gradients enter via the full analytic derivative of the corrections for RI contour-deformation $G_0W_0$ and ev$GW$, also taking into account that incomplete quasiparticle spectra are typically supplied. Comparisons to earlier approaches using a geometry-independent fixed quasiparticle correction are made. For the latter, the orbital-rotation terms are derived exactly, too. The implemented gradient scales as $\mathcal{O}(N^4)$, and the three-index integrals are processed in batches with a memory demand of $\mathcal{O}(N_\mathrm{aux}^2 + N_\mathrm{occ}^2 N_\mathrm{aux})$. Excited-state geometries of a set of small molecules are compared to EOM-CCSD references and to TD-DFT. It is shown that the full quasiparticle gradient removes most of the systematic underestimation of the bond lengths in singlet excited states. A comparison along the C$-$C stretch of acetylene shows that the neglected derivative of the quasiparticle corrections is modest, but becomes erratic for $G_0W_0$ near poles of the self-energy, which ev$GW$ avoids.

items.title: A Dual-Frequency-Constrained Structure-Function Kirchhoff Model for Near-Nadir Ocean Backscatter -- Part I: Theoretical Framework
items.summary: Most operational near-nadir geophysical model functions (GMFs) are empirical and fitted one radar band at a time, and do not explain the difference between Ku and Ka band. This paper derives a backscatter model in which one local description of the sea surface serves both bands. The near-nadir Kirchhoff integral is written in terms of the elevation difference between two surface points separated by a horizontal lag. The surface then enters through the structure functions of that difference, and the scattering kernel selects the lags each band samples, about 2.5-1.4 cm at Ku and 1.0-0.5 cm at Ka band. Geometric optics is recovered as the quadratic, isotropic limit, without a spectral cutoff. With a logarithmic second-order structure function, one wind-dependent log-slope sets both the incidence shape and the Ku-Ka shape difference, and band transfer reduces to evaluating one curve at a second lag. Same-footprint dual-frequency radar data show that one band alone does not determine this transfer. The log-slope is the level of the short-wave saturation range and grows about as the square of the wind speed; a physical short-wave spectrum reproduces this growth but overestimates the level. Dual-frequency radars thus measure the centimetre-scale roughness level, although they do not separate a scale-dependent structure function from non-Gaussian surface statistics. A companion paper delivers and evaluates the resulting GMF, KuKa-Mod.

items.title: Investigation of the Asymptotic Properties of Active Impedance in Large Finite Array Antennas
items.summary: This paper presents an improved full-wave solver for finite array antennas, and uses this solver to examine asymptotic properties of active impedance for large regular arrays. The improved solver is based on a preconditioning scheme that has been adapted for use on more general finite geometries, and an improved data structure. These two improvements result in a fast and stable solver with a lower memory footprint. By investigating the active impedance of the center element in finite arrays it is found that, even for arrays with 1000 elements, asymptotic behavior may differ appreciably from infinite arrays. Tied to these properties, different predictors on how the active impedance of the center element in the array behaves are presented. The two best predictors work very well for the wideband arrays investigated, and may be used to decide when array approximations, such as unit cell methods, are appropriate, rather than general statements on array size.

items.title: Consistent Mapping for Fluid Structure Interaction with Geometrically Nonlinear Isogeometric Beams
items.summary: Isogeometric beam formulations provide an efficient reduced-dimensional representation of slender structures, combining accurate geometry and high-order continuity with few structural degrees of freedom. Their application to fluid--structure interaction (FSI) requires transferring motion and loads between the one-dimensional beam centerline and the surrounding fluid interface. While mapping strategies exist for conventional finite element beams, geometrically nonlinear isogeometric formulations require operators consistent with their spline-based kinematics and distinct descriptions of cross-sectional rotation. This work develops consistent beam-to-surface mappings for geometrically nonlinear isogeometric Bernoulli and Timoshenko beams in partitioned FSI. Fluid-interface points are attached to the beam in the reference configuration and reconstructed using the nonlinear kinematics of each formulation. Consistent linearization yields a configuration-dependent mapping operator whose transpose ensures work-conjugate load transfer. The formulations are verified through analytical deformation tests, convergence studies, and virtual-work checks, and evaluated in beam-based adaptations of the Mok and Turek--Hron benchmarks and the Goland wing flutter benchmark. The results confirm accurate interface reconstruction and work-conjugate load transfer under large deformations, while demonstrating the applicability of both beam formulations to coupled FSI problems.

items.title: Spin-valve effect through electrostatic coupling
items.summary: We propose a spin-valve effect in which an insulating magnetic van der Waals multilayer controls the conductance of an adjacent non-magnetic conductor by electrostatic coupling, without transport-electrons entering the magnetic layers. The coupling is induced by the variations of the electronic structure when the relative orientation of the magnetization of adjacent monolayers changes from parallel to antiparallel, modifying both the dielectric constant and band alignment. We consider two types of coupling and device concepts: charge transfer to a graphene monolayer and capacitive coupling in a single-electron transistor. We use density functional calculations to assess the magnitude of the effect in various materials, including CrI$_3$, CrBr$_3$, CrCl$_3$ and NiBr$_2$. We predict magnetoresistance ratios in the range of 1.14-1.20 for the charge-transfer device and up to $10^3$ in the single-electron transistor.

items.title: Effects of pulse durations in atom interferometry with double Raman diffraction
items.summary: Double Raman diffraction is a key enabling technique for future space missions relying on atom interferometry that offers enhanced sensitivity and intrinsic suppression of systematic effects. This diffraction mechanism naturally arises when employing a retro-reflection configuration in microgravity, but then accelerations can no longer be determined through a frequency-chirp scan. As a consequence, measurements become much more sensitive to systematic effects associated with pulse timing and duration. Indeed, the finite pulse duration can introduce additional phase shifts and small modifications of the arm trajectories, which are critical sources of error in high-precision measurements. In this work, we present the first complete analytical results of these effects for double Raman diffraction, building upon previous work for single diffraction and extending the standard literature. Our analysis determines the impact of finite pulse durations on the full interferometer sequence, quantifying the shifts of the atomic wave packets' trajectories and the acquired phases. The description relies on a comprehensive framework describing matter-wave propagation in terms of central trajectories and centered wave packets, and can be easily incorporated into relativistic treatments. Furthermore, we make use of group theoretic methods that are particularly useful when accounting for residual accelerations and frequency chirps, which are also relevant for ground-based applications. Our study includes time-dependent accelerations and frequency chirps, gravity gradients, retardation effects, AC Stark shifts induced by the Raman pulses, and external forces such those due to magnetic fields or temperature gradients in the black-body radiation.

items.title: Vendor-Agnostic Pseudocontinuous Arterial Spin Labeling Using Pulseq: Cross-Vendor Quantitative Evaluation
items.summary: Purpose: Inter-scanner variability in cerebral blood flow (CBF) quantification limits reproducibility in multi-center arterial spin labeling (ASL) studies. We developed and validated a vendor-agnostic pseudo-continuous ASL (PCASL) sequence using the open-source Pulseq framework, and assessed its extensibility to advanced perfusion imaging. Methods: A vendor-independent PCASL sequence was implemented in Pulseq and deployed on 3T scanners from Siemens, GE, and United Imaging. Seven healthy volunteers underwent single-post-labeling-delay (PLD) PCASL on all platforms, including test-retest scans. An in-house adapted Siemens vendor-based PCASL sequence served as reference. Reproducibility was assessed using within-subject coefficient of variation (CVwithin), root mean square error (RMSE), regional CBF correlation, and voxel-wise variation ratio maps. Multi-PLD PCASL and planning-free VE-PCASL were implemented as proof-of-concept extensions. Results: Mean gray matter (GM) CBF was similar across implementations. Test-retest GM CVwithin was below 4% on all platforms; Siemens-Pulseq had the lowest value (2.65%), versus 3.64% for the native sequence. GM RMSE between Siemens-Vendor and Pulseq implementations was comparable to test-retest RMSE, and all inter-scanner CVwithin values were below 3%. Voxel-wise variation ratio distributions were centered near 100%, suggesting cross-vendor variability comparable to physiological baseline fluctuations. Multi-PLD and VE-PCASL ran successfully on all platforms, yielding consistent CBF/ATT maps and vascular territory delineations. Conclusion: Pulseq-based PCASL enables vendor-agnostic perfusion imaging with low inter-scanner variability. This open-source approach provides a reproducible, standardized solution for multi-center ASL studies and facilitates deployment of advanced ASL techniques in clinical research.

items.title: Ab Initio Molecular Dynamics-Guided Machine-Learning Potentials for Mapping Nitric Oxide Interactions with Oxygen-Covered Graphite
items.summary: Exploratory ab initio molecular dynamics is used to construct machine-learning interatomic potentials for NO interactions with highly oriented pyrolytic graphite at 33\% bridge-site oxygen coverage. Representative configurations sampled across surface temperatures and incidence energies provide reference energies and forces for training and validation. The selected potential enables relaxation of 300 adsorption configurations and construction of spatial and angular interaction maps. These maps reveal increasingly restricted attractive regions during vertical approach and reduced short-range repulsion upon molecular reorientation. The resulting adsorption geometries and interaction landscapes guide further first-principles sampling toward refining potentials for NO oxidation dynamics.

items.title: Distinguishing thyroid nodule malignancy using digital palpation
items.summary: Accurate pre-operative diagnosis of thyroid nodules remains a major clinical challenge. Current diagnostic techniques rely on fine-needle aspiration and demonstrate high rates of inconclusive results, often leading to avoidable thyroidectomies with lifelong implications. Here, we introduce a mechanics-based diagnostic method that leverages Digital Palpation to determine malignancy and identify tissue subtypes in human thyroid nodules. From a cohort of patients undergoing thyroidectomies, we evaluated ex vivo thyroid specimens and processed the resulting mechanical data from 36 tests in 10 thyroid nodules. Principal Component Analysis reveals that these experimental results are distributed within a three-dimensional space of interpretable scalar features reflecting tissue grittiness, strength, and toughness, which map closely to descriptions of malignant and benign nodules given by clinicians. Our results further demonstrate that malignant nodules exhibit distinct mechanical signatures compared to their benign counterparts. This revealed a statistically significant difference (p = 9 x 10^-4) and separability (95% lower-bound Hedges' g = 1.08) between benign and malignant nodules along a direction in principal component space representing effective stiffness. Preliminary clustering patterns were also observed among malignant subtypes, including follicular, oncocytic, and papillary thyroid carcinomas. Together, these results highlight the potential of Digital Palpation as a novel mechanics-based method for tissue characterization and motivate its further development toward diagnostic applications.

items.title: Analysis of Xe-131 Prompt Gammas
items.summary: The prompt gammas of Xe-131 from thermal neutron capture were measured for the first time at the Fission Product Prompt gamma-ray Spectrometer by irradiation of isotopically enriched Xe-130 in a high-purity quartz ampoule. Through gamma-gamma coincidences, 42 new prompt gammas were measured and 14 new nuclear states determined.

items.title: Memory in biological Lévy walks from the dynamic-entropy formalism
items.summary: Lévy walks are recognized by the histogram of their flight lengths, while the renewal hypothesis on which the textbook model rests, that every flight is drawn afresh, is seldom tested. We test it with the dynamic-entropy formalism. Maximizing the causal entropy of a sequence of logarithmic flight lengths at fixed lagged correlations yields a chain of continuous spins on a compact interval, whose depth, selected by the data, tells a renewal walker from a Markovian one and from one with a longer memory. With one lag the chain is exactly solvable. A duality that exchanges long and short flights locates a first-order condensation of the flights at the upper cutoff, with the logarithmic range of the flights in the role of system size, and a positive memory makes the histogram heavier-tailed than the rule that generates each flight. For groups, the same construction separates the memory of each individual from delayed interactions and from drives common to all units, which an analysis of the group average confounds, and it gives the collective speed a critical point. On open data, renewal is rejected in seven of ten conditions of Drosophila larvae and in every termite, whose memory reaches a few flights back and lowers the exponent of the histogram by more than half a unit below that of the one-step rule. Wild baboons align with where their nearest neighbors, those ahead above all, were heading 10 to 30 s earlier, and homing pigeons are coupled across their small flocks. Zebrafish T cells, a negative control, remember their own speed, but no delayed coupling between the speeds of different cells survives the controls.

items.title: Teamknitt: Configuring, Observing and Intervening in LLM-Agent Teams through the Lens of Dynamical-Systems and Human-Team Theory
items.summary: Most frameworks for teams of large language model (LLM) agents fix the team's shape inside the software: who talks to whom, how much is passed along, and what a human can do once a run has started. Human-team research has long asked those questions: where team phenomena live (in members or in their interaction), how team-level properties arise, and what separates what a team does from how a team is. I propose using that theory as the organizing lens for configuring, observing and intervening in LLM-agent teams, without assuming its findings transfer. I introduce teamknitt, a framework and open reference implementation in which a user configures a team of 1-16 AI agents for task completion, solution generation, achieving a goal or a research mission; selects one of fourteen deterministic routing topologies or a custom directed graph; chooses a sharing profile that limits what may travel along permitted routes; and binds sources, representations, work dependencies, handoffs and an expertise directory. The recorded process can be observed through non-system views (member reports and behavior) and system views (distributed problem-solving, differentiated transactive memory, interactive coordination, team dynamics). Interventions are explicit and human-led: reviewed reconfiguration between runs, planned disturbances, and private feedback, pause, resume or stop applied at dependency-wave boundaries, with "queued", "applied", "assembled", "understood" and "improved" kept as separate claims. Emergent states such as trust and shared understanding are declared unmeasured. This is an idea and system-description paper with falsifiable hypotheses on topology, information flow and intervention timing, including whether the fractal scaling of communication output between members, and between members on different models, relates to task and team performance. No comparative result is reported.

items.title: Graph Symbolic Distillation: Decoding Graph Data into Interpretable Formulas across Materials and Chemistry
items.summary: Graph data provide a natural representation of the interconnected structures and interactions underlying many chemical and materials systems. Graph neural networks (GNNs) can learn complex relationships from such data, yet translating these representations into interpretable descriptors and scientific insights remains challenging. Here we introduce graph symbolic distillation (GSD), a framework for decoding graph data into interpretable symbolic formulas. GSD identifies task-relevant message-passing architectures and distills their learned transformations while preserving graph connectivity and aggregation operations.
