Further results establish norm discretization and regularized recovery from function values, and infer target regularity from approximation rates under coefficient or separation conditions. Altogether, these results describe how parameter geometry governs approximation accuracy, the stability of coefficient representations, discrete recovery, and the regularity information contained in convergence rates.

items.title: An AFLT-type generalization of the $q$-Baker--Forrester ex-conjecture
items.summary: The Habsieger--Kadell $q$-Morris constant term identity, which is equivalent to the famous $q$-Selberg integral, has been generalized in numerous ways since the 1980s. Among these, there are two important generalizations: (i) the $q$-Baker--Forrester ex-conjecture, which was conjectured by Baker and Forrester in 1998 and proved by Károlyi, Nagy, Petrov and Volkov in 2015; (ii) the AFLT-type $q$-Morris identity (equivalently, the AFLT-type $q$-Selberg integral), which was obtained by Albion, Rains and Warnaar in 2021, as a $q$-analog of the result of Alba, Fateev, Litvinov and Tarnopolskiy (AFLT). In this paper, by the Gessel--Xin method and the Macdonald polynomials with prescribed symmetry, we unify these two generalizations.

items.title: Gelfand-Kirillov dimension of constants of algebraic $q$-skew derivations
items.summary: Let $δ$ be an algebraic $q$-skew $σ$-derivation of an algebra $R$ over a field of arbitrary characteristic, where $σ$ is an algebraic automorphism of $R$, and let $R^δ$ be the algebra of constants of $δ$. We show that $GKdim(R) = GKdim(R^δ)$ whenever $R$ is semiprime and $R^δ$ is a PI algebra containing no infinite direct sum of nonzero ideals. The polynomial identity cannot be dropped. For every $r \geq 1$ we construct a primitive algebra $R$ with an inner derivation $d$ such that $d^{3} = 0$, $GKdim(R) \geq 2r$ and $GKdim(R^{d}) = 0$, while $R^{d}$ contains no direct sum of two nonzero ideals.

items.title: Harmonic problems arising from continuous time random walks limit processes
items.summary: In this paper, we develop a universal method that identifies the (non-local) governing evolution equations for Continuous Time Random Walks' (CTRWs) limit processes. Given one of these processes, our method provides the form of a non-local operator, acting on space and time variables jointly, such that the (generalized) harmonic problem associated with it represents an evolution governing equation for this process. Then, the well-posedness of this problem must be established case by case. In this paper, we establish well-posedness when the process is a Feller process (on a locally compact separable metric space $E$) time-changed with the overshooting of a subordinator. Also, we will show how our method applies to several cases when the equation and its well-posedness are already known, hence unifying several different approaches in the literature.

items.title: Special Loci in the Moduli of Curves
items.summary: We introduce new techniques to study mixed-characteristic special loci in moduli spaces and give several applications, focusing in particular on the moduli space $\mathsf{M}_g$ of curves. These applications include Zariski density results for split Jacobians, non-density results for supersingular loci, and lifting results for algebraic cycles, all under appropriate numerical conditions. Our methods generalize to more-or-less arbitrary moduli spaces mapping to Hodge-type Shimura varieties (and even some settings beyond the Shimura case), and relate to questions raised by Oort and de Jong.

items.title: An additively idempotent semiring of least order generating a limit variety
items.summary: We construct an additively idempotent semiring of order five that generates a limit variety and is not strongly nonfinitely based. The generated variety has exactly two maximal proper subvarieties, both hereditarily finitely based. We also prove that no ai-semiring of order at most four generates a limit variety. Consequently, five is the least possible order of a finite ai-semiring generating a limit variety.

items.title: Global weak solutions to nonlinear kinetic Fokker--Planck equations in bounded domains under physical initial data
items.summary: We establish the global existence of weak solutions to a nonlinear kinetic Fokker--Planck equation with degenerate diffusion, under either inflow or partial absorption-reflection boundary conditions. The novelty of our approach lies in constructing solutions under solely the physical assumptions on the initial and boundary data, namely finite mass, kinetic energy, and entropy, with no additional regularity imposed. To overcome the lack of uniform ellipticity, we develop a compactness principle based on weighted Fisher information, which yields strong $L^1$ convergence of approximate solutions. This framework provides a robust existence theory under only the physically relevant conditions, and applies uniformly to both inflow and partial absorption-reflection boundary settings.

items.title: BONuS: Multiple multivariate testing with a data-adaptive test statistic
items.summary: We propose a new adaptive empirical Bayes framework, the Bag-Of-Null-Statistics (BONuS) procedure, for multiple testing where each hypothesis testing problem is itself multivariate or nonparametric. BONuS is an adaptive and interactive knockoff-type method that helps improve the testing power while controlling the false discovery rate (FDR). The BONuS procedure is closely connected to many existing FDR-controlling methods, such as the counting knockoffs procedure and Benjamini-Hochberg procedure with conformal p-values. Contrary to procedures that start with a $p$-value for each hypothesis, BONuS analyzes the entire data set to adaptively estimate an optimal $p$-value transform based on an empirical Bayes model. Moreover, it can iteratively refine the model fit by peeling off synthetic null statistics to reduce noise in a highly adaptively way. Our method controls FDR in finite samples even if the empirical Bayes model is incorrect or the estimation is poor. An extension, the Double BONuS procedure, validates the empirical Bayes model to guard against power loss due to model misspecification. We demonstrate the power gain of BONuS procedure on multi-trait GWAS, asset pricing, and LLM evaluation.

items.title: A Dynamical Fekete-Szegő Theorem
items.summary: Let $E\subset\mathbb{C}$ be a compact set, symmetric with respect to the real axis and regular for the Dirichlet problem. A classical theorem of Fekete and Szegő asserts that if $cap(E)\ge 1$ then every neighbourhood of $E$ contains infinitely many complete sets of conjugate algebraic integers. We prove a dynamical strengthening: $cap(E)\ge1$ if and only if every neighbourhood of the polynomially convex hull $Pc(E)$ contains filled Julia sets of monic integral polynomials of arbitrarily large degree. When $cap(E)=1$, we show that the minimal polynomials $P_n$ of distinct algebraic integers whose entire Galois orbits approach $E$ have filled Julia sets $K_{P_n}$ converging to $Pc(E)$ in the Klimek metric, and Brolin measures converging to the equilibrium measure $μ_E$. The key step is that algebraic numbers of small Rumely height $h_E$ have minimal polynomials that are asymptotically minimal on $E$. As an arithmetic application, we show that the Call--Silverman canonical heights $\hat{h}_{P_n}$ converge to $h_E$ uniformly on $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$.

items.title: On Monotonicity in Mean Field Games Induced by Discount Factor Transformations
items.summary: This paper is devoted to the well-posedness of a class of infinite horizon discounted Mean Field Games (MFGs) problems, where both an exponential discount and a so-called cheap control factors are present simultaneously, and scale in a possibly different way. We introduce a new class of transformations of variables, at the level of both the MFG PDE and the corresponding FBSDE systems. We then show how these transformations reveal a new mechanism that generates semiconvexity estimates for the value function and ensures the existence of mean field equilibria, as long as the parameters land in a suitable regime, that we quantitatively describe. This new mechanism demonstrates furthermore how discount factors lead to a source of strong displacement monotonicity for the Lagrangian, without any initial monotonicity assumptions on the running costs. Consequently, in such regimes of parameters uniqueness of solutions manifests. Our approach uses a Lagrangian point of view, which lets us treat general non-separable Lagrangians and both deterministic and idiosyncratic noise driven models in a transparent, unified way. For a specific class of quadratic Lagrangians, using turnpike-type methods, we further obtain an exponential contractivity estimate for the mean field equilibria.

items.title: Do we really need the Rademacher complexities?
items.summary: We study the fundamental problem of learning with respect to the squared loss in a convex class. In the subgaussian setting, the sharpest known sample complexity bounds are characterised via fixed points associated with the limiting gaussian process. In more general settings (for example, heavier-tailed scenarios) the state-of-the-art bounds rely on localised Rademacher complexities, which are often difficult to control and can be considerably larger than their limiting gaussian counterparts. We show that if one has access to coarse information on the covariance structure of the underlying class, it is possible to derive an upper bound on the sample complexity that matches the state-of-the-art rates in the gaussian setting---even in heavy-tailed regimes. As a consequence, under rather minimal assumptions, learning problems that share the same $L_2$-structure---even those involving heavy-tailed distributions---admit the same upper bound on the sample complexity as if the problem were fully gaussian. This constitutes the first universality result for general convex learning problems. The proof is based on a novel learning procedure, and its performance is studied by combining optimal mean estimation techniques for real-valued random variables with Talagrand's generic chaining method.

items.title: Transforms between multivariate Laguerre and Meixner polynomials and their applications to gateways
items.summary: We establish gateways in both directions between the Laguerre process and a discrete Markov process for every inverse temperature $2θ\geq 1$. Here, a gateway is an intertwining relation between Markov processes with continuous and discrete state spaces. A key ingredient is a pair of generating function identities that relate two double generating functions for multivariate Meixner polynomials to a single and a double generating function for multivariate Laguerre polynomials, respectively. These identities reveal a close relationship between the two families of polynomials and yield integral transforms that underlie the gateway relations. Gateway relations provide a means of transferring properties between continuous and discrete processes. As an application, we derive the Feller-Dynkin property and the uniqueness of the invariant distribution for the Laguerre process from the corresponding properties of the discrete process.

items.title: Lengthscale Estimation for the Gaussian Kernel and Deterministic Response Functions
items.summary: The uncertainty estimates Gaussian processes output rely on the chosen covariance kernel and its hyperparameters. We study the fixed-domain asymptotics of the maximum likelihood and cross-validation estimators of the lengthscale parameter of the popular infinitely smooth Gaussian kernel when the observations are produced by a fixed univariate response function. No theoretical results for Gaussian lengthscale estimation exist in this setting. We prove lower bounds on the lengthscale estimators that depend on the regularity of the response function, as measured by the rate of decay of its Fourier transform. If the response function lives in the Hilbert space of the Gaussian kernel with lengthscale $\ell$, the lower bounds have a straightforward dependency on $\ell$. For bandlimited functions and functions whose Fourier transforms decay as $\exp(-a \lvert ω\rvert^γ)$ for $a > 0$ and $γ> 2$, we prove that the estimators blow up essentially at least as fast as $(\log n)^{(γ-2)/(2γ)}$ in the number of data points, $n$. Bandlimited functions are identified with $γ= \infty$. Unlike analogous results for finitely smooth Matérn kernels, our results make no assumptions on the geometry of the observation points. Numerical experiments illustrate the results.

items.title: Thin-Shell implies small-ball deviation via Gaussian tilts
items.summary: We show that uniform thin-shell estimates for isotropic log-concave measures $μ$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ yield precise and explicit deviation estimates for the Euclidean norm $|X|$ below the expectation, improving the square-root dependence of Klartag-Lehec to a quadratic one (which is best possible, up to numeric constants). Using the recent Chen-Klartag sharp variance bound, we deduce: $$ μ\left(|X|\le \sqrt{n}-s\right) \le \exp\left\{ -\frac{s^2}{4} \left(1+O\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\right) \right\} \qquad \forall\, s\in(0,\sqrt{n}). $$ In particular, this yields a new and transparent proof that Thin-Shell implies Slicing (by passing through small-ball estimates). Our method is based on using central Gaussian tilts, recently introduced by Brazitikos, which may be thought of as a deterministic version of Eldan's stochastic localization. An anisotropic variant (when $μ$ has general covariance structure) of these deviation estimates is also obtained.

items.title: Asymptotic Bayes Optimality of Sparse Multiple Testing Procedures under One-Factor Dependence
items.summary: In this paper, we study sparse multiple testing under a Gaussian two-group model with known one-factor covariance and centered Gaussian signals. We derive a first-order risk expansion for the observed-data Bayes Oracle, including a finite-dimensional loading average for heterogeneous loadings and an explicit limiting constant for homogeneous loadings. Under the stated factor-estimation and signal-calibration conditions, the homogeneous one-factor Oracle has strictly smaller leading risk than its independent-coordinate counterpart; observing the latent factor yields no further first-order reduction. We establish asymptotic Bayes optimality under sparsity (ABOS) for the Maximum Residual Down (MRD) step-down procedure with Gavrilov--Benjamini--Sarkar (GBS) stagewise calibration (MRD--GBS). Uniform control of residual errors along the rejection path permits comparison with a fixed factor-known rule without requiring the rejection paths to coincide. Fixed-residual versions of GBS and Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) attain the same leading risk. We also prove ABOS for the Bayesian Step-Down (BSD) rule when supplied with the true mixture, signal variance, covariance, and loss parameters; this is an Oracle-parameterized result. When the expected signal count grows faster than the logarithm of the reciprocal signal proportion, BSD and the observed-data Oracle disagree on several coordinates negligible in probability relative to the expected signal count, explaining BSD's near-Oracle behavior in companion simulations. The results cover diverging and bounded positive expected signal counts, including every fixed polynomial sparsity rate up to the bounded-count regime, under the stated calibrations. A fixed-dimension simulation illustrates absolute-risk behavior but does not establish ABOS.

items.title: Effective Joint Equidistribution of Subspaces of Bounded Height in Rigid Adelic Spaces
items.summary: We prove effective joint equidistribution for subspaces of fixed dimension in a fixed rigid adelic space over a number field. The joint distribution records the rescaled height, the archimedean position, and the shapes of the subspace and its quotient. More generally, we obtain counting estimates for regions in which the height bound may depend on the position and both shapes. Under a Hölder-type bound for the measure of boundary layers, the estimates have explicit power-saving error terms. We apply these results to counting problems involving slopes, freeness, and semistability, and to Diophantine approximation with prescribed shapes.

items.title: An Equivariant Coarse Green-Julg Theorem for Proper Actions
items.summary: We prove an equivariant coarse Green--Julg theorem for proper isometric actions of countable discrete groups on bounded geometry metric spaces. We introduce the $(Γ, X)$-controlled proper $C^{*}$-algebra, and show that the evaluation-at-zero map between the equivariant localization and Roe algebras with such coefficients induces an isomorphism on $K$-theory.

items.title: N -phase flow simulations using X-Mesh and an explicit marker interface representation
items.summary: We present a marker-based X-Mesh framework for incompressible N-phase flow simulations with sharp, explicitly tracked interfaces. The interface is represented by Lagrangian marker chains, while the computational mesh is deformed so that selected mesh edges conform to the tracked geometry without changing mesh connectivity. This combination preserves the advantages of body-fitted finite element discretizations while allowing highly distorted and nearly degenerated elements to capture fine interfacial features on relatively coarse meshes without requiring mesh refinement. The arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) finite element solver uses a pressure field that is continuous within each phase and discontinuous across the fitted interface. Surface tension is introduced through a variational membrane, so the pressure jump is resolved without prescribing a curvature-dependent correction; a Young wall energy provides the corresponding treatment of fluid-fluid-solid triple points. Topological changes are handled geometrically from the marker representation. Numerical experiments illustrate the ability of the approach to transport complex interfaces and to control topology changes through marker-based feature-size criteria.

items.title: Generalized Frobenius manifolds: symmetries and their classification in 2-dimensions
items.summary: A theory of symmetries of generalized Frobenius manifolds is developed. This is used to study the solution space of all generalized Frobenius manifolds that are "above" a specific Frobenius manifold. Since all (semi-simple) Frobenius manifolds in 2-dimensions are known, by constructing all homogeneous Legendre fields associated to these manifolds we classify all 2-dimensional generalized Frobenius manifolds. With this description, the known examples of generalized Frobenius manifolds correspond to distinguished points in this solution space. For Hurwitz-Frobenius manifolds the action of a Legendre transformation on Hurwitz space data, and in particular the primary differential, is given.

items.title: Feedback Vertex Set, Max Cut, and Edge Coloring on the Strong Product of a Graph and a Path
items.summary: We examine the computational complexity of well-known problems on subgraphs of the strong product of two paths. Namely, for Max Cut we show NP-hardness on induced subgraphs of $P \boxtimes P$ answering a question by Dvořák, Huynh, Joret, Liu, and Wood (2021). For 3-Edge Coloring we show NP-hardness on subgraphs of $P \boxtimes P$ and that it is equivalent to 3-Edge Coloring on planar graphs for induced subgraphs of $P \boxtimes P$. It is a long standing open question whether 3-Edge Coloring on planar graphs is NP-hard. As a second contribution, we consider graphs of the form $G \boxtimes P$ and show that Feedback Vertex Set on these graphs is FPT in the clique-width of $G$. Furthermore, we show that it can be solved in polynomial time if $G$ is chordal or co-comparable and that the computational complexity depends on the parity of $P$ if $G$ is bipartite. Namely, it is solvable in polynomial time if $P$ has an even number of vertices but is NP-complete otherwise. For Max Cut, we show that it can be solved in polynomial time if $G$ is bipartite.

items.title: Dual-Space Preconditioning for Variational Inequalities and Root-Finding Problems
items.summary: This paper develops a dual-space preconditioning framework for variational inequalities and root-finding problems beyond classical cocoercivity and Lipschitz continuity assumptions. To this end, we introduce both a novel cocoercivity-type condition and a relaxed Lipschitz continuity condition, and derive convergence of deterministic and stochastic methods under these generalized conditions. For isotropic preconditioners, the resulting algorithms can be interpreted as variable-stepsize variants of classical methods, extending recent analyses based on $(L_0, L_1)$-type growth conditions while allowing simpler proofs and larger stepsize ranges. We also show that the framework naturally handles variational inequalities through weak Minty-type arguments. Finally, we study the associated continuous-time dynamics and derive a variational and optimal control interpretation of the preconditioned flow. Overall, the results show that dual-space preconditioning provides a flexible mechanism for designing and analyzing operator methods beyond the standard Euclidean Lipschitz setting.

items.title: Pólya's conjecture for hyperbolic balls and Berezin--Li--Yau type inequalities
items.summary: We prove the strict shifted Dirichlet Pólya inequality \[ λ_k(B_R)>\frac{(d-1)^2κ^2}{4}+4π^2\left(\frac{k}{ω_d\operatorname{Vol}_κ(B_R)}\right)^{2/d},\qquad k\ge1, \] for every geodesic ball $B_R$ in hyperbolic space of constant sectional curvature $-κ^2$, in every dimension $d\ge2$. As a consequence, we obtain the shifted Berezin--Li--Yau type inequality for hyperbolic balls, thereby providing a concrete family of domains satisfying both conjectures proposed by Laptev in 2023. For arbitrary nonempty open subsets $Ω\subset\mathbb{H}^d_κ$ of finite volume, we establish the weak Berezin--Li--Yau type inequality \[ \sum_{j=1}^{m}λ_j(Ω)\ge a_{d,κ}m+\frac{d}{d+2}\,4π^2\left(\frac{m}{ω_d\operatorname{Vol}_κ(Ω)}\right)^{2/d}m,\qquad m\ge1, \] with the optimal leading coefficient, where $a_{2,κ}=κ^2/4$ and $a_{d,κ}=d(d-1)κ^2/6$ for $d\ge3$. We also establish the global two-sided estimate for the renormalized eigenvalue sum on hyperbolic space, originally proposed by Strichartz in 1996 and valid for $d\ge3$.

items.title: The Role of Insurance in Power-System Risk Management: A Critical Review
items.summary: Modern power systems are becoming more renewable-rich, digitalized, and interconnected, making risk propagation and economic consequences increasingly complex. Physical mitigation remains the primary means of risk control, but technical and economic limits leave residual risk. Insurance can complement these measures by transferring associated economic losses and influencing power-system decisions through risk-responsive terms. Despite growing interest, the literature remains fragmented across power-system engineering, actuarial science, and risk finance. This review develops an integrated physical-financial perspective for reviewing insurance in power systems. It examines how power system risks generate residual economic losses and the conditions under which these losses can be insured and transferred. It then develops an actuarial framework for insured-loss assessment and pricing. Insurance-aware decision-making is synthesized through four coupling levels describing how financial protection interacts with power-system decisions. Further progress is constrained by weak physical-financial loss validation, incomplete representation of systemic and evolving portfolio risk, and limited empirical and actuarial grounding of insurance-decision feedback. Research priorities include stronger physical-financial data linkage, forward-looking portfolio assessment, multi-timescale decision feedback, and empirical validation. Addressing these priorities would help move power-system insurance from fragmented applications toward a more coherent approach to residual-risk management in future power systems.

items.title: Connectivity and the equilibration of Boltzmann-type equations on dense graphs
items.summary: We investigate the equilibration of solutions to a homogeneous Boltzmann-type equation whose collision kernel is given by a graphon encoding the connectivity structure of interacting agents. For a broad class of Lipschitz-continuous binary interaction rules, we show that, under suitable conditions relating the interaction parameters to the connectivity properties of the graphon, solutions converge exponentially fast towards those of the classical homogeneous Boltzmann-type equation without preferential connections, and hence towards its equilibrium distributions. We then consider in detail compromise-diffusion interaction rules and establish a quasi-invariant limit leading to a Fokker-Planck-type equation parametrised by the graphon connectivity. This limiting equation allows us to characterise explicitly both connectivity-independent and connectivity-dependent equilibrium distributions.

items.title: An Accelerated Dynamic Stochastic Primal-Dual Method for Multi-stage Stochastic Optimization
items.summary: We consider multi-stage stochastic optimization problems with smooth convex stage costs and linear linking constraints. Dynamic stochastic approximation (DSA), a stochastic first-order method, uses a recursive structure whose memory requirement grows only linearly with the number of stages. Its implementation, however, requires an exact solution of the proximal subproblem associated with the stage cost, and this subproblem often admits no closed-form solution. To resolve this issue, we develop an accelerated dynamic stochastic primal-dual (A-DSPD) framework that retains the recursive value-function structure and only requires the gradient of the stage cost. Within this framework, each stagewise saddle-point subproblem is solved by an inexact accelerated stochastic primal-dual method (iASPD), which applies Nesterov acceleration to the smooth stage cost and uses recursively generated stochastic $ε$-subgradients for the nonsmooth downstream value function. For the stochastic composite saddle-point problem, after $N$ primal-dual updates, iASPD yields optimality and feasibility bounds in which the contribution of the smooth stage cost decays at a faster rate $O(1/N^2)$, while the terms associated with stochastic $ε$-subgradients of the nonsmooth value function decay as $O(1/\sqrt{N})$, up to the prescribed oracle inexactness. We also develop bounds for the stochastic $ε$-subgradient estimators and the dual iterates, which yield complexity guarantees for A-DSPD. Specifically, A-DSPD computes an $ε$-solution using $O(1/ε^4)$ sampled scenarios and $O(1/ε^5)$ primal-dual updates for three-stage problems. We further extend the method and its convergence analysis to problems with an arbitrary finite number of stages. Numerical experiments on three-stage stochastic portfolio models illustrate the empirical advantage of the proposed method.

items.title: Thermodynamic Formalism for Non-Invariant Probabilities: Entropy, Divergence, Channels
items.summary: Let $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{M}_σ$ denote, respectively, the sets of Borel and $σ$-invariant probabilities on the uncountable set $Ω=\{1,2,...,d\}^\mathbb{N}$. Given a Hölder Jacobian $J$, the dual Ruelle operator $μ\in \mathcal{M} \mapsto \mathcal{L}_{J}^* (μ)$ will play the role of a dynamical channel; generalizes the action of a stochastic matrix on probability vectors. Since $\mathcal{L}_{J}^*$ generally breaks $σ$-invariance, we introduce the \emph{ni-entropy} $h_{ni}(μ)$ for non-invariant measures, employing the concept of the expected value function on cylinders of size one. $h_{ni}(μ)$ differs from Shannon entropy but extends the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy from $\mathcal{M}_σ$ to $\mathcal{M}$; $h_{ni}$ is concave and u.s.c. This leads us to the concept of ni-pressure $\mathcal{P}(A)$ of a potential $A:Ω\to \mathbb{R}$. $μ\in \mathcal{M}$ is not a density with respect to a dominating measure. We define an {\it ni-Kullback-Leibler divergence} $D_{ni}(ρ|| ν)$ not assuming absolute continuity. We investigate concepts of Information Theory such as Minimal Output Entropy, Donsker-Varadhan variational principle, a variational formula for $h_{ni}$, bounds for divergence, information projections, and their connections to the ni-pressure $\mathcal{P}$.

items.title: Coverage and shape of conformal highest-density sets: A minimax theory
items.summary: We study conditional coverage and geometric efficiency of conformal highest-density sets. The excess volume of such a set over the conditional highest-density set, the smallest set with the required conditional coverage, splits into a coverage error and an excess mass. We show that, among procedures whose volume is accurate up to a constant, the coverage error has the minimax rate of nonparametric regression on the covariate, and that the excess mass has the squared minimax rate of conditional density estimation. The usual split conformal construction calibrates these sets with a single threshold, which corrects the bias of the density estimate only on average over the covariate. We prove that its coverage error can then be of the order of the slower density rate. We therefore propose two-stage calibration, which estimates the coverage of the super-level sets of a density estimate by a regression on the covariate and uses this estimated coverage as the conformity score. Since these sets are fixed at each covariate value, their coverage is as smooth as the conditional density, and, under mild regularity conditions, the coverage error attains the regression rate even when the density estimate is inconsistent. The shape of the set still depends on the accuracy of the density estimate: sup-norm accuracy controls it at the minimax excess-mass rate, whereas accuracy in an integrated norm, even of minimax order, does not. With a local polynomial density estimate, two-stage calibration attains both minimax rates up to logarithmic factors. Simulations and an application to bike-sharing demand illustrate the results.

items.title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training
items.summary: Foundation models pretrained on large natural-image collections are increasingly adapted for medical image segmentation, in the expectation that they will replace models trained for each task. Most comparisons, however, use data from the training distribution and a single task-specific baseline whose configuration is rarely justified, and therefore provide limited evidence of performance at new clinical sites. It also remains unclear how much of a foundation model must be adapted, and what determines this. We adapted a foundation model, DINOv2, with strategies ranging from tuning only its bias terms to full fine-tuning, and compared it with U-Nets and ResU-Nets trained from scratch. Experiments covered colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and dermoscopy, with testing on held-out data from the training source and on independent datasets from other institutions. The adapted foundation model generalised better on every external dataset. Within the training distribution, the task-specific models remained competitive when training data were abundant, and delineated boundaries more precisely, while the foundation model more often missed small lesions. Only a small fraction of the foundation model required adaptation, and the capacity needed was determined by the imaging domain rather than by the adaptation method. A widely used polyp test set was also found to duplicate images from another benchmark. Foundation-model adaptation is therefore warranted where models must work across sites, with capacity selected on the target domain.

items.title: Multimodal Model Diffing for Feature Discovery and Control
items.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit strong visual understanding, yet the internal features that cause these behaviors remain difficult to identify, audit, or control. While applicable to post-hoc inspection, hidden states that are decomposed into interpretable feature directions using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) neither readily isolate which features are changed by multimodal training, nor are they directly useful for targeted control. We introduce MMDiff, a multimodal model-diffing framework that trains multimodal SAEs and turns them into feature-level interfaces for discovering and controlling multimodal behavior. MMDiff supports three uses: (i) feature isolation, by diffing a base-LM SAE against its multimodal-adapted counterpart to identify features altered by multimodal training; (ii) task-specific feature detection, via per-token contrastive firing analysis that isolates causal features; and (iii) feature-level control, by causally removing or steering the discovered feature directions. We train multimodal SAEs for three MLLM families, LLaVA-MORE, PaliGemma 2, and InternVL3.5, and evaluate on visual-spatial understanding, multimodal safety, and OCR. MMDiff discovers sparse, causally specific features whose removal selectively degrades target behaviors by an average of 12% on spatial tasks and 17% on OCR, and reduces attack success rate by 24% on multimodal safety attacks, with no impact on VQA performance. Steering these features improves spatial and OCR accuracy by +3.6% and +1.8% on average over a standard single-layer steering baseline. These results show that multimodal SAEs can serve not only as interpretability tools, but as mechanisms for auditing, steering, and controlling MLLMs behavior toward safer and more capable generations.

items.title: Toward Foundation Detection Models via Example-Based Grounding in EM-DETR
items.summary: DeepLearning (DL)-based Computer-Aided Diagnostic (CAD) systems have shown great promise in supporting clinicians, but their performance heavily depends on the availability of large, well-annotated datasets. In medical lesion detection, the scarcity of comprehensive, stan dardized annotations and the heterogeneity of existing datasets limit the development of robust foundation models. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to building a multi-domain foundation model for le sion detection by integrating diverse medical image datasets annotated for both anatomical structures and abnormalities. We first propose a student-teacher training strategy to effectively combine datasets with heterogeneous label spaces, mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and im proving feature learning. In addition, building on our previously pro posed example-based EM-DETR framework, we adapt it to jointly learn from multiple domain-specific datasets, enabling fine-grained, example driven detection across modalities. Our model achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results, with image-level AUC scores exceeding previous SOTA by 1% point on four key findings in CXRs. We achieve a leading mAP50 in CXRs and mammography, surpassing EM-DETR trained on a single dataset by 2-3% points. This approach paves the way for scalable foundation models in medical imaging that leverage heterogeneous data while maintaining robust and generalizable performance.

items.title: DynaCrys: Crystal Generation with Dynamic Space-Group Diffusion
items.summary: The search for new crystalline materials spans an enormous compositional and structural space. Generating candidates in this space requires modeling the relationships between elemental composition, crystallographic symmetry, and crystal geometry. The space group specifies the crystal's symmetry and determines the admissible Wyckoff positions and geometric degrees of freedom; fixing it in advance prevents this global symmetry choice from being revised using information from evolving Wyckoff occupations and elemental composition. We introduce DynaCrys, the first framework for complete crystal generation in which the space group co-evolves with Wyckoff occupations and elements. We develop physics-informed space-group diffusion that explicitly incorporates crystallographic group-subgroup relations, and a legality-constrained stochastic decoder that jointly samples compatible space groups, Wyckoff occupations, and elements, followed by symmetry-constrained geometry generation. In large-scale evaluations on standard benchmarks, DynaCrys achieves state-of-the-art performance in symmetry-aware crystal generation while supporting fast sampling.

items.title: TorchCurves: Differentiable Parametric Curves
items.summary: We present TorchCurves, a PyTorch library that treats vector-valued parametric curves as learnable primitives. Its central operation maps batches of scalar inputs to points on curves represented in B-spline or Legendre polynomial bases, with differentiation through both inputs and coefficients. Curve coefficients can be optimized jointly with the surrounding model or produced by another network. The library provides trainable modules, reusable basis modules, and a functional interface, supporting applications ranging from continuous feature embeddings to Kolmogorov-Arnold networks and functional regression. Its implementation combines classical evaluation algorithms with vectorized PyTorch operations, emphasizing readability and maintainability without custom hardware kernels. Timing experiments compare curve evaluation against NumPy and SciPy and KAN training against EfficientKAN across a range of problem sizes. The results illustrate where this generality remains computationally practical and where overhead is substantial. Library is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexshtf/torchcurves.

items.title: AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models
items.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) produces rich training experience, yet outcome rewards reduce each attempt to a single number and leave most of this information unused. Training-time scaffolds, such as strategies or hints added to the prompt during training, offer a natural way to turn this information into guidance, but their design and adaptation are largely left to humans and tailored to specific domains. We introduce AutoScaffold, a unified AI-for-AI framework that turns a student's training experience into adaptive scaffolds, with minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention during training. A frozen teacher periodically examines this experience, diagnoses bottlenecks, and designs scaffolds in two forms: (i) strategies shared across a class of tasks and (ii) hints for individual hard tasks, adjusting the content and amount of support as the student learns. The scaffolds are removed at evaluation. We apply the same framework to ALFWorld, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation. When evaluated without scaffolds, students trained with AutoScaffold outperform those trained with the corresponding RL baselines in all four domains, with gains of 7.2 points in ALFWorld success and 4.0 points in average QA exact match. On GPU kernel generation, AutoScaffold increases the fraction of tasks with a correct kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference by up to 5.0 points. On math, our student surpasses QuestA's reported accuracy using approximately one-third as many student training steps. Analyses show that the teacher identifies a different failure in each task class and shifts its scaffolds from step-by-step workflows to targeted fixes as the student improves, and that its revised scaffolds help the student learn more than keeping the previous scaffold or using no scaffold.

items.title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
items.summary: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. When evidence rejects $h$, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, $89\%$ of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve $73\%$ of these candidates to a specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves $67\%$ more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded study, $38$ human experts chose the same explanation on $78\%$ of resolved questions and on $82\%$ of questions where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget.

items.title: RepFusion: Leveraging Multimodal Priors for Denoising in Representation Space
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used in text-to-image (T2I) systems, but they are typically limited to text encoding, while denoising is handled by newly trained generative backbones. The emergence of representation autoencoders (RAEs) shifts the generation target toward semantically structured visual representations, creating a latent space that is more compatible with pretrained LLM priors. Inspired by multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), where an MLP projector is sufficient to align clean visual representations with a pretrained LLM, we repurpose the MLLM itself as a noisy representation encoder, extending this mechanism from clean to noisy inputs. We present RepFusion, which uses the resulting MLLM outputs as the conditioning signal for a diffusion transformer. In controlled comparisons at similar inference budgets, RepFusion outperforms baselines that devote comparable capacity to newly initialized denoisers. Reusing MLLM outputs across denoising steps further accelerates inference while retaining performance comparable to per-step MLLM recomputation. These results demonstrate that MLLMs provide strong priors for denoising visual representations.

items.title: Layer-Based Width for PAFP
items.summary: The Path Avoiding Forbidden Pairs problem (PAFP) asks whether, in a directed graph $G$ with two of its vertices labeled $s,t$ and a set $\mathcal F$ of forbidden vertex pairs, there is an $s$--$t$ path that contains at most one endpoint from each pair in $\mathcal F$. We initiate the study of PAFP through a layer-based width measure. We first look at the directed union digraph $G\cup\mathcal F$, which is obtained by adding one arc per forbidden pair to $G$, oriented according to a fixed reachability-compatible order. Let the BFS layer $L_d$ be the set of vertices at directed shortest-path distance $d$ from $s$, and define the BFS-width from $s$ as $\max_d |L_d|$. We show that if $G\cup\mathcal F$ has BFS-width $b$ from $s$, and $p$ is the maximum, over BFS-layer cuts, of the smaller of the numbers of distinct heads and distinct tails of backward arcs crossing the cut, then PAFP is FPT parameterized by $b+p$. Here a backward arc goes from a later BFS layer to an earlier one. In contrast, we show that bounded BFS-width alone does not suffice: PAFP remains $\mathsf{NP}$-complete when the union digraph has BFS-width 2. We also study layer-based width parameters on the input graph. We show that if the input DAG has BFS-width at most $2$ and only $k$ backward input arcs, then PAFP can be decided in $2^k |I|^{O(1)}$ time, with unrestricted forbidden pairs, and this result is tight. Moreover, we study exact-length layers in the input graph, where the $d$-th exact-length layer consists of the vertices reachable from $s$ by a directed path of length exactly $d$. We show that for DAGs of exact-length width at most $2$, PAFP is polynomial-time decidable by a $2$-SAT encoding of fixed-length paths. Unlike previously known polynomial-time regimes our 2 input -graph tractability results simultaneously allow unrestricted forbidden pairs and input graphs with exponentially many $s$--$t$ paths.

items.title: Pyrite: Building and Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Pose Ranking Agents
items.summary: Predicting how a ligand binds to its target is central to small-molecule drug discovery. Modern cofolding models can generate diverse candidate poses, but reliably ranking these candidates remains challenging. We introduce Pyrite, a pairwise pose-ranking benchmark comprising 1,500 pose pairs across diverse protein-ligand complexes. Expert chemists equipped with 3D visualization tools and physics-based scores perform near chance, highlighting the difficulty of interpreting available chemical signals. To investigate automated ranking, we introduce PyriteRep, a structured representation of molecular geometry, protein-ligand interactions, and physicochemical scores, and develop two LLM-based agents: PyriteReasoner, which directly compares poses through text-based reasoning, and PyriteFeaturizer, which generates executable code to construct features for logistic regression, optionally incorporating features derived from LLM subcalls. These agents achieve up to 67% and 74% accuracy, respectively, exceeding observed expert performance. LLM-guided feature discovery generally outperforms direct reasoning, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves open-weight models, enabling them to match or surpass closed-source frontier models in our evaluations. These results establish Pyrite as a challenging test of pose-ranking ability and highlight LLM-guided feature discovery as a promising approach to interpret and combine the outputs of computational chemistry tools.

items.title: Artificial Currency and Separate Selling: A 3-Approximation for Consumer Surplus
items.summary: We study the allocation of indivisible items to buyers with additive values drawn from independent distributions. The objective is consumer surplus net of burnt payments. We consider artificial-currency mechanisms: buyers receive personalized budgets of a currency worthless outside the mechanism and use them to bid across items. The better of separate selling and artificial-currency mechanisms provides a 3-approximation to optimal consumer surplus. The guarantee holds at every Bayes--Nash equilibrium, without equilibrium selection. Both branches are necessary: either alone may capture only a vanishing share of the optimum. The proof decomposes benchmark surplus into a stable part captured by artificial currency and a variation covered by separate selling.

items.title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology
items.summary: Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function. Such comparisons can confound wiring with how the models are tuned: a connectome fixes who connects to whom, not the excitability, gains or plasticity rates the model also needs, and modellers often tune these until the real-wiring model works. We separate three estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 restricted to physiology consistent with independent data (P3). The biases involved are known in machine learning (under-tuned baselines, inherited weights, winner's curse); we measure what they do to biological conclusions, using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models. Some claims survive every protocol we test: segregated reward and punishment dopamine improves learning, and head-direction topography is required for a persistent bump. Others do not. In the mushroom body, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 under P1 and P2 but loses to it by 0.09 under P3 (95% CIs exclude zero; held-out runs confirm). The verdict is set by the share of alpha'beta' cells among active Kenyon cells, which P1 selects low; at the share implied by imaging (about 44%) the real-wiring model fails to learn, exposing a model inadequacy rather than a deficit of the fly's wiring. In flyvis, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome, which has a constructed solution within 0.07 (median) of the real error, more than a spatially shuffled one in 50 of 50 members; the ranking survives ten-fold longer retraining but depends on the checkpoint at fifty-fold. A credible structural claim needs matched optimisation, data-constrained physiology and a model that still works there.

items.title: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime
items.summary: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. No harness-based method gains on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.

items.title: Uniform-in-Time Weak Propagation-of-Chaos in Shallow Neural Networks
items.summary: We consider one-hidden layer neural networks trained in the feature-learning regime using gradient descent, and relate the output of the finite-width network $f_{\hatρ_t^m}$ to its infinite-width counterpart $f_{ρ_t^{MF}}$, which evolves in the mean-field dynamics. While constant-time horizon bounds for $\|f_{ρ_t^{MF}} - f_{\hatρ_t^m}\|$ may be obtained via standard Grönwall estimates, the long-time behavior of the fluctuation is a more delicate matter. Uniform-in-time bounds often rely on (local) strong convexity in the landscape or Logarithmic Sobolev inequalities present in noisy gradient dynamics. In this work, we establish non-asymptotic weak propagation-of-chaos that holds uniformly in time, obtained by exploiting instead the convergence rate of the mean-field deterministic Wasserstein-gradient-flow dynamics. Specifically, denoting by $L_t$ the mean-field excess MSE loss at time $t$ and $m$ the number of neurons, under standard regularity assumptions and the condition $\int_0^\infty L_t^{1/2} dt =O(\log d)$, we obtain the uniform in time bound $\|f_{ρ_t^{MF}}- f_{\hatρ_t^m}\|^2 \lesssim \text{poly}(d) m^{-\min(1,c/6)}$ whenever $L_t \lesssim t^{-c}$. Our result holds in a noiseless setting and does not make any assumptions on the geometry of the landscape near the optimum, and extends seamlessly to other forms of discretization, including finite number of samples and time discretization. A key takeaway of our result is that whenever the convergence rate of the mean-field, population-loss dynamics is faster than $t^{-2}$, we can attain a loss of $ε$ with only $\text{poly}(d/ε)$ neurons, training samples, and GD steps.

items.title: Emergent Biological Capabilities in a Foundation Model for Molecular Interactions
items.summary: Foundation models trained on large unlabeled corpora develop emergent capabilities, tasks that go beyond the training objective. We extend this paradigm to multimodal biology with Bonbon, a foundation model for molecular interactions trained on approximately 3.2 trillion tokens of paired protein-ligand sequences. From a single representation space, Bonbon exhibits three zero-shot emergent capabilities at hierarchical levels of resolution: functional (mechanism of action), residue (binding site localization, including orthosteric/allosteric discrimination), and bond (covalent versus non-covalent engagement). All three capabilities generalize to out-of-distribution complexes. Bonbon was trained on protein-ligand sequences alone, without any task-specific supervision and without structural coordinates. We conducted controlled scaling experiments across six model scales from 42M to 1.6B parameters; every capability evaluated shows a sharp jump at the largest scale on continuous metrics, even as pretraining loss decreases smoothly. This demonstrates that loss-based scaling laws alone are insufficient to predict when zero-shot emergent capabilities become available. The capabilities reported here emerge after training at a 1:2,000 parameter-to-token ratio to accommodate the sparsity of paired biological interaction data. The same frozen representations achieve state-of-the-art binding and affinity prediction at five orders of magnitude greater speed than co-folding methods. In prospective wet-lab validation across nine disease targets spanning seven protein families, Bonbon achieves a 61.5% dose-response hit rate on de novo compounds, yielding structurally novel molecules not previously reported to inhibit these proteins, including for out-of-distribution targets.

items.title: Analyzing Linear Layers in Related-Differential Cryptanalysis
items.summary: In AES-like ciphers, diffusion layers are commonly instantiated using MDS matrices, since their optimal branch number yields strong diffusion guarantees and underpins classical resistance arguments against differential and linear cryptanalysis. However, Daemen and Rijmen (2009) showed that linear layers may still exhibit related-differential structure beyond what the MDS criterion captures, and Bardeh and Rijmen (2022) demonstrated that this phenomenon can be exploited in attacks on reduced-round AES. In this work, we systematically investigate the conditions under which linear layers avoid or exhibit these differentials, identifying matrix classes for which such structure is unavoidable. We first prove that every non-MDS matrix admits a nontrivial pair of related differentials, showing that the MDS property is necessary for avoiding them. We then establish that every odd-order symmetric MDS matrix admits related differentials, which rules out broad families of Cauchy-based constructions. We also substantially strengthen the circulant case by proving that related differentials are unavoidable for every circulant matrix of order $n$ with $n \not\equiv \pm 2 \pmod{12}$. Finally, we revisit the characterization of $3 \times 3$ MDS matrices over $\mathbb{F}_{2^m}$ for the absence of related differentials, and derive an explicit necessary and sufficient criterion in terms of $15$ polynomial constraints.

items.title: Measuring Robustness and Efficiency in a Connectome-Constrained Fly Visual System Model: Linking an Adversarial and a Perceptual Illusion
items.summary: Biological visual systems compute reliably under tight metabolic and wiring constraints, whereas artificial vision systems consume far more energy and can be sensitive to adversarial perturbations. Whether networks with brain-like wiring are more robust at lower computational cost is unclear. We address this by benchmarking a task-optimized, continuous-time recurrent neural network of the fly visual system constrained by its synaptic connectome (FlyNet) against artificial neural networks. We compare it against CNNs, RAFT, and continuous-time recurrent neural networks without detailed connectome constraints (sCTRNN, CTRNN) on a collision-detection task within a differentiable 3D rendering pipeline. FlyNet is adversarially vulnerable but, relative to its compute, more robust to common video corruptions than RAFT, while using up to five orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs. The CTRNNs remain more robust than FlyNet across almost all tested perturbations, suggesting that connectome constraints benefit efficiency, through their low edge count, over robustness. Recurrence improves robustness to white-box attacks in RAFT and temporal context improves robustness to common corruptions. FlyNet's position and velocity representations degrade under adversarial textures but recover under counterfactual textures that restore correct classification while staying equally far from training, ruling out unfamiliar textures as the cause of failure. The reverse-phi illusion similarly disrupts these representations and inverts the same low-level motion statistic as the adversarial textures. Optimizing this input statistic alone, without access to the network, suffices to induce classification failure, attributing both perturbations to the same circuit vulnerability. Connectome-constrained models can thus surface adversarial failure mechanisms as testable hypotheses about biological perceptual vulnerabilities.

items.title: RS-JEPA: Remote Sensing Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with Scan-Path Views for Cross-Sensor Image Retrieval
items.summary: Cross-sensor remote sensing image retrieval aims to find scenes with the same content across heterogeneous sensors, such as SAR and optical or panchromatic (PAN) and multispectral (MS) imagery, without manual labels. Existing self-supervised methods either reconstruct sensor-specific pixel detail, align each image only with its co-registered twin, or rely on large transformers with 118-173M parameters (and up to 398M). We introduce RS-JEPA, a compact joint-embedding predictive framework built on a Vision Mamba encoder shared by both sensors. Since a state-space encoder reads an image as an ordered sequence of patches, we propose scan-path views, which treat two reading orders of the same image as two views with identical pixels and predict the hidden patches in one order from the visible patches in the other.To keep this prediction challenging, we propose Adversarial View Coupling (AVC), which learns the hardest split of the visible patches, and a neighbourhood consensus loss that aligns the scene similarities of both sensors. Extensive experiments on SAR-optical (BEN-14K, CBRSIR-VS) and PAN-MS (DSRSID) benchmarks demonstrate that RS-JEPA achieves the highest F1@5 among twelve re-implemented methods (72.92, 80.35 and 94.43) with a retrieval network of only 3.88M parameters (14.57M in training, 8-16times fewer than prior JEPA retrievers). Like prior methods, RS-JEPA trains on co-registered pairs. Our results highlight reading order as a source of self-supervised views. code: https://github.com/Tanishq251/RSJEPA.

items.title: SkipLane: Write-Once, Conflict-Free Accumulation for Zero-Skipping CNN Engines on FPGAs
items.summary: Skipping zero activations saves multiplications in CNN accelerators, but it complicates accumulation: the products in a compressed input window belong to different output columns and must be merged. In our earlier engine, this merging was done by read-modify-write (RMW) of a row buffer, which made sparse inputs slower than dense ones even at 87% sparsity. Existing designs either merge kernel rows through RMW or reduce bank conflicts with extra hardware, without eliminating them. SkipLane makes the entire accumulation path write-once. Each kernel row is processed in its own lane, which holds partial sums in three registers and retires up to three finished columns per cycle into memory banks that cannot conflict. Lanes and input channels are summed only at readout, so no partial sum is ever read back. Multipliers left idle by zero weights compute a second filter in the same pass. In RTL simulation, the engine stays within 0.5% of its frontend bound up to 70% sparsity and is 1.10-1.26$\times$ faster than an SCNN-style scatter accumulator with 18 banks and ideal RMW at 50-80% sparsity. Six engines meet 140 MHz on a PYNQ-Z2 using 21.1k LUTs and run LeNet-5 bit-exact on the board. For conv1, the engine needs 1.94$\times$ fewer cycles than a dense engine (1.26$\times$ faster end to end); for conv2, whose rows are only 13 pixels wide, it reaches 0.87$\times$ the dense speed.

items.title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
items.summary: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation.

items.title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows
items.summary: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent's reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On $79$ procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach $93.8\%$ completion, against $96.8\%$ for the agent, at $24\%$ lower cost per task. On $τ^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent.

items.title: TimeSeek: Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Pretraining for Generalized Time Series Analytics
items.summary: Time series analytics has been widely applied across various domains. While existing time series foundation models (TSFMs) have demonstrated promising results, they still face two major challenges: 1) Most TSFMs mainly rely on stacking Transformer layers to increase parameter size, lacking the ability to adaptively model complex time series patterns from multi-domain data. 2) Current TSFMs are primarily pre-trained for specific tasks, e.g., forecasting or anomaly detection, and a few models support multiple tasks, but they fail to fully leverage task specificity and commonality, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we propose TimeSeek, a novel generalized time series analytics model that adaptively models time series patterns from multi-domain data and unifies multiple tasks in pre-training. Conceptually, TimeSeek is guided by selective information sharing under domain and task heterogeneity. From the perspective of multi-domain data, we propose a Multi-Domain Feature Extractor that adaptively captures temporal dependencies and channel correlations based on domain-specific characteristics, including progressive multi-scale modeling and adaptive slot channel modeling. From the perspective of the diversity of tasks, we propose multi-task collaborative training, which leverages task specificity and task commonality through task customization and cross-task training, effectively unifying multiple tasks in pre-training and better adapting to diverse downstream scenarios. After pre-training on large-scale time series data, TimeSeek achieves state-of-the-art performance in forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification tasks across both few-shot learning and zero-shot situations, together with favorable inference efficiency.

items.title: Second-Best Trade Is Half Efficient in Multidimensional Markets
items.summary: We prove that at least half of the first-best gains from trade can always be achieved in multidimensional two-sided markets with additive values and costs and arbitrary downward-closed feasibility constraints. The guarantee is achieved by a mechanism satisfying Bayesian incentive compatibility, interim individual rationality, and strong budget balance, and is tight already in single-item bilateral trade. Types are independent across agents, while the coordinates of each agent's type may be arbitrarily correlated. Feasibility constraints may couple trades across items and agents. This extends the known tight one-half guarantee for single-item bilateral trade. Our proof develops a new application of the Cai--Devanur--Weinberg duality framework. We show that the objective of every feasible dual is at least half of the first best. Strong duality then yields the guarantee without characterizing an optimal mechanism or dual. The key observation is that every feasible dual induces continuous-time Markov chains that, when stopped by exponential clocks, recover true types as expectations of virtual types. The dual constraints control the rate at which these chains change the prior distributions. We establish our bound by combining this control with a coupling of the agents' clocks.

items.title: Is Your Robot's Memory Just a Clock? Temporal Shortcuts in Memory-Augmented VLA Policies
items.summary: Memory-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policies are meant to remember what happened. Many of them, however, fill memory by time: they sample frames uniformly across the episode and stamp each frame with its time step. Because time passes even when nothing happens, such a memory may not tell waiting from working. We show that it does not. On the counting tasks of RoboMME, we make the robot briefly pause or fidget its wrist. Such a null event changes nothing the task depends on, yet a released memory VLA counts the interval as work done and stops early. We call this failure phantom progress. It cuts success from 47 to 16 of 50 on one task and from 44 to 10 on the other. When the same frames are withheld from memory, success returns, so the cause lies in memory rather than in the interruption itself. We trace the failure to a temporal shortcut: because demonstrations proceed at a steady pace, elapsed time predicts progress. Indeed, rescaling the time stamps alone makes the policy stop early when the clock runs fast and repeat when it runs slow. Surprisingly, removing the time encoding does not cure the failure, because the frames of a null event still occupy slots of the time-sampled memory. Across RoboMME's released designs, vulnerability follows how memory is indexed. Of the fixes the diagnosis suggests, training with injected pauses does not remove the failure and impairs counting, whereas indexing memory by events recovers half or more of the loss without retraining. A memory meant to remember what happened should count events rather than clock ticks.

items.title: Re-Search: Dissecting LLM Ideation Through a Two-Player Questioning Game
items.summary: Research ideation is iterative: researchers refine their ideas step by step based on feedback. Yet existing evaluations obscure this search process, making it difficult to understand how LLMs explore the space of research ideas and what limits their progress. We introduce Re-Search, which adapts the format of Twenty Questions to research ideation: given only the research problem of a published paper, a model must rediscover the paper's core idea by asking yes-or-no questions. Built from 200 ICML 2026 papers, Re-Search tracks how a model's idea evolves as it asks questions and receives binary oracle feedback, isolating ideation from execution. Across six recent LLMs, nearly all progress happens within the first 30 of 100 questions, which largely decide how the game ends; after that, most models plateau. Through controlled interventions on the candidate questions and the hypothesis space, we find that the bottleneck is generation, not judgment: models recognize a good idea or a good question when one is offered, but often cannot produce it on their own. We further analyze the ideation traces and find that models fail by either over-exploiting one direction or over-exploring too many. These findings point to concrete design principles for autoresearch systems: since models can judge candidates they cannot produce, enriching the search with externally sourced ideas and questions may be more effective than improving any single model's generation ability.

items.title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs a Logic of Inference
items.summary: Neural networks are increasingly studied not merely as predictive systems, but as complex systems whose internal computations are themselves objects of scientific inquiry. Recent progress in mechanistic interpretability (MI) has made it possible to identify neurons, features, circuits, population structures, and dynamical patterns associated with model behavior. As these tools improve, attention is shifting from what can be observed inside a model to how those observations support mechanistic explanations. We examine the parallel efforts of neuroscience and MI to address this question and identify recurring inferential bottlenecks when inferring mechanisms from complex neural systems. We propose five principles and organize them into a recursive logic for a more rigorous procedure of mechanistic inference. These principles provide a framework that supports scientific discovery in two senses: it helps turn local interpretability findings into cumulative knowledge of mechanisms within models, and it makes those mechanisms sufficiently precise to generate testable hypotheses about domains beyond the models. Evidence beyond MI is ultimately required to establish what model mechanisms reveal about the world.

items.title: Beyond the Mean Gap: What Transferred-Angle QAOA Retains on a Superconducting Processor
items.summary: Hardware executions of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) are often validated by comparing the device's mean cost with a simulation, a check that can miss what matters for optimization. Under global depolarization, the mean normalized gap and the floor-corrected probability of every set of bitstrings, the optimum included, retain the same fraction of their noiseless improvement over uniform sampling. We test this prediction with depth-2, transferred-angle QAOA circuits for binary subproblems of an alternating-direction decomposition on the IBM Heron processor \texttt{ibm\_marrakesh}, with and without dynamical decoupling and twirling. At 12 qubits, the main-family circuits retained 29\% to 46\% of their mean-gap improvement but only 5\% to 15\% of their probability of the optimum, lower on at least nine of ten instances per run. Near-optimal bitstrings were lost about as much as the optimum, whereas the avoidance of poor bitstrings was retained best. In the first submission, a device-matched noise model reproduced the pattern but overestimated the retention of the optimum five- to eightfold. On a rugged planted family, the device found the optimum in 62\% of 768-shot blocks (noiseless: 98\%), within the range of local heuristics. Validations of optimization circuits should report retention of the optimum and of near-optimal sets.

items.title: $A^2$: Smaller Self-Supervised ViTs Localize Better than Larger Ones
items.summary: Robust visual classification often depends on localizing the main foreground objects in an image while ignoring contextual distractors. Surprisingly, we find that the last layer attention maps of smaller self-supervised ViTs localize foreground objects better than those of larger ViTs. However, we still need large ViTs, because they extract richer representations from each patch. To get the best of both worlds, good localization and rich representations, we propose $A^2$, a simple method that leverages this inverse scaling finding by decoupling where to look (a small attention model) from what to extract (a large embedding model): we crop around the attention peaks of a small model and embed the crops with a larger model. $A^2$ uses entirely pretrained features, requires no group labels, and does not require per-dataset attention or backbone training. Across 5 benchmarks, $A^2$ is competitive with backbone-matched loss-level methods like DFR, and outperforms end-to-end attention training under stronger distribution shifts.

items.title: Pterodactyl: Pushing the Limits of Efficient Automated Translation Evaluation
items.summary: In this paper, we present 1020 Group's submission to the WMT26 shared task on automated quality evaluation. Our system, Pterodactyl, was engineered specifically for subtasks 2 and 3, that is, segment-level quality score prediction and the detection of error-free segments. Pterodactyl is a highly customizable, ultra-low cost system optimized for binary classification in translation triage and data curation. It is based on an LLM-as-a-judge approach, with prompt engineering and model selection guided by ROC analysis. We also developed several variants of Pterodactyl that were specifically adapted for subtasks 3.

items.title: FERN: Cross-Benchmark Table Retrieval for Text-to-SQL with Frozen Retrievers and Learned Ranking
items.summary: Text-to-SQL systems over large pooled catalogs must first retrieve the tables a question needs. We compare against the published table recall of RASL, which uses Claude 3.5 models to extract keywords and select tables, on pooled BIRD, Spider, and Fiben catalogs. FERN (Feature-Engineered Ranking with No generative LLM) instead fuses three frozen retrievers into 100 candidates, describes each with up to 120 features, and reorders them with LightGBM rankers fitted once on BIRD's training questions. On Spider, where it was not fitted, its candidate pool alone reaches RASL's published recall at fifteen tables (98.0), and the ranker raises the share of questions with every gold table in the top five (complete@5) from 83.9% to 95.6%. At five tables, FERN's recall is within one point of RASL's on Spider (96.7 vs 97.0) and on BIRD with its evidence hints (96.6 vs 97.5), and 8.2 points below on BIRD without them (89.3). On 121 real BEAVER questions, without BEAVER fitting, its recall at fifteen (82.1) falls between two BEAVER-trained retrievers (80.8, 84.5), but its complete@15 is below both (49.6 vs 54.5 and 62.0). On Fiben, it falls far short at fifteen tables (54.2 vs 69.2, different question sets), although its recall at fifty is numerically close to RASL's question-only retrieval result (80.7 vs 79.4). On BIRD dev with evidence, non-retrieval features raise complete@5 by 7.7 points over retrieval signals alone. On BIRD dev, median latency is 208 ms per question on one A100, without hosted model calls.

items.title: BoviShift: A Six-Year Multi-Attribute Audit of Visual Cattle Phenotyping Across Animals and Time
items.summary: Computer vision offers a scalable, non-contact means of estimating livestock traits, but correlated images and video frames make reliable evaluation difficult. Image-random splitting can place views of the same animal in both training and test sets, while deployment further requires transfer to animals captured in future years. We introduce BoviShift, a corpus reconstructed from six consecutive annual cohorts of an operational cattle marketplace collected from 2021 to 2026. It contains 2{,}657 cattle, 10{,}610 still images, and 2{,}566 walk-around videos across nine recorded breed categories. We evaluate three splitting strategies through four configurations: image-random and pooled cattle-disjoint splits over the same development cohorts, followed by separate future-2025 and locked future-2026 evaluations. Using a fixed ResNet-50 multi-task baseline, we assess weight, age, height, breed, and coat color. Differences between image-random and cattle-disjoint splitting are task-dependent rather than a universal leakage penalty. Future-cohort behavior is also attribute- and cohort-specific: breed declines relative to pooled evaluation; mean weight and age performance fails to beat constant baselines in 2025; height remains above baseline; and color transfers well to 2025 but degrades in 2026. Multi-task training improves all five point estimates in a single-seed ablation, still-view aggregation helps selectively, and zero-shot video-frame aggregation exposes a still-to-video domain gap. To our knowledge, BoviShift is the longest-spanning cattle-vision resource combining consecutive annual cohorts with physical and visual attributes.

items.title: Learning to Reason from Reference Samples Alone: Reinforced Adversarial Learning for Modern LLM Post-Training
items.summary: In many settings where LLM post-training is desirable, high-quality answers are recognizable but difficult to score with explicit rewards. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is limited to tasks where an explicit correctness signal is available.
