The asymptotic prediction optimality of the REML-guided early stopping time is established for fixed-design in-sample risk and random-design out-of-sample risk. Deep learning models in fixed-kernel gradient regimes provide canonical instantiations for our results. Numerical experiments and a UK Biobank proteomics application show competitive accuracy of the REML-guided early stopping time with reduced reliance on validation splits and repeated checkpoint evaluation.

items.title: Optimal Radial Weighting for Robust Mutual Fund Selection
items.summary: Identifying skilled mutual funds requires methods that distinguish positive alphas from sampling variation when many funds are evaluated simultaneously. Heavy-tailed returns and dependence across funds complicate this task. We propose a robust selection procedure based on radially weighted alpha estimation in linear factor pricing models. The method uses both the directions and lengths of standardized residuals, estimates marginal scales from pairwise residual differences, and accounts for the estimation of factor loadings. Within the proposed class, inverse-norm weighting minimizes the asymptotic variance of the alpha estimators and maximizes the local asymptotic power of individual tests at a common significance level. For radial weights fixed conditional on the factor design, we establish asymptotic false discovery rate control under elliptically symmetric errors and show that the proportion of sufficiently strong positive-alpha funds selected tends to one. The theory accommodates comparable cross-sectional and time-series dimensions and nonvanishing alphas. We also develop a smoothed implementation and assess its finite-sample properties. Simulations show higher true discovery proportions than least-squares and spatial-sign methods under heavy-tailed distributions and improved numerical stability from smoothing. An application to U.S. equity mutual funds examines the subsequent performance of portfolios formed from the selected funds.

items.title: Breaking the $\sqrt{d}$ Communication Barrier in Federated Sampling with Adaptive Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
items.summary: This work proposes the Adaptive Federated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (AFHMC) for Bayesian federated learning (FL) tasks. The prior work on HMC applications for FL achieves $O(\sqrt{d}/ε)$ communication cost under log-convex distributions, already demonstrating its advantage over the Langevin dynamic-based counterpart. Based on a refined analysis, this paper further reveals the benefit of HMC for the FL regime by incorporating a control mechanism for local node shifts. We prove that AFHMC at most requires $O(\{d/ε^2\}^{1/3})$ communication cost up to a logarithmic term, which is significantly better than the existing results. Moreover, the proposed method adapts to client heterogeneity. Under low-heterogeneity settings (i.e., the target sampling precision $ε^2$ is higher than the heterogeneity level), the communication rate of AFHMC can be as good as $O(\log(d/ε^2))$, resembling the communication costs for FL optimization tools. To the best of our knowledge, this provides the first logarithmic communication complexity result for federated sampling, even though it requires low heterogeneity. Numerically, we also justify AFHMC's advantage under the low-heterogeneity regime. Our code is available at https://github.com/laaaarrywang/Adaptive-Federated-HMC

items.title: A Review of Measurement System Uncertainty Handoffs Across the Manufacturing Decision Lifecycle
items.summary: Measurement systems generate uncertain information that downstream manufacturing decisions often consume as if fixed. This structured integrative review examines how measurement error, uncertainty, GR\&R estimates, calibration evidence, and drift information are handed off into capability inference, retrospective Phase I reference estimation, prospective Phase II monitoring, operational action, and requalification. Studies are compared by the upstream uncertain object, whether it is known, calibrated, or estimated, its propagation mechanism, the downstream decision, and the validation boundary. The synthesis distinguishes recorded production data from latent-process targets: measurement-system information calibrates limits, uncertainty statements, replication, guard bands, or losses, but does not reveal the realized random error in an individual record. Within the retained literature, measurement-to-capability and measurement-to-monitoring mechanisms are more extensively represented by model-based studies, whereas prospective evidence is thinner where statistical results must support source attribution, cost-sensitive action, and requalification. A decision-handoff spine separates measurement generation, statistical inference, and operational validation so that capability, stability, attribution, and intervention effectiveness are not conflated. The review is integrative rather than exhaustive. Its contribution is an auditable measurement-science framework that preserves provenance, information status, validity conditions, and downstream use while identifying claims that are model-supported, conditionally calibrated, or not yet operationally validated.

items.title: Can the Remaining Answers Change the Prediction? Worst-Case Stability Checks for Personalized Rating Models
items.summary: Missing ratings can overturn a personalized model's current prediction. For completed models with additive response scores, exact worst case bounds check all missing assignments without changing the current predictor. We evaluate this audit retrospectively in two self-triage cohorts, 108 clinicians rating three simulated psychiatric interviews, and 126 counseling demonstrations annotated by ten experts. Under shared random half histories, Fisher adaptation based on observed ratings reduces log loss relative to response frequency by 0.1071 nats in the clinician audit (95% CI [0.0867,0.1261]) and 0.0223 in counseling (95% CI[0.0121,0.0321]). The counseling test excludes target experts and source videos from training. Certification covers 5.4% and 10.5% of targets; fixed width acquisition raises coverage to 13.7% and 28.6% at the same budgets. With weights and responses held fixed, the observed-rating update also has lower loss than an affine partial update while certifying exactly the same evaluated targets. The certificate establishes agreement with the completed model, not correctness or stability at intermediate updates. These rating tasks test the method; clinical usefulness remains untested.

items.title: MML Probabilistic Principal Component Analysis
items.summary: Principal component analysis (PCA) is perhaps the most widely used method for data dimensionality reduction. A key question in PCA is deciding how many components to retain. This manuscript describes a new approach to automatically selecting the number of principal components based on the Bayesian minimum message length method of inductive inference. We derive new estimates of the isotropic residual variance and loadings, and establish their bias and asymptotic distributions. For moderate latent dimensions, the residual variance estimate improves on maximum likelihood, and the implied eigenvalue shrinkage approaches the Stein-optimal shrinkage for strong signals.

items.title: The Dark Matter of Clinical Data: An Identification Limit on Disentangling Physiology from Care Process in electronic health records
items.summary: Representations learned from electronic health record (EHR) data encode patient physiology together with the clinical process that decides what is measured, when, and for whom. We formalize the data-generating process with latent physiology, ordering intent, laboratory values that exist only when measured, a learned representation, and clinical environments, and analyze two strategies for undoing this entanglement. First, no division of the information carried by laboratory "value" and "ordering" channels is identified from a single dataset: when ordering depends on the analyte, its distribution among untested patients is not recoverable, and a sentinel code for the undefined recorded value makes it carry all the entropy of the ordering indicator, fixing partial information decomposition (PID) for every redundancy measure satisfying the Williams-Beer axioms and invariant under injective re-encoding. Second, cross-site invariance of representation-conditional outcomes is a falsifiable implication of biological invariance taken jointly with exclusion and representation-sufficiency conditions, but not an identification strategy: we construct observationally equivalent models that disagree about biological invariance, whether the invariance test fails or passes. For binary physiology this happens exactly when case mix differs, the representation is lossy, and physiology affects the outcome. A worked example yields a 9.6-percentage-point cross-site gap under an unchanged biological mechanism. Tests performed for every patient remove the ordering gate, and measured tests can restore identification: biological invariance is identified when a test exactly summarizes outcome-relevant physiology, or, for binary physiology, when two tests with independent errors are available at sites with different case mix. Cross-site analyses should be reported as tests of a stated joint hypothesis.

items.title: Informed Posterior Sampling: More Efficient Online Learning with Few Offline Demonstrations in Average-Reward MDPs
items.summary: We study efficient online reinforcement learning in the infinite horizon setting when there is an offline dataset to start with. We assume that the offline dataset is generated by an expert but with an unknown level of competence, i.e., it is not perfect and not necessarily using the optimal policy. We show that if the learning agent models the behavioral policy (parameterized by a competence parameter) used by the expert, it can do substantially better in terms of minimizing cumulative regret than if it does not do that. We establish an upper bound on regret of the exact informed PSRL (iPSRL) algorithm that scales as $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$. This requires a novel prior-dependent regret analysis of Bayesian online learning algorithms for the infinite horizon setting. We then propose the informed RLSVI (iRLSVI) algorithm to efficiently approximate the iPSRL algorithm. Empirical results show that small offline expert datasets are sufficient for iRLSVI to outperform online-only algorithms on hard exploration domains.

items.title: A lift for input-convex neural net training
items.summary: Input-convex neural nets parametrize the convex potentials of density models and transport maps, and their convexity requires the inter-layer weights to be non-negative. Projected gradient descent enforces this by projecting after each step, and due to mini-batch noise the boundary is re-crossed indefinitely, which leads to an active set the projection never identifies. The differentiable alternative, direct softplus, optimizes a free latent weight through a softplus positivity map. Where that latent weight is well below zero, the derivative of the map is exponentially small and scales down both the gradient and its noise. We call this region the shoulder, and a weight that reaches it therefore barely moves and stays for an exponentially long time. We propose the lift, which replaces the free latent weight by a learnable slack plus the output of a hypernetwork that reads a permutation-invariant summary of the training batch. The latent weight then varies with the same batch that forms the gradient, so the two are coupled. We show that this coupling adds a term to the variance of the update at first order, and that the slack, the batch dependence, and the shared batch are each needed for it. Where the coupling aligns positively with the loss curvature, a weight on the shoulder crosses the barriers of the loss sooner under the lift than under direct softplus, also under preconditioned stochastic gradient descent. We compare the lift with the two existing methods on several applications. Where a constrained weight of direct softplus reaches the shoulder, the lift fits the target more closely than direct softplus and reaches the same reconstruction about three times sooner. Where almost none reaches it, the methods agree.

items.title: Invariant Image Reparameterisation: Bridging Symbolic and Numerical Methods for Identifiability Analysis, Model Reduction, and Prediction
items.summary: Structural and practical parameter non-identifiability issues are common when mathematical models are used to interpret data. Such issues motivate model reparameterisation and reduction methods. Here, we consider Invariant Image Reparameterisation (IIR), which asks when symbolic reparameterisation conditions can be replaced by numerical derivative calculations at a single reference point. The central object is the invariant image: a reduced, basis-independent representation of the parameter combinations controlling observable model behaviour. We show that when a one-to-one componentwise transformation makes observable behaviour depend only on fixed linear combinations of the transformed parameters, a single numerical Jacobian determines the associated lower-dimensional reparameterisation space. This includes models depending on monomial combinations of the original parameters. We also give a first-order invariance condition that can rule out a minimal reduction of this form and extracts candidate invariant null directions for an exact non-minimal reduction. In structurally identifiable but practically weakly informed settings, the same calculations separate strongly and weakly informed parameter combinations. The invariant image admits multiple coordinate representations: the SVD gives a default orthonormal basis ordered by local identifiability, while sparse monomial bases are often more interpretable. Treating these coordinates as interest parameters in Profile-Wise Analysis gives likelihood-based uncertainty quantification and prediction. We demonstrate the method on parameterised normal models with Poisson-limit, extended Poisson-limit, and non-limit cases, and on the repressilator, a nonlinear differential equation model of gene regulation. A Julia implementation of IIR, with these and further examples, is available at https://github.com/omaclaren/reparam.

items.title: Comparing randomized trials: a formal approach
items.summary: Disagreements between randomized trials that address the same causal question pose challenges for the interpretation and synthesis of evidence. We sketch a causal framework for comparing the results of randomized trials that explicitly accommodates the possibility of trial engagement effects. Using counterfactual outcomes defined under joint interventions on treatment assignment and trial-related actions, we compare trial-native treatment effects with the effects transported from one trial to the population of another in a common target population. We show that standard conditions for transporting treatment effects across trial populations are not sufficient to guarantee agreement between transported and trial-native effects. Agreement additionally requires conditions governing how trial-related actions affect outcome across studies - for example, absence of trial engagement effects, equivalence of such effects across trials, or lack of interaction between trial engagement and treatment assignment. Our framework clarifies potential sources of disagreement across trials and extends existing approaches to study comparison to settings in which trial engagement effects may be present.

items.title: ATHOS: Agreement-based Testing of Hypotheses in Overlapping Subgroups
items.summary: We study confirmation of treatment benefit in a prespecified family of overlapping subgroups of a randomized trial. Maximum-statistic procedures exploit the correlation between subgroups' statistics, but calibration decides what they protect. Re-randomization controls error exactly when treatment has no effect, but not when only an average effect is zero, whereas a multiplier bootstrap protects average effects only asymptotically. Our first result characterizes when re-randomization alone protects average effects. It reverses the arms' weights in the statistics' covariance, so with unequal allocation and heterogeneous effects it can overstate their correlations; in one such family of 50 subgroups, its limiting familywise error is 0.064 at nominal 0.025. We propose a step-down procedure called ATHOS, short for agreement-based testing of hypotheses in overlapping subgroups, which confirms a subgroup only when both calibrations reject it. Given assignments exchangeable within strata, ATHOS controls familywise error exactly when treatment has no effect and, under complete randomization, asymptotically for average effects, even in large families. Our second result shows that requiring agreement costs no first-order local power in balanced trials. In a null simulation with 200 patients and 1,497 subgroups, the bootstrap step-down alone made false claims in 40% of trials and ATHOS in 2.6%. In two comparisons in an HIV trial, ATHOS confirmed 188 and 73 subgroups and Holm's procedure 179 and 62.

items.title: Query- and Candidate-Aware Long User Sequence Modeling for Sponsored Product Ranking in Search
items.summary: User sequence modeling is widely used in recommendation and advertising. Search ranking presents an additional challenge: the current query expresses immediate intent, while a candidate product determines which parts of a user's long-term history are relevant. We present a production sequence framework for sponsored-product ranking that augments recent behavior with two retrieval channels over long-term history: candidate-nearest-neighbor retrieval and query-nearest-neighbor retrieval. The selected actions are encoded together with dedicated query and candidate context tokens, while candidate-aware early fusion injects the candidate into every history token. Offline ablations show that dual retrieval improves major ranking metrics relative to the production baseline. In an online A/B test on sponsored-product search traffic, the model increased CTR, attributed conversion rate, and orders per impression.

items.title: Nonasymptotic causal structure learning in generalized linear DAGs with continuous optimization
items.summary: We study the problem of learning directed acyclic graphs from observational data in nonlinear models and provide finite-sample, nonasymptotic statistical guarantees in these models. Although widely studied, statistical guarantees for gradient-based methods in nonlinear models are missing from the literature. Under a generalized linear model for each node, we analyze a global nonsmooth objective combining an exact acyclicity constraint with a quasi-minimax concave penalty, which can be optimized via standard gradient-based solvers. We establish finite-sample guarantees under this model, including the most widely used logistic and Poisson models. Experiments corroborate structure recovery accuracy and computational performance, including both standardized data and negative controls as baselines.

items.title: A Trust Region Approach for Learning Schrödinger Bridges
items.summary: We study the numerical approximation of Schrödinger Bridges in the setting where samples from the target distribution are unavailable and only an unnormalized target density is given. In this regime, the widely used iterative proportional fitting (IPF) procedure (and its variants) often exhibits severe numerical instabilities, stemming from ill-conditioned underlying control problems and from the fact that the optimal solution may lie far from the initialization. To address these issues, we propose a trust region variant of IPF that constrains successive updates to remain at a fixed Kullback-Leibler divergence from the current iterate. This restriction significantly improves numerical stability. Moreover, we show that the resulting method admits an interpretation as a mirror descent scheme with an adaptively chosen step size. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several challenging sampling tasks.

items.title: Nearest-Neighbor Radii under Dependent Sampling
items.summary: Nearest-neighbor methods are fundamental to classical and modern machine learning, yet their geometric properties are typically analyzed under independent sampling. In this paper, we study the nearest-neighbor radii under dependent sampling. We consider strong mixing dependent observations and ask whether dependence changes the scale of nearest-neighbor neighborhoods. We establish distribution-free almost sure convergence under polynomial mixing and sharp non-asymptotic moment bounds under geometric mixing. The moment bounds depend on the local intrinsic dimension rather than the ambient dimension, making the results applicable to high-dimensional data supported on lower-dimensional manifolds. Synthetic experiments and real-world time-series benchmarks illustrate the theory, showing that nearest-neighbor geometry remains informative under dependent sampling.

items.title: The optimal information complexity of VC learning
items.summary: Steinke and Zakynthinou(2020) introduces the Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) framework of analyzing the information complexity of learning algorithms based on algorithm-dependent information-theoretic quantities. We study one of these quantities, the evaluated Conditional Mutual Information (eCMI). It has been an interesting question whether the optimal PAC guarantee for VC classes can be recovered from the algorithm-dependent analyses via CMI. And we show that it is possible to recover this guarantee by constructing a learning algorithm whose eCMI is of order O(d) in the realizable case, where d is the VC-dimension of the concept class. Specially, our algorithm is a randomized Majority-of-5 base learners with optimal in-expectation generalization guarantee.

items.title: Graph Fourier Neural Kernels: Learning Full PDE Trajectories Across Geometries and Anisotropic Parameter Fields
items.summary: High-fidelity simulations of time-dependent nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) are expensive to repeat across families of domains and parameter fields, a cost that recurs in design optimization, uncertainty quantification, and computational medicine. Most neural-operator surrogates require each domain to be mapped onto a common grid or reference shape, and few predict the full time course. We introduce Graph Fourier Neural Kernels (G-FuNK), a neural operator for second-order semilinear PDEs with a diffusive principal part that transfers across geometries and anisotropic diffusion tensors without coordinate maps or diffeomorphisms. A weighted graph and its Laplacian supply a spectral basis that encodes geometry and anisotropy. Shared layers act in this basis, at a cost linear in mesh size after one partial eigendecomposition per geometry, and a neural ODE integrator propagates the learned generator to full spatiotemporal trajectories on unseen domains. Across anisotropic heat flow, stiff reaction-diffusion, FitzHugh-Nagumo, and patient-specific left-atrial electrophysiology on CT-derived surfaces, G-FuNK reproduces held-out trajectories with relative $L^2$ error between 0.046 and 0.160. Its accuracy is comparable to that of a geometry-aware Fourier neural operator on regular domains, and its predictions are unchanged when a rectangular domain is rotated. On left atria, whose venous and valvular openings prevent mapping onto a reference shape, it predicts an 85-ms trajectory in under half a second, against about 5 minutes for finite elements, with a mean activation-time error of 1.73 ms. Accuracy depends on graph construction and is highest when the learned generator is integrated at its training time step.

items.title: Robust Gaussian process regression: posterior contraction
items.summary: Gaussian processes form a popular and flexible class of prior distributions with principled uncertainty quantification, but the Gaussian likelihood on which the corresponding posterior relies makes them highly sensitive to outliers and contaminated observations. We study Gaussian process regression when among the $n$ observations, $m$ of these are possibly contaminated. A generic framework to obtain posterior contraction rates in this setting is considered, from a frequentist perspective as the sample size $n$ and the number of corrupted observations $m$ grow. We adopt a generalized Bayes approach in which the log--likelihood is replaced by a robustified version; we discuss various choices thereof, such as one recently proposed by Altamirano et al. that preserves conjugacy. We investigate the minimax rate of estimation under adversarial contamination in terms of the Sobolev smoothness $β$ of the regression function and $m$. The question of building adaptive procedures to both $β$ and $m$ is investigated, and we show that a polynomial loss for adaptation must be paid in general. We instantiate our results for Matérn Gaussian process and deep ReLU network priors. Numerical experiments for existing and new robust algorithms are provided, illustrating the practical applicability of our results.

items.title: Attention as In-Context Empirical Bayes: A Two-Stage View via Particle Dynamics
items.summary: We study minimal attention-only transformers under all-token corruption and show they admit a two-stage empirical Bayes interpretation. A single attention step computes a kernel-weighted posterior mean with respect to the empirical distribution defined by the context. Depth refines this distribution through particle dynamics (Stage 1), while a long-range skip-connection carries the noisy input as a query for posterior inference (Stage 2), revealing distinct statistical roles for depth and attention residuals. The framework isolates a minimal setting in which the context itself induces a depth-dependent energy landscape governing in-context inference. We show that effective denoising can emerge without an explicit noise schedule: a fixed kernel bandwidth and finite integration horizon suffice, yielding a principled depth-noise relationship. We further establish a posterior-mean recovery guarantee for Gaussian priors, showing the empirical estimator converges to the Bayes-optimal predictor under sequential asymptotic conditions. Connecting these dynamics to reverse-diffusion limits, our results provide a statistical interpretation of attention as in-context inference via sample-based posterior estimation, without explicit density modeling.

items.title: Toward a Unified Statistical Theory of Multi-View Pretraining for Neural Knowledge Graph Learning
items.summary: Knowledge graph learning offers a powerful framework for representing and inferring structured knowledge, with broad practical applications. Two obstacles limit current methods: labeled triples are scarce for each entity and relation, which makes expressive models hard to train, and scoring functions are designed ad hoc, which limits their generalizability and leaves them without theoretical grounding. We address both obstacles with a theoretically grounded framework, with end-to-end guarantees, that extends and subsumes existing methods. The framework proceeds in two stages: multi-view unsupervised pretraining that integrates heterogeneous sources of entity side information into a shared representation, followed by supervised learning across multiple relation types. We establish a unified nonasymptotic risk bound that combines the subspace recovery error of pretraining and the sample complexity of the labeled data in a single guarantee, quantifying formally how large-scale unlabeled data from multiple views benefits downstream knowledge prediction. Synthetic experiments validate each component of the theory, and experiments on large-scale real-world knowledge graph benchmarks confirm the effectiveness of our approach.

items.title: Express Language Modeling
items.summary: We introduce a new tool, Express, for converting a non-causal attention approximation into a causal approximation with matching approximation guarantees. When combined with the state-of-the-art Thinformer approximation, Express improves upon the best known causal attention guarantees, delivering $\log^{3/2}(n)/s$ approximation error with only $O(s)$ memory and $O(s^2 \log^2(n))$ compression overhead for a sequence of length $n$. We pair these developments with an efficient I/O-aware Triton implementation, demonstrate substantial speedups over FlashAttention 2, and use Express to overcome four resource bottlenecks in the language modeling pipeline: long-context prefill, KV cache compression, long-form memory-constrained decoding, and long-form compute-constrained decoding.

items.title: Addressing Bias Early in the AI Lifecycle: Social Determinants of Health in Functional and Cognitive Assessment Labels of Nursing Home Residents
items.summary: Fairness in clinical artificial intelligence (AI) is usually evaluated after model training, yet bias can enter earlier in the AI lifecycle, during data collection and labelling. When routine clinical assessments serve as target variables, systematic differences in these labels across sociodemographic groups are carried into model development, validation and updating. This study addresses this early lifecycle stage by auditing labels from three standardised instruments used in residential care: the Barthel Index (BI), the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and the Global Deterioration Scale (GDS). Using electronic health records of 2,407 residents from 12 nursing homes in the Basque Country, Spain (2011-2021), we assessed four social determinants of health (SDoH) - sex, educational attainment, lifetime work activity and marital status - with two group fairness metrics, Disparate Impact (DI) and Statistical Parity Difference (SPD), computed for each outcome category with bootstrap confidence intervals. Disparities were found for all four attributes and across the three instruments: men, residents with intermediate education and never-partnered residents were more frequently classified in categories indicating preserved function or cognition. These disparities may reflect genuine differences in health status, measurement properties of the instruments, assessment practices or selective admission to residential care, and cannot be attributed to a single cause with the present design. Regardless of their origin, any model trained on these labels would inherit them, and they could persist through later lifecycle stages unless explicitly examined. These findings support pre-training label auditing as the first step of a continuous fairness assessment spanning model development, validation, deployment and updating.
authors: Miguel A. Armengol de la Hoz

items.title: A Stability Analysis of AdamW: Unstable Equilibria and Non-Convergence
items.summary: AdamW is ubiquitous in deep learning, yet its behavior remains poorly understood. We analyze its dynamics through the lens of dynamical systems and show that AdamW admits an implicit fixed-point objective: its fixed points coincide with the stationary points of a constrained and regularized optimization problem. However, not all of these fixed points are stable under AdamW's dynamics, and stability depends sensitively on curvature, weight decay, and momentum parameters. Even in one-dimensional settings, equilibria may be unstable, and trajectories can exhibit persistent oscillations rather than convergence to them. We further extend the analysis to higher dimensions, deriving sufficient conditions for local stability of the continuous-time dynamics, and propose a convergent modification that preserves AdamW's fixed points. These results clarify what optimization problem AdamW is associated with, when its convergence can be expected, and how its dynamics could inspire more reliable optimizers.

items.title: Personalized Pricing with Invalid Instrumental Variables: Identification, Estimation, and Policy Learning
items.summary: Pricing based on individual customer characteristics is widely used to maximize sellers' revenues. We study how a firm can learn such a personalized pricing policy from historical transactions when unobserved factors affect both the prices it charged and the revenue it earned. Standard instrumental variable (IV) methods either focus on a discrete treatment space or require that the IV affect revenue only through price. This exclusion restriction is difficult to justify in pricing, where the most natural candidate IVs are price-setting levers that may also affect revenue directly. We propose PRINT (Personalized pRicing using Invalid iNsTrumental variables), a policy learning method for continuous prices that uses such candidate IVs. Relying on structural models of revenue and price, we show that the optimal pricing policy can be identified with invalid IV that shifts higher moments of historical prices, when the unobserved factors that drive customers' price sensitivity are separated from those used by the historical pricing rule. Based on this identification, which leads to conditional moment restrictions with generalized residual functions, we construct an adversarial min-max estimator that accommodates flexible machine learning models and establish regret bounds for the learned pricing policy. Simulation studies and an application to a U.S. online auto lender illustrate the method's performance. Our results give a principled way to learn personalized prices from observational data using imperfect price-setting levers, and clarify when doing so is justified.

items.title: Amortized Bayesian Experimental Design with In-Context Knowledge Conditioning
items.summary: Amortized Bayesian experimental design (BED) enables real-time design strategies by shifting acquisition cost offline, but existing methods remain tied to the prior and task distribution they were trained on and cannot exploit additional information available at deployment. We introduce in-context amortized BED with unified knowledge encoding (IMBUE), a BED framework that admits external knowledge at deployment through a unified in-context interface. IMBUE accepts two forms of such knowledge without retraining, namely user-specified prior knowledge and observations from previous instances of the experiment. Both are encoded as additional input tokens and processed in-context with the accumulated observations by a shared Transformer, and a learned reliability filter scores each external token against the observations and excludes inconsistent ones. Across four benchmarks, IMBUE accelerates early-stage information acquisition when the external knowledge is reliable, and remains close to the no-external baseline when it is not.

items.title: A Workflow for Lipid Nanoparticle (LNP) Formulation Optimization Using Designed Mixture-Process Experiments and Self-Validated Ensemble Models (SVEM)
items.summary: We present a Quality by Design (QbD) styled approach for optimizing lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulations, aiming to offer scientists an accessible workflow. The inherent restriction in these studies, where the molar ratios of ionizable, helper, and PEG lipids must add up to 100%, requires specialized design and analysis methods to accommodate this mixture constraint. Focusing on lipid and process factors that are commonly used in LNP design optimization, we provide steps that avoid many of the difficulties that traditionally arise in the design and analysis of mixture-process experiments by employing space-filling designs and utilizing the recently developed statistical framework of self-validated ensemble models (SVEM). In addition to producing candidate optimal formulations, the workflow also builds graphical summaries of the fitted statistical models that simplify the interpretation of the results. The newly identified candidate formulations are assessed with confirmation runs and optionally can be conducted in the context of a more comprehensive second-phase study.

items.title: Multilevel and Sequential Monte Carlo for Training-Free Diffusion Guidance
items.summary: We address the problem of accurate, training-free guidance for conditional generation in trained diffusion models. Existing methods typically rely on point-estimates to approximate the posterior score, often resulting in biased approximations that fail to capture multimodality inherent to the reverse process of diffusion models. We propose a sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) framework that integrates over the full denoising distribution to construct an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of $p_θ(y\mid x_t)$, avoiding the bias of existing training-free guidance methods. To ensure computational tractability, we incorporate variance-reduction schemes based on MultiLevel Monte Carlo (MLMC). We evaluate on three image generation tasks. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet classifier guidance, our approach improves accuracy by 18 and 38 points respectively over the strongest training-free baseline. On CelebA-HQ joint-attribute guidance, three existing methods (DPS, LGD, TFG) used within our framework all outperform the closest SMC-based comparator (TDS) by 25-37 points, and improve over the strongest baseline by 2-14 points.

items.title: On the Burden of Achieving Fairness in Conformal Prediction
items.summary: Conformal prediction is often calibrated with a single pooled threshold, but this can hide cross-group heterogeneity in score distributions and distort group-wise coverage. We study this phenomenon through the population score distributions underlying split conformal calibration. First, we derive a conservation law and lower bound showing that pooled calibration incurs irreducible group-wise coverage distortion at a scale set by cross-group quantile heterogeneity. Second, we demonstrate that the two leading fairness definitions for conformal prediction, Equalized Coverage and Equalized Set Size, are fundamentally in tension. Third, we quantify the cost of moving between policies which treat groups separately or pool them. Experiments on synthetic and real data confirm the same bidirectional trade-off after finite-sample calibration. Our results show that, for the policy families studied here, calibration choice does not remove cross-group heterogeneity; it determines whether the resulting distortion appears in the coverage or size dimension, providing a principled lens for analyzing fairness-oriented calibration choices in practice.

items.title: A Bayesian approach to the survivor average causal effect in cluster-randomized crossover trials
items.summary: In cluster-randomized crossover (CRXO) trials, groups of individuals are randomly assigned to one of two or more sequences of alternating treatments. Since clusters serve as their own control, the CRXO design is typically more statistically efficient than the usual parallel-arm design. CRXO trials are increasingly popular in many areas of health research where the number of available clusters is limited. Further, in trials among severely ill patients, researchers often want to assess the effect of treatments on secondary non-terminal outcomes, but frequently in these studies, there are patients who do not survive to have these measurements fully recorded. In this paper, we provide a causal inference framework and treatment effect estimation method for addressing truncation by death in the setting of CRXO trials. We target the survivor average causal effect (SACE) estimand, a well-defined subgroup treatment effect obtained via principal stratification. We propose causal structural assumptions and standard parametric modeling assumptions that together enable estimating the SACE within a Bayesian paradigm. We evaluate the small-sample performance of our proposed Bayesian approach for estimation of the SACE in CRXO trial settings via simulation studies. We apply our method to a previously conducted two-period cross-sectional CRXO study examining the impact of proton pump inhibitors compared to histamine-2 receptor blockers on length of hospitalization among adults requiring invasive mechanical ventilation.

items.title: Graph-regularized synthetic control for spatial panels with post-only treated locations
items.summary: Spatial policy panels can contain treated locations that are observed only after an intervention and therefore have no pre-treatment outcome history. Without a pre-treatment trajectory to match, choosing donor weights for such post-only locations requires an additional source of information. We propose Graph-SCM, which estimates donor weights jointly across treated locations and encourages geographically neighboring locations to use similar donor combinations. GeoEco-SCM keeps the same geographic graph but adjusts the strength of its existing edges using pre-treatment economic similarity. Both methods handle complete, partial, and absent histories within one convex weight-estimation problem. Monte Carlo experiments compare them with covariate-balanced synthetic controls, equally weighted donor averages, ordinary synthetic control where estimable, and nonseparable spatio-temporal imputation and direct prediction. No method dominates. Graph-based borrowing improves on covariate balancing in several settings, but a selective-coverage design favors covariate balancing. Economic adjustment helps when geography alone misses relevant donor relationships. The results support graph regularization as a way to extend synthetic-control coverage when connected locations share similar donor representations, with its usefulness depending on the structure of the available information.

items.title: Learning through Capacity Awareness to Minimize Hospital Readmissions
items.summary: Predictive algorithms are increasingly used to guide hospital discharge decisions, yet these models can exhibit censoring bias for vulnerable patients due to insufficient historical data or past discharge decisions. When biased readmission risk predictors are used to inform discharges, the training data generated by discharge decisions may perpetuate similar biases when predictors are re-trained, leading to a vicious cycle. We extend a queueing-based Markov decision process for hospital discharge to incorporate periodically retrained readmission risk predictors. Our key insight is that cost-optimal, "capacity-aware" operational decision policies can naturally diversify the lengths of stay at which patient outcomes are observed, enabling consistent estimation of readmission risk without explicit fairness constraints. We prove that repeated retraining under discharge-up-to policies converges to unbiased risk estimates under well-specification. In synthetic experiments and calibrated simulations based on patient-level data from a partner hospital, we find that where commonly used threshold-on-risk policies can remain persistently biased, discharge-up-to policies reduce learning error over status quo decision policies (such as thresholding on risk) by 24%-25%. These improvements to estimation also mitigate some forms of bias, reducing readmission cost disparities (adjusted for baseline risk differences between demographic groups) by 38%-63%. Our results demonstrate how capacity-aware decision policies can improve both predictive performance and fairness by addressing censoring bias.

items.title: Transductive Generalization for GNNs via Optimal Transport
items.summary: Analyzing the generalization of graph neural networks (GNNs) on node classification is challenging: message passing induces dependencies that break the i.i.d. assumption underlying standard inductive generalization theory. While distribution-free transductive theory resolves this dependency issue, existing classical bounds are either intractable or correlate poorly with empirical generalization. To fill this gap, we propose a transductive generalization bound based on optimal transport, connecting generalization to intra-class concentration and inter-class separation in the feature space. Empirically, our bound aligns strongly with the generalization gap. Building on this representation-based approach, we analyze how feature geometry evolves under repeated message passing. This explains the non-monotonic relationship between GNN depth and generalization, providing new insights into oversmoothing research. Practically, our bound serves as a geometry-aware regularizer that corrects the harmful behavior of message passing, yielding consistent performance improvements. The code is available at https://github.com/ml-postech/Transductive-OT-Gen-Bound.

items.title: GPU-accelerated Regularized Vector Multiplicative Error Models for Positive-valued Financial Time Series
items.summary: The logarithmic vector multiplicative error model (log-vMEM) provides a methodology for modeling and forecasting multivariate positive-valued time series. However, the number of autoregressive parameters increases rapidly with the system dimension and lag order, posing challenges for estimation and model selection. This paper develops a regularized estimation framework for the log-vMEM with multivariate Gamma errors by incorporating hierarchical lag structures to induce sparsity and accommodate heterogeneous lag dynamics. We consider three hierarchical lag structures: componentwise, own-other, and elementwise, in combination with group lasso, adaptive group lasso, group MCP, and group SCAD penalties. Parameter estimation is carried out through an alternating block-coordinate optimization algorithm with sequential Gauss-Seidel updates, while GPU-accelerated numerical quadrature is employed to address the computational burden of evaluating the multivariate Gamma likelihood. Simulation experiments investigate parameter recovery and lag selection under different sparsity structures. The real data analysis is carried out on the realized volatility measures for Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) which allows a comparison of the competing regularization approaches in an empirical financial setting. Together, these developments provide a computational framework for sparse multivariate volatility modeling with flexible lag structures and dependent Gamma errors.

items.title: Causal Machine Learning for Multilevel Studies with Unmeasured Cluster-Level Covariates via Variational Autoencoders
items.summary: Unmeasured confounders are a key obstacle to accurately estimating treatment effects in observational studies, and in multilevel data, they often arise at the cluster level. Flexible machine learning methods cannot directly resolve such unmeasured confounding. To address this, we propose the variational autoencoder-augmented R-learner (VAE-R), which leverages variational autoencoders (VAEs) to infer unmeasured cluster-level covariates from the within-cluster dependence of outcome and treatment residuals, and uses the resulting adjustments to estimate the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) and the average treatment effect (ATE). The VAE decoder is specified through an offset likelihood so that the latent variables capture only the cluster-level variation left unexplained by measured covariates. VAE-R accommodates unmeasured cluster-level confounders in observational studies and unmeasured cluster-level predictors of the outcome in multisite randomized trials. We also provide data-driven strategies for selecting the two hyperparameters of the VAE, the latent dimension size and the Kullback-Leibler weight. Our simulation study shows that VAE-R nearly eliminates the bias of the ordinary R-learner's CATE and ATE estimates in multilevel observational data and improves their precision in multisite randomized trials. Finally, we illustrate VAE-R with two datasets, one from a multilevel observational study and the other from a multisite randomized trial.

items.title: Identification-aware Markov chain Monte Carlo
items.summary: In Bayesian analysis, a proper posterior can exist even when identification fails, but its existence does not ensure reliable posterior computation. More broadly, posterior simulation can be slow when local samplers must move between separated regions or along ridges and weakly curved directions. We develop identification-aware Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samplers that combine local updates with moves across observationally equivalent parameter values, thereby giving identification analysis a constructive role in modern Bayesian analysis. Under uniform mixing and communication conditions, we establish spectral-gap comparisons in which local-sampler upper bounds vanish as modes separate or likelihood-flat fibers expand, while lower bounds for identification-aware samplers remain bounded away from zero. Simulations illustrate these mechanisms. Structural vector moving-average (SVMA) applications at two scales demonstrate substantial sampling improvements under weak priors, with limited additional gains under strong priors.

items.title: Identifiable alignment of unpaired representations
items.summary: Aligning two models without paired data requires a distance that both share, yet existing methods use Euclidean or spherical geometry. This is either an arbitrary choice or imposed by their loss function. We show that, under a precise form of the manifold hypothesis, the pullback of the data metric gives such a distance for any two models of one data-generating process. This holds whether the models are encoders, decoders or both, and whatever their architecture, loss, prior or training data. The alignment map preserves this distance and the distribution of representations, and is identifiable if and only if the data distribution breaks every symmetry of the data manifold. We show that this symmetry breaking holds generically. Identifiability makes the alignment coupling the unique optimum of Gromov--Wasserstein and of its weighted combinations with a linear program. The linear program alone has the same optimum if almost every data point has a distinct distribution of distances. The coupling, and with it the alignment map, is recovered exactly from permuted samples, even without identifiability, and consistently from independent ones. Our method, Neural Gromov--Monge Alignment (NGMA), uses no pairs or labels and outperforms every unpaired and label-informed baseline. It relies on pullback distances to align image models with different priors and single-cell models trained on disjoint cells, where Euclidean distances fail.

items.title: Anchored Extra-Proximal Methods: Optimal Higher-Order Methods for Monotone Inclusion Problems
items.summary: We characterize, up to logarithmic factors, the optimal higher-order oracle complexity of finding approximate solutions to composite monotone inclusion problems, formed by the sum of a smooth single-valued monotone operator and a maximal monotone set-valued operator. We introduce the Anchored Extra-Proximal (AEP) framework, which combines an anchored extrapolation step with an inexact anchored proximal update satisfying a relative-error condition. This framework recovers the composite Fast Extragradient method in the first-order setting and yields natural higher-order extensions through Taylor approximations of the smooth operator at the extrapolated point. For every $p\geq 2$, assuming that the $(p-1)$th derivative of the single-valued operator is $L_p$-Lipschitz continuous and the initial distance to a solution is at most $R$, we combine AEP with a bisection line search to obtain a $p$th-order method that attains a tangent residual of at most $\varepsilon$ in $\widetilde{O}((L_p R^{p}/\varepsilon)^{\frac{2}{3p-1}})$ oracle calls. We complement this result with a worst-case lower bound of $Ω((L_p R^p/\varepsilon)^{\frac{2}{3p-1}})$ for every deterministic algorithm in the $p$th-order oracle model, without imposing any prescribed update structure. For the subclass of smooth nonexpansive fixed-point problems, we further establish a lower bound of $Ω(\min\{R/\varepsilon, {(L_p R^{p}/\varepsilon)}^{\frac{2}{3p-1}}\})$. By choosing between AEP and Halpern iteration, we match this lower bound up to logarithmic factors, thereby also settling the deterministic oracle complexity of smooth nonexpansive fixed-point problems.

items.title: Model-assisted semi-supervised estimation of the Mann-Whitney probability under right censoring
items.summary: We study semi-supervised estimation of the full-lifetime Mann-Whitney probability under right censoring using finite covariate-only samples from two populations. A model-assisted estimator is constructed by adjusting censored pair comparisons with differences between labeled and auxiliary feature means. Resource weights minimize first-order variance within the working projection class. Under joint independent censoring and regularity conditions, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality through a four-pool influence representation that accounts for censoring distributions estimated from the same labeled records. Consistent variance estimation from all four sample pools yields Wald confidence intervals. The efficiency analysis relates variance reduction to projected comparison signals and auxiliary sample sizes and characterizes the gap to the semiparametric bound. A fixed-horizon extension accommodates half-weighted ties and the terminal mass induced by capping follow-up. Simulations show increasing precision gains with auxiliary sample size under moderate or strong projected signals, with finite-sample losses in some settings with zero or weak projected signals. A five-year Rotterdam breast-cancer comparison illustrates precision gains and variability across label allocations when auxiliary samples are formed by controlled outcome withholding.

items.title: ZIO: Order-Based Structure Learning for Zero-Inflated Count Data under Data Heterogeneity
items.summary: We propose a structure learning method for directed acyclic graph (DAG) models of zero-inflated multivariate count data. Although causal structure learning with zero-inflated Poisson models is identifiable, existing algorithms rely on local search over the DAG space, leading to poor scalability and a tendency to converge to suboptimal solutions. To address these limitations, we develop a novel order-based scoring framework that searches over variable orderings rather than directly over DAGs. Building on this framework, we further extend the method to multiple heterogeneous datasets by identifying a shared variable ordering while allowing each dataset to have its own edge set. We implement a stochastic hill climbing algorithm with a random-to-random (R2R) proposal operator to efficiently explore the ordering space. Simulation studies show competitive performance against existing methods and improved graph estimation accuracy as more heterogeneous datasets are jointly analyzed under a shared causal ordering. We apply the method to single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from a major depressive disorder study.

items.title: Exploring complex dependence structures using Bayesian bi-clustering and log-linear graphical modelling
items.summary: Bayesian partitioning is utilised simultaneously on subjects and categorical variables to reveal complex dependence structures. Clusters of variables are referred to as views. Variable selection highlights the variables that drive the clustering of the subjects within each view. We derive theoretical results on the relation between the variables' dependence structure and the inferences derived from bi-clustering. The results relate to marginal independence and conditional independence. Using simulated and real data, we demonstrate the applicability of bi-clustering results in assisting log-linear graphical model determination, leading to the efficient exploration of typically vast model spaces. This work sheds light on the relation between two very different but equally popular Bayesian approaches; mixture modelling, that benefits from a large number of variables, and graphical log-linear modelling, which describes explicitly the variables' dependence structure and allows to evaluate the uncertainty associated with model determination.

items.title: Diffusion Path Samplers via Sequential Monte Carlo
items.summary: We develop diffusion-based samplers for target distributions known up to a normalising constant. To this end, we rely on the well-known diffusion path that smoothly interpolates between a simple base distribution and the target, popularised by diffusion models. We tackle the score estimation problem by developing an efficient sequential Monte Carlo sampler that evolves auxiliary variables from conditional distributions along the path, providing principled score and density estimates for time-varying distributions. To control the variance of score estimates, we further propose practical control variate schedules that incur minimal overhead. We adapt this general framework to paths induced by the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) time-reversal process, stochastic interpolants, and diffusion annealed Langevin dynamics, outlining their trade-offs. Finally, we provide theoretical guarantees and empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several synthetic and real-world datasets. Our code is available at: https://github.com/akyildiz-group/dpsmc.

items.title: Schrödinger--Föllmer Actor--Critic: Diffusion Policy Improvement with Finite-Sample Analysis
items.summary: Diffusion policies represent multimodal action distributions, but a $Q$-weighted update does not specify how to sample from the resulting target distribution. We propose Schrödinger--Föllmer Actor--Critic (SFAC), an offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) method for Kullback--Leibler (KL)-regularized policy improvement through conditional diffusion. A minimax Bellman critic estimates the action-value function, which defines an exponentially tilted target policy. A Doob $h$-transform expresses this update as a correction to the reference diffusion drift. The target drift is a weighted conditional mean of Brownian-bridge labels. We fit it by weighted regression using endpoints from the current policy and pointwise action-value evaluations. In the small-update regime, the KL-regularized update follows the natural policy-gradient direction, and the Doob correction represents the same local change in the space of diffusion drifts. Under suitable conditions, we derive finite-sample bounds that separate the errors from critic estimation, weighted neural drift regression, and diffusion discretization through a reverse-KL actor bound. The average-performance bound depends explicitly on the comparison coefficients over the policy iterations. Across six D4RL offline-to-online tasks, the final scores of the $Q$-guided bridge-regression implementation exceed its offline initialization on every task and Cal-QL on five tasks. We also compare with offline RL and online-only baselines.

items.title: Uniform inference for $U$-statistics of exchangeable arrays under degeneracy
items.summary: Many $U$-statistics of row-column exchangeable arrays become degenerate at natural null hypotheses: their convergence rates change and their limiting laws may or may not remain Gaussian. We establish conditions under which inference based on the classical unbiased variance estimator is uniformly valid across these changes, without knowledge of the degeneracy order. It is known that $U$-statistics can be decomposed into orthogonal projections indexed by bipartite graphs. Under uniform fourth-moment assumptions, we establish that the standardized statistic is asymptotically Gaussian and the classical unbiased variance estimator is ratio-consistent, as long as a certain measure of concentration for projections indexed by disconnected graphs tends to zero. Under compactness of the normalized projections, both properties hold if and only if the proportion of variance contributed by disconnected graphs tends to zero. The necessity of this condition follows from a general limit theorem for these $U$-statistics, in which each graph contributes to a Wiener chaos of order equal to its number of connected components. We note that the row-column jackknife variance estimator, although nonnegative, does not generally give a studentized statistic with a standard normal limit in degenerate regimes. We illustrate our theory with an application to estimation and testing based on a distance from product form, exhibiting Gaussian and non-Gaussian limits at various rates depending on the model. We also propose a conservative inference procedure that does not require a Gaussian limit, valid under additional moment and projection conditions.

items.title: Orthogonal Updates for the Win: Towards Accelerated Adaptive Minimax Optimization
items.summary: Single-loop minimax methods are appealing for modern machine learning, but standard stochastic gradient updates can be unstable and oscillatory under tightly coupled primal-dual dynamics, making performance notoriously sensitive to stepsizes. To fundamentally improve stability, we develop an orthogonal update framework tailored to minimax optimization, which applies updates along orthogonalized directions to reduce update anisotropy. However, orthogonalization reshapes the optimization geometry and makes coordinating primal-dual stepsizes even more delicate. To overcome this challenge, we develop AdaSGDA, which equips orthogonal updates with an adaptive stepsize rule driven by accumulated gradient norms. This mechanism automatically balances coupled primal-dual progress under orthogonalization, yielding an effectively parameter-free method for nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax optimization. We prove that AdaSGDA avoids problem-dependent tuning while attaining the state-of-the-art $\mathcal{O}\left(T^{-1/4}\right)$ convergence rate. We further propose AdaSGDA-VR, which incorporates a carefully designed variance reduction scheme and achieves the faster $\mathcal{O}\left(T^{-1/3}\right)$ rate. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our methods deliver competitive performance compared to existing minimax optimization methods.

items.title: What Travels Across Languages? Reading, Transfer and Erasure of Cross-Lingual Concept Subspaces in Bangla Idioms
items.summary: Cross-lingual concept analysis requires distinguishing the information that a subspace retains from the classifiers and erasers that transfer through it. We study these operations in six frozen encoders using 10,359 Bangla (Bengali) idiom senses, eight input conditions, and figurative-class and sentiment labels. Class-mean directions provide the most consistent evidence of shared coarse meaning: in post hoc analyses, they outperform random-subspace, permuted-label and covariance-matched nulls in all 12 model-label tests under balanced accuracy. A prospective internal re-split supports idiom-alone sharing in 10 of 12 tests, spanning five encoders. The original confirmatory logistic-regression family rejects both planned nulls in 4 of 12 tests, where English directions gain only a few accuracy points above the majority-class floor (3.0-7.3). Classifier transfer depends on the input map and regularization: English-trained class-mean readouts beat both zero-shot nulls in 8 of 12 discovery tests, and stronger source-selected penalties improve transfer through logistic and LEACE directions. These readouts use Bangla-validation-selected layers and unlabeled target preprocessing. Input controls show greater coarse-class sharing for explicit glosses than for idiom counterparts. Reading, however, does not imply effective erasure: English-fitted LEACE removes less than one percentage point of Bangla figurative-class accuracy, compared with 4-11 points for Bangla-fitted LEACE; INLP shows a similar asymmetry. Pattern-filter analysis, covariance-weighted input maps and a binary Gaussian overlap bound explain how these operations can diverge. The analogous multiclass ordering is an empirical diagnostic, observed in 11 of 12 cells. The results support an estimator-sensitive account of cross-lingual concept sharing and motivate evaluating reading, classifier transfer, erasure and overlap separately.

items.title: Does Predictive Performance Translate to Causal Performance? Evaluating tabular foundation models as nuisance learners for causal effect estimation
items.summary: Tabular foundation models based on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) achieve strong predictive performance, but their value for causal inference is unclear. We evaluated whether PFNs, which predict through in-context learning, could match or outperform conventional nuisance learners in supporting accurate causal estimation and reliable uncertainty quantification (inference). Learners modeled propensity scores and outcome regressions within doubly robust estimators of average causal effects, with and without cross-fitting, across synthetic and semi-synthetic settings with varying confounding complexity and effect heterogeneity. Under simple parametric data-generating processes, the PFNs were competitive with correctly specified parametric regressions and ensembles containing them. In more complex settings, they outperformed all conventional learners evaluated, including richly specified Super Learner ensembles, for both accuracy and uncertainty quantification. As sample size increased, only the two PFN models (TabPFN and Mitra) consistently approached nominal confidence interval coverage, whereas under-coverage persisted for conventional learners. In some settings, PFNs achieved near-nominal coverage and well-calibrated standard errors even without cross-fitting. At the smallest sample size (n=200) and in the higher-dimensional semi-synthetic settings, PFNs and other flexible learners exhibited poor coverage without cross-fitting. For PFNs, this appeared to be driven by propensity score overfitting consistent with in-sample memorization of treatment labels. These findings highlight the promise of prior-data fitted networks as in-context nuisance learners for causal estimation, while underscoring the need for further evaluation in challenging settings.

items.title: Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers for Nonlinear Matrix Decompositions
items.summary: We present an algorithm based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) for solving nonlinear matrix decompositions (NMD). Given an input matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ and a factorization rank $r \ll \min(m, n)$, NMD seeks matrices $W \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times r}$ and $H \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times n}$ such that $X \approx f(WH)$, where $f$ is an element-wise nonlinear function. We evaluate our method on several representative nonlinear models: the rectified linear unit activation $f(x) = \max(0, x)$, suitable for nonnegative sparse data approximation, the component-wise square $f(x) = x^2$, applicable to probabilistic circuit representation, and the MinMax transform $f(x) = \min(b, \max(a, x))$, relevant for recommender systems. The proposed framework flexibly supports diverse loss functions, including least squares, $\ell_1$ norm, and the Kullback-Leibler divergence, and can be readily extended to other nonlinearities and metrics. We illustrate the applicability, efficiency, and adaptability of the approach on real-world datasets, highlighting its potential for a broad range of applications.

items.title: When Sensors Fail: Coverage Auditing with Incomplete Sensor Records
items.summary: Sensor outages can conceal prediction-interval coverage deficits behind acceptable marginal performance, while unavailable future readings leave some issued forecasts unscorable. We present a measurement-record audit that links issue-time outage duration, original target availability, and time-uniform statistical evidence. The audit retains complete forecast keys, batches all sensors and overlapping horizons at each measurement tick, and projects simultaneous covered-count and scored-count bounds onto a cumulative conditional expected coverage ratio. This target is distinguished from empirical coverage and outage-conditional population coverage. Selected traffic and air-quality results illustrate the gap between pooled and long-outage coverage; in METR-LA, only 7.6% of issued long-gap forecasts have originally observed targets. Of 30 primary sequential outage-state audits, 26 are inconclusive and four lack scored support. This concise presentation gives the core construction and selected aggregate evidence without the full experimental supplement.

items.title: Debiased Machine Learning for Partially Linear Accelerated Failure Time Models
items.summary: The Cox model remains the default for survival analysis, but the proportional hazards assumption is often violated and hazard ratios can be difficult to interpret. Accelerated failure time (AFT) models provide an intuitive time-scale alternative, yet flexible covariate adjustment while preserving valid inference on a target exposure remains challenging. For the partially linear AFT model under right censoring, a rank-based debiased machine learning (DML) framework has not been developed. The rank-based pairwise moment is not Neyman orthogonal, and standard cross-fitting does not directly apply to U-statistics. We develop the first such framework by combining an orthogonalized rank-based U-statistic, a censoring-corrected influence function, and block-pairwise cross-fitting, yielding valid inference for a finite-dimensional exposure effect under flexible machine-learning nuisance estimation. In the primary simulation study, the proposed estimator attains near-nominal coverage under independent and covariate-dependent censoring at rates up to 60%, whereas the nonorthogonal plug-in estimator remains biased. Using All of Us electronic health record data from adults with diabetes and advanced chronic kidney disease, we apply the proposed method to estimate the associations of serum albumin, estimated glomerular filtration rate, and systolic blood pressure with incident cardiovascular outcomes.

items.title: Causal discernment and the direction of clinical research
items.summary: A clinical trial can establish an intervention's effects while leaving their causal pathways unresolved. We call causal discernment the practice of identifying explanations that fit the evidence but imply different decisions or research directions, and seeking studies that distinguish them. METHOD: We combine causal graphs and prose around four questions: delivery of the intended target change, routes of benefit and harm, stability of causal relations across regimes, and whether unresolved pathways could change the decision. With quantitative assumptions, graphs support plausible reasoning by showing which findings could distinguish explanations even when effects are not identified. Prose specifies clinical meaning, effect size and timing, and supporting evidence. We use conceptual analysis, hypothetical calculations, CAST and lipid-lowering therapy. SUBSTANTIVE RESULTS: Concordant coronary associations for HMGCR and PCSK9 perturbations support LDL mediation over target-specific explanations predicting unequal effects per unit of LDL reduction, but leave a shared receptor pathway possible. Diabetes associations leave LDL lowering, receptor-mediated uptake and weight gain as possible explanations. An illustrative causal record specifies a genetic comparison and assumptions under which it could distinguish them. CONCLUSION: The causal record formalises the reasoning behind the choice of the next study by making competing explanations, evidence and assumptions explicit and stating what each design could resolve. Prepared before a design or recommendation is adopted, it enables scrutiny of that reasoning and interpretation of results in relation to the stated explanations. Its added value over ordinary rationale review remains to be assessed.

items.title: Sharp bounds for posterior causal attribution given complete factual records
items.summary: Retrospective causal attribution evaluates whether altering an earlier event would have prevented an observed outcome. Observational data determine marginal potential-response probabilities at fixed inputs while leaving cross-world joint distributions unspecified. Conditional on a complete factual record in a finite Markovian structural causal model, independence across mechanisms is preserved and each unobserved conditional response distribution is restricted to a capped probability simplex. Every collection of conditional distributions satisfying these local bounds is jointly attainable within a single compatible structural causal model. Optimizing the counterfactual expectation over the resulting product domain yields sharp attribution bounds for multistage interventions and mediated effects, and compatible response-vector polytopes extend these bounds to structural response restrictions. Exact algorithms for causal chains and general directed acyclic graphs, consistent plug-in endpoint estimators, and finite-sample and asymptotic confidence intervals are developed and illustrated using synthetic reactor experiments and health survey data.

items.title: Maximin Robust Bayesian Experimental Design
items.summary: We address the brittleness of Bayesian experimental design under model misspecification by formulating the problem as a max--min game between the experimenter and an adversarial nature subject to information-theoretic constraints. We demonstrate that this approach yields a robust objective governed by Sibson's $α$-mutual information~(MI), which identifies the $α$-tilted posterior as the robust belief update and establishes the Rényi divergence as the appropriate measure of conditional information gain. To mitigate the bias and variance of nested Monte Carlo estimators needed to estimate Sibson's $α$-MI, we adopt a PAC-Bayes framework to search over stochastic design policies, yielding rigorous high-probability lower bounds on the robust expected information gain that explicitly control finite-sample error.

items.title: Mamba Can Learn Low-Dimensional Targets In-Context via Test-Time Feature Learning
items.summary: Mamba, a recently proposed linear-time sequence model, has attracted significant attention for its computational efficiency and strong empirical performance. However, a rigorous theoretical understanding of its underlying mechanisms remains limited. In this work, we provide a theoretical analysis of Mamba's in-context learning (ICL) capability by focusing on tasks defined by low-dimensional nonlinear target functions. Specifically, we study in-context learning of a single-index model $y \approx g_*(\langle \boldsymbolβ, \boldsymbol{x} \rangle)$, which depends on only a single relevant direction $\boldsymbolβ$, referred to as feature. We prove that Mamba, pretrained by gradient-based methods, can achieve efficient ICL via test-time feature learning, extracting the relevant direction directly from context examples. Consequently, we establish a test-time sample complexity that improves upon linear Transformers -- analyzed to behave like kernel methods -- and is comparable to nonlinear Transformers, which have been shown to surpass the Correlational Statistical Query (CSQ) lower bound and achieve near information-theoretically optimal rate in previous works. Our analysis reveals the crucial role of the nonlinear gating mechanism in Mamba for feature extraction, highlighting it as the fundamental driver behind Mamba's ability to achieve both computational efficiency and high performance.

items.title: Tail behaviour of infimum of Gaussian processes
items.summary: We investigate the upper tail of $\inf_{t\in\mathcal T}X(t)$, where $X$ is a centred Gaussian process (GP) with continuous sample paths on a nonempty compact metric space $\mathcal T$. As suggested by the findings of [1], the exponential rate is governed by an optimal-measure problem, while the exact prefactor depends on the local geometry of the corresponding contact set. In the full-contact regime, we strengthen the known Gumbel max-domain of attraction property of the distribution of $\inf_{t\in\mathcal T}X(t)$ by establishing the von Mises condition. For fractional Brownian motion on $[a,b]$, $0<a<b$, with Hurst index $H\in(0,1/2)$, we also determine the order of the logarithmic correction to the leading Gaussian exponential. For finite contact sets, we distinguish dominated, smooth-critical, and rough-critical regimes and derive exact asymptotics of $P\{\inf_{t\in\mathcal T}X(t)>u\}$ as $u\to\infty$ under suitable local assumptions. We illustrate our findings with examples including fractional Brownian motion and the fractional Brownian sheet.

items.title: Zero Replacement and Latent Profiles in Short Media Diaries: Checking Recording Status Before User Segmentation
items.summary: Short media diaries contain many zeros because many activities go unrecorded during the observation period. Log-ratio analysis of time allocation requires these zeros to be replaced with small positive values; as a result, all respondents who did not record an activity receive nearly the same value. We examined how such zero replacement affects classification in latent profile analysis and propose checks to perform before profiles are interpreted. Three-day diaries of 8,089 adults from the 2025 Korea Media Panel Survey were converted into nine-part time-use compositions. Gaming was not recorded by 88.9% of the respondents, and in every model with two to eight profiles and a covariance matrix held equal across profiles, respondents who recorded gaming and those who did not were classified into different profiles. Even when the replacement value equaled the minimum recording unit (5 min/day), the two-profile classification largely matched gaming recording status, and the two groups separated more sharply as the replacement value decreased, until the separation was complete. Before naming profiles, researchers should therefore check the proportion of respondents who did not record each activity and its replacement value, the same proportion within each profile, and the distribution of usage time among those who recorded the activity.

items.title: Global Trends and Heterogeneity in Modified Adjusted Net Savings
items.summary: Modified adjusted net savings is a derived weak sustainability indicator obtained by subtracting education expenditure from adjusted net savings (ANS). Because ANS equals net national savings plus education expenditure minus natural-resource depletion and carbon dioxide damage, MANS isolates the savings and depletion components and is useful when education expenditure would otherwise dominate cross-country comparisons. This study documents the global distribution, long-run trends, and cross-country heterogeneity of MANS excluding particulate emission damage over 1990-2021. The accounting base is the World Bank World Development Indicators series NY.ADJ.SVNX.CD, and MANS is constructed by subtracting education expenditure from this series. We combine global maps, aggregate time series, country-level heatmaps, distributional statistics, and income group comparisons. The results show that global MANS has increased substantially in aggregate, but its evolution as a share of nominal GDP has been more volatile and uneven across countries. Per capita MANS and global MANS totals remain concentrated in high-income and large economies, whereas low-income and lower-middle-income groups display persistently lower and more volatile outcomes.
