The distribution then determines the *required directions*, along which the dual transports mass, and the preference determines the *covered directions* of each bundle; optimality is full coverage. This separation enables comparative statics in the preference: raising a complementarity premium on bundles containing a core of goods widens their covered directions. Two premium thresholds describe the optimum: above a lower threshold the grand bundle must be offered; above an upper threshold a *core-peripheral* menu --- a bundled core with optional add-ons not sold standalone --- is optimal, and every optimal menu is core-peripheral. The upper threshold is finite if and only if the menu is *inclusive*: it excludes no near-top buyer.

items.title: Advancing AI Capabilities and Evolving Labor Outcomes
items.summary: This paper examines how labor market outcomes have evolved across occupations as AI capabilities advanced from generative AI chatbots to reasoning models and AI agents. We construct an occupational AI exposure score that measures the share of each occupation's work that AI could perform at each capability stage, and link the change in exposure to the Current Population Survey from January 2023 through June 2026, using first-difference and fixed-effects designs at the occupation and individual level, with 2017 to 2022 as a placebo period. We find that occupations with larger increases in exposure show no change in employment or unemployment relative to occupations with comparable workforces. However, the composition of the workforce in these occupations changed. The number of workers under 30 decreased by about 8 percent per standard deviation of the change in exposure, and the decline is concentrated among workers without a college degree and builds gradually from 2023. It is not accompanied by higher unemployment among young workers who were already in these occupations, which suggests a decline in entry rather than an increase in exit. The decline is smaller when remote work is held fixed, but it remains. On the other hand, college graduates aged 30 to 49 gained full-time employment. Part-time work declined, weekly hours increased slightly, and the workforce in these occupations became older and more educated. In sum, the early effects of AI appear in the composition of the workforce rather than in the number of jobs.

items.title: The invisible hand as an emergent property
items.summary: We develop a multi-sector competitive economy where firms reallocate across sectors under myopic profit-seeking behaviour and quadratic reallocation costs. The dynamic path, formalised as a gradient flow in Wasserstein space, yields two emergent properties: (i) short-run equilibria can be seen as solutions to sequential aggregate optimisation problems; and (ii) the long-run equilibrium is globally stable and efficient. Linearizing around the common long-run equilibrium, we show that convergence can be faster or slower under a planner who accounts for reallocation costs than under decentralized adjustment.

items.title: Local Projections Inference with High-Dimensional Covariates without Exact Sparsity
items.summary: This paper develops a high-dimensional local projections framework for estimating impulse responses in the presence of many potential controls. Other approaches often rely on exact sparsity assumptions, but empirical macroeconomic applications may involve nuisance relationships better described by structured coefficient decay. Building on the orthogonal greedy algorithm with high-dimensional AIC (OGA+HDAIC), I propose a double-selection procedure that separately addresses the shock equation and the outcome equation within local projections. The method allows for nonexact sparsity through polynomially decaying nuisance coefficients, with rates indexed by the decay exponent rather than by an effective sparsity level. Under suitable moment, dependence, and approximation conditions, the estimator achieves asymptotic normality with HAC standard errors. Simulation evidence shows reliable coverage under shock contamination and lower point-estimation error under predictable high-dimensional outcome nuisance. I illustrate the method's practical feasibility in a monetary policy application using the FRED-MD dataset.

items.title: Estimating multidimensional poverty under incomplete data in North Macedonia
items.summary: Multidimensional Poverty Indices (MPIs) are available for more than 100 countries, but rarely below the national or regional level. Local estimates require knowing how deprivations overlap within households, yet the sources that cover every locality, such as censuses and geospatial data, cannot be linked at the household level. We show how to measure local multidimensional poverty under such incomplete data, using North Macedonia as a case study. Combining settlement-level access to services with municipal census data, we pair an independence-based point estimate with sharp bounds over all joint distributions consistent with the data. We find that, nationally, 5.01 percent of households are multidimensionally poor, with bounds of 2.01 to 17.44 percent. Also, poverty is concentrated in small rural municipalities, which are poorer than nearly all municipalities of the capital city under any dependence structure. Validating our index against official statistics, the Global MPI, and a fieldwork deprivation index indicates that the socio-economic part of the index is consistent with external measures of deprivation, while the geographic part captures a distinct dimension of remoteness. Our approach thus presents a promising way to measure multidimensional poverty at the local level in countries where linked household data are unavailable.

items.title: Coordination Mechanisms with Partially Specified Probabilities
items.summary: A mediator coordinates play in a finite game, but instead of revealing a fully known correlation device it discloses only some statistics of the process that generates players' private messages. Players complete the partially specified process by minimizing a loss over the set of distributions consistent with what is disclosed: maximum Shannon entropy is the leading case, and the analysis covers every strictly convex and symmetric loss that never excludes an event the data do not exclude. We obtain four sets of results. (i) With unrestricted message spaces, the implementable outcomes are exactly the jointly coherent outcomes, namely distributions supported on the support of the set of correlated equilibria. (ii) The characterization is unchanged when players' partial knowledge also concerns the joint distribution of messages and actions, whether or not players know the strategy profile. (iii) Under direct implementation, implementability depends on the loss and reduces to a single optimality condition linking the outcome to some correlated equilibrium: among all distributions on the line joining the equilibrium and the outcome, the equilibrium must be the one with the lowest loss. (iv) In single-agent decision problems the designer can induce, with probability one, any action that is a best response to some interior belief.

items.title: Exact Inference in Fixed-Effect Regressions with Concentrated Identifying Variation
items.summary: In fixed-effect regressions with many groups, a handful of observations can carry most of the identifying variation left after fixed effects are removed. Conventional $t$-tests can then reject a true null more than half the time. This paper specializes the exact $t$-test of Pouliot to such designs. Contrasts chosen from the design eliminate the nuisance coefficients exactly; sign flips give finite-sample valid tests under independent symmetric errors, or compatible independent symmetric error blocks, allowing arbitrary heteroskedasticity. In two-way designs, the annihilating space is the cycle space of the bipartite observation graph and contains all within variation. This makes the choice of contrasts a graph problem. The observable capture ratio $κ_{\mathcal C}\in[0,1]$ measures retained identifying variation and, under diffuse homoskedastic conditions, gives the efficiency relative to an oracle test. Structured packing trades capture against the number and balance of usable signs. The matched-weight test is also asymptotically valid without symmetry when independent centered contrast scores satisfy a fourth-moment negligibility condition. In the Grunfeld investment regression, where one observation carries $73.9\%$ of the realized squared score, 32 contrasts capture $κ_{\mathcal C}=0.627$ and give a symmetry-based exact $95\%$ confidence interval of $[0.150, 0.450]$.

items.title: Identification in Auctions with Truncated Transaction Prices
items.summary: This paper studies nonparametric identification in auction models with truncated transaction price data arising from either binding reserve prices or endogenous entry. I characterize identification under alternative information structures that differ according to whether the number of potential bidders is fixed or varies across auctions and whether the econometrician observes the number of potential or active bidders. A central insight is that identification hinges on recovering the screening threshold that determines bidder participation. The analysis provides a unified characterization of identification in first- and second-price auctions under both truncation mechanisms.

items.title: Backtesting High-Dimensional Expected Shortfall
items.summary: Forecast evaluation increasingly uses high-dimensional predictors, but estimation and regularization of large predictive models can distort conventional backtests. This issue is particularly important for forecasting downside risk, where the signal-to-noise ratio is low. We develop out-of-sample Expected Shortfall (ES) backtests that remove the large first-order bias effects of estimating high-dimensional Value-at-Risk, ES, and the evaluation instrument. In a linear ES specification, the proposed methods are easily implemented as Double Lasso with a tail-size-adjusted score as a generated dependent variable. More generally, we characterize orthogonal ES backtesting moments, and establish oracle equivalence and valid inference under time-series dependence and repeated estimation with overlapping and expanding training windows. Simulations show that conventional backtests can severely overreject ES optimal forecasts, whereas orthogonalization improves size control. An application to downside-growth forecasting for G7 economies finds evidence against a US growth-only ES specification, even though forecast-oriented regularization selects no additional financial predictors. The application also shows that accounting for estimation can change rejection decisions in either direction. These findings highlight the distinct roles of predictive variable selection and backtesting in the evaluation of high-dimensional tail-risk models.

items.title: Economic Benefits of Cross-Border Electricity Trade and Domestic Electricity Production in Switzerland
items.summary: This paper assesses the economic benefits of cross-border electricity trade in the context of rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty. Switzerland provides a particularly compelling case because of its geographical location and limited integration into the EU electricity market. We first use the Nexus-e framework to simulate the generation capacity and transmission grid expansion required under autarky and free-trade scenarios. Based on these capacity configurations, a fundamental power market model simulates wholesale market outcomes under projected demand and generation conditions for 2040. By jointly accounting for consumer and producer surplus, as well as investments in generation capacity and grid infrastructure, we provide a comprehensive assessment of the welfare effects of cross-border electricity trade, leading to an estimated EUR 1.5 billion gain. More specifically, open access to cross-border electricity trade implies a EUR 1.8 billion transfer from largely publicly owned producers to consumers. Finally, we provide an illustrative, non-causal mapping of broader macroeconomic effects. Under a price-convergence assumption, the implied demand adjustment corresponds to a GDP-equivalent effect of approximately EUR 7 billion.

items.title: Have wind and solar energy increased electricity price volatility? And what is electricity price volatility, anyway?
items.summary: It is widely held that wind and solar power increase the volatility of electricity prices. This paper argues that the literature conflates two distinct types of price variation: across delivery time and across trading time. Determined simultaneously in the same day-ahead auction, prices for power to be delivered in distinct quarter-hours differ. This price dispersion, which I call "variability", is rooted in non-storability. After that auction, trading continues in intraday markets until imbalance settlement. The price for the same delivery period changes as new information arises, e.g., weather forecasts. Such price "volatility" is ultimately caused by uncertainty. This paper develops a simple algebraic model of day-ahead and imbalance markets that provides a formal definition of variability and volatility, allows for a decomposition and derives the fundamental drivers, uncertainty and non-storability. It then provides empirical data on price variability and volatility for the past 25 years in Germany, during which the share of wind and solar energy increased from zero to nearly 50 % of generation. Volatility is measured with imbalance prices, intraday price indices and intraday transaction data. Variability followed a U-shaped trajectory, falling from the 2000s to the 2010s but increasing since then. Volatility, in contrast, declined over time. Across 24 European bidding zones, variability has risen since the late 2010s in almost all zones and increases with the share of solar power.

items.title: Optimal Regulation and Information Institutions with Hidden Network Equilibria
items.summary: Aggregate outcomes can conceal network configurations that expose households to uninsurable risk and require different public services. We study a regulator's joint choice of a corrective activity charge and an information institution in a two-population network game. Although aggregate behavior follows an exact stable law, distinct specialization equilibria require different targeted interventions. With purchased Gaussian monitoring, primitive conditions imply a discontinuous switch between strong regulation without purchased information and informed specialization. The regulator may alternatively obtain signed certification or elicit a privately known state through a report backed by committed random audits. We characterize the three institutions' optimized values and the cost thresholds at which credible disclosure replaces government monitoring. The institutional choice also changes optimal regulation: even when certification and truthful reporting reveal the same state, costly audits favor less specialization and a higher corrective charge. This ordering and monotonicity in audit costs hold under an explicit interiority condition without global concavity of the audit problem. The institutional comparison is solved in the benchmark without feedback from anticipated policy, while the policy switch and strict institutional rankings admit local persistence under additional regularity conditions. Results depend on enforceable verification, restrictions on data access, and an explicitly limited institutional menu.

items.title: Herding with Multiple States: When the Prior Matters
items.summary: In sequential observational learning with more than two states, the same information structure and preferences can yield learning for some full-support priors and herding for others. This disproves a conjecture of Kartik, Lee, Liu, and Rappoport (2024, working-paper version). In the counterexample, the cascade region has nonempty interior, yet learning occurs for generic full-support priors outside it. Focusing on information and preferences, we introduce two necessary conditions for learning. Escapability requires that signals can provide arbitrarily strong evidence that any given action is ex post suboptimal; pairwise escapability is its pairwise variant. If escapability fails, herding occurs for some initial prior; if pairwise escapability fails, it occurs for every full-support prior. For a class of environments with interval optimality and monotone likelihood ratios, escapability completely characterizes learning and herding independently of the full-support initial prior. With location-shift signals, this characterization reduces to pairwise distinguishability, a generalization of unbounded beliefs (Smith and Sørensen, 2000).

items.title: Testing Exclusion and Shape Restrictions in Potential Outcomes Models
items.summary: Exclusion and shape restrictions play a central role in defining causal effects and interpreting estimates in potential outcomes models. To date, the testable implications of such restrictions have been studied on a case-by-case basis in a limited set of models. In this paper, we develop a general framework for characterizing sharp testable implications of general support restrictions on the potential response functions, based on a novel graph-based representation of the model. The framework provides a unified and constructive method for deriving all observable implications of the modeling assumptions. We illustrate the approach in several popular settings, including instrumental variables, treatment selection, mediation, and interference. As an empirical application, we revisit the US Lung Health Study and test for the presence of spillovers between spouses, specification of exposure maps, and persistence of treatment effects over time.

items.title: Do wind and solar curtail at negative electricity prices? Incentives and evidence across two decades of German renewable support schemes
items.summary: In many power systems, installed wind and solar now exceed peak electricity demand. In very sunny or windy periods, curtailing renewable generation becomes a precondition for grid stability. While turning off wind turbines and solar panels is technically easy, support schemes often give renewables an economic incentive to keep producing at negative prices. This paper studies wind and solar energy in Germany, estimating, for each cohort of generators, hour by hour the incentives implied by two decades of support policy. It then sets those incentives against observed behavior, using a new estimate of market-based curtailment built from reanalysis weather data. I find that in 2025, at prices below -50 EUR/MWh, almost all wind generators had an incentive to stop producing, but only half of them did. Nearly two thirds of solar capacity had no incentive to curtail at all, mostly because it receives a feed-in tariff that shields it from wholesale prices. Of the exposed remainder, about one in seven cut production. Low exposure and response rates inflate subsidy payments and make the power system harder to operate safely. I conclude that a further expansion of wind and solar requires them to respond to price signals, which depends on policy makers providing proper incentives and on generators acting on them.

items.title: Obvious Group Manipulations and Top Trading Cycles
items.summary: We introduce a group version of non-obvious manipulability, which is stronger than the original definition by Troyan and Morrill (2020) and weaker than group strategy-proofness, and study its implications in Shapley-Scarf housing markets. We provide several characterizations of the Top Trading Cycles mechanism using the new condition.

items.title: Feedback Design in the Shadow of Strategic Communication
items.summary: We study optimal feedback design when evaluations affect subsequent strategic communication within organizations. A firm designs public feedback about an employee's potential before the employee communicates private information about project-specific circumstances to a manager. While more informative feedback helps the manager make better decisions, it can also intensify preference conflicts and undermine the credibility of subsequent communication. We characterize the optimal feedback policy. First, full disclosure is either optimal for all prior beliefs or strictly suboptimal for all of them. In particular, it is optimal when preference conflicts are sufficiently small or sufficiently large. Second, when full disclosure is suboptimal, no disclosure is optimal for some priors, while partial disclosure is strictly optimal for some priors if and only if the number of messages in equilibrium communication varies with posterior beliefs. Third, optimal partial disclosure can conclusively identify low-potential employees when high potential is rare, but high-potential employees when it is common.

items.title: Observable Self-Restraint in Repeated Cheap Talk
items.summary: A long-lived sender seeks to persuade short-lived receivers, who cannot verify his past advice, to take his preferred action. Restrictions on recommendation histories alone can support a partially informative equilibrium. Under rolling quotas, which cap favorable recommendations within a fixed memory window, a partial order on histories ranks the cost of favorable advice. When receivers infer the reason for a violation, they can still follow the violating recommendation, so state sequences can lead the sender to exceed the quota, ending informative communication on the equilibrium path. As the sender becomes patient, suitable rolling quotas approach his normalized equilibrium payoff ceiling.

items.title: Instrumental variables with treatment clusters
items.summary: Many policy evaluations include multiple unordered treatments. A common approach is to aggregate these treatments into clusters and apply instrumental variable (IV) methods at the treatment cluster level: The clusters are treated as binary treatments and the IV assumptions are invoked at the cluster level. This paper shows that IV with treatment clusters identifies a weighted average of local average treatment effects (LATEs) under a set of assumptions at the unclustered treatment level. When data on unclustered treatment choice is available, we propose testable necessary conditions for the causal interpretation of IV with treatment clusters. We illustrate our methods with empirical applications to the causal effects of fields of study aggregated into STEM and non-STEM clusters or eight broad study directions.

items.title: Designing Markets for Screening: Optimal Composition and the Geometry of Surplus
items.summary: We characterize the structure of market compositions that generate Pareto efficient outcomes and the geometry of the surplus set in a screening model with type-dependent costs. Under mild cost-curvature conditions, agent-oriented optima use rather than suppress screening to sustain information rents: all agents are served, allocations strictly separate types, and an atom at the highest type receives the efficient allocation. Each Pareto efficient payoff is implemented by a unique market. When costs are type independent or a type with no gains from trade is feasible, we also characterize the entire surplus set and establish its convexity. Otherwise, type-dependent costs can generate nonconvexity. Market segmentation can expand attainable outcomes only on the rent-suppression side of the set, without increasing maximum agent surplus at any level of principal surplus. The characterization and comparative statics link market formation to the distribution of surplus and identify the limits on payoffs attainable under screening.

items.title: Choosing Complexity: Cognitive Ability, Overconfidence, and Task Choice
items.summary: Workers and organizations routinely choose between complex tasks that differ in their success-payment tradeoff. We study how cognitive ability and overconfidence shape this choice of task complexity, both theoretically and experimentally. Consistent with our model, we find that more cognitively able individuals choose more complex tasks. Conditional on cognitive ability, we find that more overconfident individuals also choose more complex tasks. In about 75% of the decisions, subjects pick their payoff-maximizing task, and higher cognitive ability is weakly associated with more efficient choices of task complexity. But errors are strikingly one-sided: those who fail to choose optimally pick tasks that are too complex. Our findings suggest that organizations should pair task menus and incentives for choosing more complex tasks with information and feedback that help workers assess their ability and probability of success. This preserves the benefits of self-selection while reducing costly overreach.

items.title: Dynamic investment and coordination in teams: Theory and experimental evidence
items.summary: Teamwork requires more than the general skills that team members bring. In successful teams, members invest in team-specific skill or capital that accumulates within the team and raises the return to coordinated production. We provide the first systematic analysis of dynamic investment in such team skill. Adopting a dynamic game approach, we develop a novel theoretical framework where investment in team skill creates persistent benefits but is risky because the benefits depend on successful team coordination. We then take this framework to the laboratory to study empirically the factors that influence dynamic investment in team skill. We find underinvestment compared to the efficient benchmark. However, investment responds strongly to incentives, in line with specific theory-predicted patterns. Pre-registered traits (theory of mind and propensity to coordinate) predict investment and team-level efficiency. We conclude that careful design of team incentives and selection of team members can facilitate the development of team skill.

items.title: Taste or Strategy? Nationalistic Bias and Competitor Penalties in Figure Skating Judging
items.summary: Many decisions rest on expert panels whose members have ties to some candidates, and favoritism is hard to tell from shared taste or better information. Using a rich dataset from figure skating, we find evidence of a strategic compatriot premium and a targeted penalty on the compatriot's close rivals. The premium falls along a randomly drawn start order and, before 2022/23, rises when close rivals have their own judges on the panel. The penalty grows with the compatriot's placement chances and fades once she is out of contention. A counterfactual analysis shows that these biases can shape close competitions.

items.title: On the Nonemptiness of the Core: Connecting Cooperative Games and Asset Pricing
items.summary: We show that the Bondareva--Shapley theorem for infinite cooperative games can be derived from a version of the fundamental theorem of asset pricing. The link is the Choquet extension of a game, viewed as a possibly nonlinear pricing rule on the space of measurable simple payoffs. Under this identification, balancedness translates into no arbitrage, and a linear functional dominated by the pricing rule yields an allocation in the anti-core; the core statement follows by duality. Applying the arbitrage-free pricing theorem of Cornet (2025), we recover the characterization of the nonvacuity of the core initiated by Schmeidler (1967) and established in full generality by Bartl and Pinter (2023) for bounded-below games. Unlike the earlier derivation in Cornet (2025), our argument does not require the game to have bounded variation or the collection of coalitions to be a $σ$-algebra.

items.title: State-Dependent Local Projections and Vector Autoregressions
items.summary: This paper studies the relationship between state-dependent local projections (LPs) and vector autoregressions (VARs). I show nonparametrically that state-dependent LPs estimate the projection of a convex weighted average of causal effects on the state, including continuous and multidimensional states. In contrast, conventional state-dependent VARs need not have a causal interpretation, even when they model state transitions correctly. A new backshifted VAR, conditioning every prediction step on the pre-shock state, asymptotically matches the LP estimand up to its lag order.

items.title: Identification, estimation, and robust inference of structural autoregressions for multidimensional data
items.summary: Many modern datasets such as cross-country panels have a multidimensional structure. Conventional approaches on structural vector autoregressions for identifying structural shocks are not directly suited to these settings where data are naturally organized as matrices or tensors, since the number of parameters grows rapidly and identifying restrictions become hard to impose. We introduce a class of structural autoregressions for multidimensional data that achieves tractability and global identification by assuming a Kronecker structure on the model coefficients. We develop a minimum-distance estimator and establish its asymptotic distribution. To accommodate approximate Kronecker separability, we develop confidence intervals for the structural impulse response functions that are robust to local misspecification, and we show their asymptotic validity. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate the validity of the asymptotic approximations and good finite-sample performance of the estimator and their (robust) confidence intervals. We illustrate the methods on a country panel dataset to analyze the dynamic and spillover effects of US monetary policy shocks.

items.title: Dynamic Regression Discontinuity: An Event-Study Approach
items.summary: I propose a novel argument to identify economically interpretable intertemporal treatment effects in dynamic regression discontinuity designs (RDDs). I develop a dynamic potential outcomes model and reformulate two assumptions from the difference-in-differences literature, no anticipation and common trends, to attain point identification of cutoff-specific impulse responses. Each time-specific parameter can be expressed as the sum of two static RDD contrasts, allowing for estimation with standard local polynomial methods and robust bias-corrected inference. I also propose a nonparametric approach to aggregate treatment effects across calendar time and treatment histories, and use a limited path independence restriction to reduce the number of history-specific estimands. I apply this method to estimate the dynamic effects of school district expenditure authorizations on housing prices in Wisconsin.

items.title: Learning to Choose with Categories: Theory and an Application to Algorithmic Prominence
items.summary: We introduce Coarse Q-learning, a reinforcement learning framework in which a decision-maker partitions alternatives into coarse similarity classes, chooses among available classes using logit, and learns class valuations by averaging experienced payoffs. Even in stationary bandit problems with independently drawn menus, choices change the composition of pooled feedback. By deriving the continuous-time mean field ODE limit, we show this endogenous sampling can generate a unique globally attracting mixed equilibrium with limiting indifference, multiple stable strict rankings, or persistent cycling. Learning can reduce welfare even when the coarse representation admits efficient choice. An application demonstrates how digital platforms may exploit this feedback by promoting high-quality products to sustain purchases of inferior products under a common brand.

items.title: That Time of the Year Again: Government Pay Revisions in the Aggregate Economy
items.summary: Public pay is set by law in nominal terms, so inflation erodes its real value between legal acts until the government revises it. I model each revision as the choice of a forward-looking government, shaped by two costs that push in opposite directions. A fixed cost of acting makes revisions large and rare, whereas a convex cost of financing the increase at once makes them small and frequent. Through the budget, each revision also moves debt and the risk of fiscal stress under which the next one is made. In the documented pay decisions of eleven countries, pay set at discretion erodes against prices and private earnings and is restored in discrete steps, every cut was decided during market stress or an adjustment program, and court rulings drove a wedge between the cuts legislated, the cuts paid and the cuts that lasted. Estimated on the legal acts, the model reproduces the documented paths of pay in most countries when data and simulations are measured the same way. In Portugal's estimated model, the savings that the Treasury requires once spreads rise produce the cuts, the debt overhang holds pay down after the crisis, and a court that strikes cuts after they take effect invites cuts it will strike. Review of cuts before they took effect would have lowered the social cost of Portugal's crisis relative to review after the fact, and partial indexation would have paid in Bangladesh unless its automatic increases were costly to finance.

items.title: A Game-Theoretic Framework for Resource Allocation under Institutional Asymmetry
items.summary: We develop a two-player knapsack game to investigate resource allocation under individual capacity constraints, competition over shared resources, and institutional asymmetry. Players select feasible subsets of resources, while their payoffs depend on competitive losses, allocation rules, and asymmetric institutional benefits and costs. We derive the aggregate welfare function and show that allocation coefficients redistribute payoffs without directly affecting total welfare, whereas institutional parameters influence welfare through their net contribution. Consequently, institutional arrangements with identical welfare effects may induce different strategic incentives and Nash equilibrium outcomes. We analyze how capacity constraints and institutional priority shape equilibrium configurations and their welfare properties. A central result concerns the distinction between the social efficiency and strategic stability of shared resources. We derive conditions under which sharing is socially preferable to exclusive allocation yet remains strategically unstable because the non-priority player can increase their payoff by abandoning the resource. Conversely, sharing may remain strategically stable even when exclusive allocation yields higher aggregate welfare. These findings demonstrate that social efficiency and strategic stability need not coincide under institutional asymmetry.

items.title: Fiscal Commitment and the Additionality of Philanthropy: Heterogeneous Donor Purposes in a Shared Public Budget
items.summary: Philanthropic donors often value different public services, while a budget authority allocates public spending across a shared portfolio. Policy frameworks frequently seek to ensure that private finance supplements rather than displaces public funding. We distinguish baseline additionality, which preserves pre-gift public funding, from portfolio preservation, which preserves a service's provision after all gifts are pooled under discretionary budgeting. A larger gift to one service raises the discretionary provision of every service and reduces the protection slack available to the others. This cross-donor fiscal externality yields an exact feasibility result: if a service's maximum permissible floor lies below its discretionary post-gift provision, every effective protection reform reduces that service relative to the portfolio reference, including full protection of its own appropriation. Conversely, a reform that expands at least one donor-backed service while preserving all others exists exactly when every maximum floor reaches the reference. The paper characterizes the complete preservation set and its welfare-maximizing element. Under logarithmic preferences, donation shares determine protectability, while heterogeneous donor valuations determine welfare incidence. Baseline additionality may therefore hold while a service loses fiscal benefits generated by other gifts.

items.title: Organizational Lifespan as Commitment: The Case of Foundations
items.summary: An organization's lifespan may commit future decision makers to continue, terminate, or retain discretion. We identify when each rule has value for philanthropic foundations. If the same aligned actor chooses investment and subsequent survival, discretion weakly dominates fixed rules; a commonly used investment comparison fails because it omits the option to invest enough to make continuation desirable in adverse states. With noncontractible organizational investment delegated to an earlier actor, however, perpetuity may improve incentives despite inefficient continuation in some states. The result survives an observable-investment extension. A finite terminal date is valuable under governance-induced overcontinuation, and its optimum reflects both direct operating benefits and investment incentives. We establish nonempty environments favoring each regime and distinguish institutional lifespan from payout policy, requirements to preserve the foundation's endowment capital, and the duration of grant commitments.

items.title: Fueling Inflation Risks: An Oil Shortage Scenario
items.summary: Central banks routinely use alternative scenarios to assess risks to the economic outlook, but these are usually generated from linear models that are unable to speak to the likelihood of extreme outcomes. We develop a nonlinear modeling framework that turns a narrative oil market scenario into a fully probabilistic assessment of the dynamics of oil and gasoline prices, aggregate inflation, and household inflation expectations. It combines an expert-based path for a tail event, a nonparametric model of the global oil market, and nonlinear Phillips curves for the energy, food, and core components of PCE inflation. We apply it in real time to quantify energy price and inflation risks of a severe oil shortage caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, modeled as a rapid drawdown of global petroleum inventories, using only information available in February 2026. Our analysis shows that once oil reserves hit rock bottom, oil and gasoline prices rise sharply, with risks tilted to the upside. Headline PCE inflation peaks near 4.8% in late 2026, and households expect inflation to rise by about 3 percentage points. Two years out, inflation is still highly likely to exceed the Fed's 2% target.

items.title: Inequality-Aware Regulation
items.summary: I study regulation of a screening monopolist when the regulator cares about the distribution of surplus across heterogeneous consumers and the firm. Consumers privately know their willingness to pay for quality, and the firm privately knows its production costs. Regulatory contracts specify quality-price options that the firm must offer. I show that when the regulator gives greater weight to consumers with lower willingness to pay, baseline regulation is optimal: the regulator requires affordable basic options but leaves the firm free to design and price premium options. Under strong consumer-side redistributive concerns, a single required basic option suffices. The regulator uses the firm's incentive to extract surplus from premium buyers to support low regulated prices for basic options.

items.title: Wage-Setting Constraints and Firm Responses to Demand Shocks
items.summary: This paper investigates how institutional wage-setting constraints, such as a national minimum wage or collectively bargained wages, affect firm responses to demand shocks. We develop a framework to interpret heterogeneous shock responses that depend on the constraints firms face, and provide empirical evidence on the relevance of these constraints in shaping firm behavior in Portugal and Norway, two countries with different institutional settings. We discuss the implications of our findings for conventional measures of employer wage-setting power and rent-sharing.

items.title: When the Norm is Wrong: Social Norm Misspecification and Targeting with an Application to Microfinance Adoption
items.summary: Structural models of peer effects typically capture peer influence through the average, aggregate, or in some cases through extreme peer actions. Such specifications, however, are imposed ex ante and are typically ad hoc. We study the consequences of social norm misspecification by extending the constant elasticity of substitution (CES) norm from continuous to discrete choices. Considering a binary-choice game with incomplete information, we derive results on existence and uniqueness of a rational expectations equilibrium and establish conditions for identification of the structural parameters. We estimate the model by the Nested Pseudo-Likelihood estimator, implemented using the spectral algorithm. Monte Carlo simulations show that the CES estimates of the peer effects approach their true values as the sample grows, whereas imposing a linear norm biases them even in large samples. We apply the framework to microfinance adoption in India and find a strongly max-leaning norm, with significant heterogeneity in curvature and peer effects across villages grouped by caste composition and wealth. In a counterfactual exercise that allocates a fixed subsidy budget to maximise adoption, the estimated and linear norms target very different households, with the former favouring village "leaders", who are more likely to adopt and were the first to be informed about microfinance.

items.title: Work that Counts, and Work that Doesn't: Reconciling Experimental and Observational Labor Supply Elasticities
items.summary: Do workers behave the same in experiments as they do in real life? Combining a real-effort emoji-counting experiment with platform records, self-reported expectations and recalls, and smartphone screen-time logs, we compare how the same workers on Prolific respond to wage changes in the experiment and in their actual work. Our results reveal that workers' behavior in experiments is remarkably different from their behavior in real life. In the observational window, in fact, workers respond to expected wage changes just as they do in the experiment, but are much less responsive to unanticipated changes. However, once we condition on recall error in self-reports, we find that behavior in the two windows aligns. Recall error is then both a source of error in self-reported data and the result of a process of inattention that affects effort itself, as workers do not respond to unexpected wage changes that pass unnoticed.

items.title: Individual incentives and uniform gains under symmetric constraints
items.summary: We study the division of a fixed total under symmetric joint constraints when agents have continuous, strictly single-peaked preferences over their own shares. Each agent reports a complete preference, including comparisons across the two sides of her peak. For any finite population and any nonempty closed convex permutation-invariant feasible set, we characterize the uniform-gains rule by efficiency, symmetry, individual strategy-proofness, and own-coordinate peak-onlyness. The last condition requires that a change of preference leaving an agent's peak fixed also leave her own share fixed; it places no direct restriction on others' shares. The characterization separates uniqueness from continuity and yields a continuous characterization with individual incentives for compact feasible sets that are polyhedral or relatively full-dimensional and strictly convex. We then show that, for every population of two through six agents and every nonempty compact convex permutation-invariant feasible set, efficiency, symmetry, and individual strategy-proofness alone characterize uniform gains. The proof recovers allocations from the shares attainable by unilateral reports, feasible transfers, and endpoint reports. A common induction applies at each population, with additional starting configurations for five and six agents.

items.title: Does fare communication format matter? Evidence from a randomised experiment in public transport
items.summary: Highly concentrated demand in public transport places pressure on infrastructure and reduces service quality. Pricing instruments-such as discounted off-peak single fare tickets-are a widely used tool for rescheduling demand across time. Yet no study has directly examined whether the price communication format of single fare tickets affects travel behaviour in terms of departure-time rescheduling. To fill this gap, we exploit a randomised stated preference survey conducted in Switzerland based on participants' actual journeys (n = 1,082), assigning participants to one of three price formats: absolute amounts, absolute deviations, or percentage deviations from their current fare. Estimating a multinomial logit model with price-format interaction terms, we find no significant effect of communication format on aggregate price sensitivity. However, for low-fare trips, percentage-based communication substantially amplifies price sensitivity relative to absolute amounts or absolute deviations. Moreover, when prices are shown as percentage deviations, price sensitivity increases for small price spreads and decreases for large price spreads, with a crossover point corresponding to a discount depth of approximately 47%. In summary, these findings suggest that percentage-based price communication has the potential to reinforce the demand-shifting effect of off-peak discounts, particularly for low-fare products and for discounts shallower than approximately 47%.

items.title: A Note on Qualified Majority Voting Rules
items.summary: This note characterizes every qualified majority voting rule (up to the designation of the reform) in environments with just two alternatives through anonymity, responsiveness, and q-neutrality. Crucially, the latter imposes independence of the labels of the alternatives if and only if some alternative is strictly top-ranked by at least q voters. The axioms also rule out quotas not exceeding half the electorate. Thus, this note provides a characterization in the spirit of May (1952, Theorem, p. 682) that identifies the quota of each qualified majority voting rule through its degree of neutrality.

items.title: Equilibrium Selection in Coordination Games with Planned Actions and Scouting
items.summary: We study Stag Hunt games in which every action requires planning and preparation. Before players act, they observe noisy signals of their opponent's preparations and can revise their plans, which allows players to screen for cooperation. As screening becomes more precise and cheap, small trembles ensure that, in every equilibrium, play yields the payoff-dominant outcome with a probability that converges to one, even when the safe, low payoff equilibrium is risk dominant. Across scenarios, we emphasize that decomposing an action into (i) preparation and (ii) execution allows us to analyze simultaneous-move games in which players partially observe each other's contemporaneous actions.

items.title: Risk-insurance parity
items.summary: Risk aversion and insurance are two prominent and interconnected concepts in economics and finance. To explore their fundamental connection, we introduce risk-insurance parity, which associates various classes of insurance contracts with different notions of risk aversion. We show that the classic notions - both weak and strong - of risk aversion can be characterized by propensity to different classes of insurance contracts, generalizing recent results on propensity to full, proportional, and deductible-limit contracts in the literature. We examine in depth classes of insurance indemnity functions that correspond to weak and strong risk aversion. We show that one proportional-indemnity contract is enough to obtain equivalence with strong risk aversion. Risk-insurance parity allows us to define two new notions of risk aversion, between weak and strong, characterized by insurance propensity to deductible-only and limit-only contracts, respectively.

items.title: Disappointment Aversion and Expectiles
items.summary: This paper recasts Gul's (1991) theory of disappointment aversion in a Savage framework, with general outcomes, new explicit axioms of disappointment aversion, and novel explicit representations. These permit broader applications of the theory and a better understanding of its decision-theoretic foundations. Our results exploit an unexpected connection between Gul's model and the econometric framework of Newey and Powell (1987) of asymmetric least squares estimation. Our main axiomatization result shows that a preference relation over Savage acts is probabilistically sophisticated, invariant biseparable, and disappointment hedging if and only if it admits a representation \emph{à la} Gul, and hence all explicit equivalent representations that we present in the paper. We also derive a neurocomputational foundation of the theory based on recent neuroscience findings and a novel reinforcement learning result.

items.title: Separable social welfare evaluation without completeness
items.summary: In this paper, we study incomplete social evaluation of utility vectors to capture situations in which there is disagreement in society about the degree of inequality aversion. We characterize multi-prioritarian criteria using efficiency, equity, impartiality, separability, and a condition called continuous divisible completion condition. We also provide uniqueness results and investigate comparative inequality aversion.

items.title: Distributionally Robust Rational Inattention
items.summary: We study a rational inattention model in which a decision maker chooses a stochastic choice rule while facing ambiguity about the prior distribution over states. Ambiguity is modeled through a distributionally robust formulation in which the prior belongs to an uncertainty set defined by a general phi-divergence. Our main result establishes an exact Lagrangian dual representation of the resulting max-min problem as a finite-dimensional concave optimization problem. This characterization yields necessary and sufficient conditions for the emergence of robust consideration sets and a tractable one-dimensional dual representation for the Cressie-Read family of divergences. We further connect the model to robust risk measures: Average Value-at-Risk arises from a particular non-smooth divergence, while Kullback-Leibler ambiguity is linked through Lagrangian duality to the entropic-risk multiplier representation. We then develop two extensions. The first allows the attention-cost technology and prior ambiguity to be governed by distinct phi-divergences, while the second introduces a deeper layer of ambiguity over the decision maker's baseline prior. Both extensions preserve the finite-dimensional structure of the model and encompass standard Kullback-Leibler robust rational inattention specifications as special or corresponding multiplier cases.

items.title: Realized Stochastic Volatility Models with Skew-t Distributions for Volatility and Tail Risk Forecasting
items.summary: Volatility forecasts underlie tail risk measures: value-at-risk (VaR) and expected shortfall (ES). This paper compares realized stochastic volatility (RSV) models, which add a realized measure to the stochastic volatility (SV) model, with their SV counterparts under normal, Student's t, two skew-normal, and three skew-t return distributions, and against EGARCH and REGARCH benchmarks. Estimated by Markov chain Monte Carlo on the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the Nikkei 225, the models are compared by their one-day-ahead volatility, VaR, and ES forecasts (the predictive mean for volatility). Adding realized volatility improves volatility forecasts over the main sample for both indices under every proxy and return distribution; the gains are uniformly significant for the Nikkei 225 but, for the Dow Jones, only under the realized variance used in estimation. During the COVID-19 period the gains persist for the Nikkei 225 but vanish for the Dow Jones, where the REGARCH benchmark is best. For VaR and ES the gains are confined to the Nikkei 225 and to the 5% level for the Dow Jones, and few matched-pair differences are significant. Skewed innovations lower the 1% joint loss for the Dow Jones, but no specification dominates across indices, risk levels, and sample periods.

items.title: Fairness Drift: Assessing Algorithmic Fairness in a Moving Market
items.summary: Flexible models and richer data can reduce systematic valuation errors and improve fairness. Yet algorithmic values stay fixed between updates while the market moves, so a new algorithm gains most against an intact distortion and least where uneven appreciation has eroded or just reversed it. We study property assessment, which sets tax bills and has long over-assessed cheaper homes. Cook County replaced township regressions and manual adjustments with a gradient-boosted model and richer data on its triennial cycle: Chicago in 2021, northern suburbs in 2022, southern in 2023. We estimate difference-in-differences in how the assessment-to-price ratio varies with sale price and neighborhood minority share. In Chicago, the reform halved the relative over-assessment of cheaper homes and, among equally priced homes, weakened the link to neighborhood racial composition. In the suburbs the price gradient was unchanged: the North's legacy values were already accurate, and the South's cheap neighborhoods had appreciated faster under frozen values, correcting part of the distortion, then stalled in the reassessment year, leaving the new values too high where prices had gained and accuracy unimproved. Fairness thus drifts with the market between updates, and single-deployment evaluations may credit or blame the algorithm for what the market did.

items.title: Jornada de trabalho, produtividade e informalidade: uma avaliacao quantitativa para o Brasil
items.summary: This paper quantifies the total factor productivity (TFP) gain required to offset the short-run output loss associated with alternative weekly working-hour ceilings in Brazil. We combine moments from the 2024Q4 PNAD Contínua with a static partial-equilibrium model in which formal and informal labor are imperfect substitutes, hourly efficiency depends on working hours, and formalization wedges govern the composition of employment. To represent reductions from 44 to 40 and 36 hours, we initially cap formal workers' usual hours at 44 as a baseline measurement assumption. The 40-hour alternative requires 1.53-1.57% higher TFP. Moving to 36 hours requires 6.52--8.38%, depending on the efficiency assumption below 40 hours; informality rises by 2.28-2.92 percentage points in the same counterfactual. Decompositions show that fewer physical formal hours account for the largest negative component of the output change. Comparison with Brazil's historical TFP path and welfare exercises suggests an important quantitative difference between moderate reforms and the 36-hour ceiling. Magnitudes depend on fatigue and baseline hours: retaining the observed usual-hours tail above 44 reduces the requirement at 40 hours to approximately 0.07%. The results motivate the assessment of gradual paths and transition instruments, without providing a causal estimate of the effects of a specific legislative proposal.

items.title: Difference-in-differences with a mediator
items.summary: Causal mediation analysis is a powerful tool for decomposing the total effect of a treatment into its direct effect on the outcome and its indirect effect mediated through an intermediate variable. However, in observational studies, confounding between treatment and potential outcomes typically renders the total and natural effects non-identifiable. In this work, we advance the mediation analysis within the difference-in-differences framework. Under a mediator-adjusted parallel trends assumption and additional conditions, we demonstrate that natural indirect, direct, and total effects are identifiable in the treated group. We further derive efficient influence functions for these estimands, enabling the construction of multiply robust and nonparametrically efficient estimators. Applying our methodology to data from the Job Corps Study, we find that job training has a positive direct effect on short-term earnings, holding employment intensity fixed at its level under training, which is masked in the total effect by reduced work time; in the longer run, the total effect is positive and operates mainly through higher employment intensity.

items.title: What is Work For? Labor, Politics, and Meaning in the Age of AI
items.summary: This paper investigates the role of work in providing meaning, purpose, community, and other non-monetary benefits. Using an original cross-national survey of 8,234 working-age adults across the UK, US, Denmark, and India, I study the factors that motivate people in their work, with an eye toward the future AI economic transformation. I find that 81% of respondents report being satisfied with their job, and a majority across all four countries are strongly motivated by the non-monetary components of their employment. Using an original "Work Values" Index, I show that one third of working respondents are motivated intrinsically by their job--valuing their role for its own sake. Nearly one quarter are driven by social and community-related aspects of their employment, 17% by social status, and just over one quarter by the transactional financial benefits of their job. Although a majority of people would leave their role if offered their current salary as a guaranteed income, one fifth of workers would stay even if offered up to 120% of their salary. Intrinsically motivated workers were disproportionately likely to refuse a basic income at any substitution level. Groups attached to their job for non-monetary reasons were also more likely to pursue volunteering or work-like activities if they received guaranteed income substitution but could no longer perform their role. Crucially, these non-monetary work motivations are evenly distributed across the income distribution and between white- and blue-collar workers. I argue that these findings have implications for managing the AI transition, understanding attitudes to AI, and making sense of policy preferences. Guaranteeing a basic income may indeed be necessary for managing any future AI labor shock, yet it could ultimately fail to compensate workers for any loss of the non-monetary benefits they derive from work.

items.title: Whom Do AI Agents Serve? Role-Induced Sponsorship Bias in Decision Models and Generative LLMs
items.summary: Consumers increasingly delegate product search to AI shopping agents powered by generative large language models (LLMs) or non-generative decision models. Because retail platforms monetize through sponsored listings that consumers typically discount, we examine whether an AI agent's evaluation of sponsored listings depends on who delegates it. Across six LLMs and six decision models in Study 1, consumer-delegated agents penalize sponsored listings, whereas naming a booking platform as principal significantly attenuates this sponsorship penalty without instructions to favor advertisers. This sponsorship bias replicates across prompt wordings and LLM reasoning efforts and operates through reduced pre-choice skepticism in LLMs. In Study 2, attributing the paid placement to the platform amplifies sponsorship bias across both model families, and stricter disclosure wording ("Sponsored" vs. "Promoted") fails to eliminate it. In Study 3, prompt-level mitigation removes platform leniency but can over-correct the sponsorship penalty, whereas consumer-aligned fine-tuning eliminates sponsorship bias and better preserves baseline preferences.

items.title: Interacting Principal-Agent Games
items.summary: In many economic environments, multiple principals simultaneously design incentive systems while interacting strategically with one another. The resulting incentive constraints are interdependent: whether a mechanism is incentive compatible for one principal may depend on the mechanisms chosen by the other principals. This interdependence makes exact equilibrium fragile: small changes in one principal's mechanism can alter the incentive-compatible mechanisms available to others. We establish two complementary equilibrium-existence results. First, for environments with multidimensional type, action, and outcome spaces, we show that, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a Bayesian-Nash principals' equilibrium under $\varepsilon$-relaxed incentive compatibility: principals best respond exactly over mechanisms whose agents' ex ante expected deviation regret is at most $\varepsilon$. Thus equilibrium existence can be recovered with arbitrarily small expected incentive regret. In contrast to Myerson's quasi-equilibrium, which keeps incentive compatibility exact but relaxes the principals' optimality requirement, this concept keeps principals' optimization exact and relaxes the agents' incentive constraints. Second, motivated by Myerson's nonexistence example, in which each principal has a single privately informed agent, we examine a one-member team-contest specialization of the general model with voluntary participation. This specialization retains the basic structure of Myerson's setting (competing principals, privately informed agents, and interdependent incentive constraints) while imposing primitive conditions under which exact feasibility varies continuously. In this environment, we establish existence of an exact Bayesian-Nash principals' equilibrium.

items.title: Continuous difference-in-differences with double/debiased machine learning
items.summary: This paper extends difference-in-differences to settings with continuous treatments. Specifically, the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) at any level of treatment intensity is identified under a conditional parallel trends assumption. Estimating the ATT in this framework requires first estimating infinite-dimensional nuisance parameters, particularly the conditional density of the continuous treatment, which can introduce substantial bias. To address this challenge, we propose estimators for the causal parameters under the double/debiased machine learning framework and establish their asymptotic normality. Additionally, we provide consistent variance estimators and construct uniform confidence bands based on a multiplier bootstrap procedure. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we revisit a previous study on the 1983 Medicare Prospective Payment System reform, reframing it as a DiD with continuous treatment and non-parametrically estimating its effects.

items.title: Conventional Inference under Nonstationary Heavy Tailed Fractional Processes & Arrays
items.summary: Existing regression inference methods for nonstationary heavy tailed data are largely limited to unit roots tests. Functional central limit theorems (FCLTs), which are commonly used for the asymptotic analysis of nonstationary models, are inapplicable to nonstationary data characterized by a memory parameter $d<1$ and a stability parameter $α<2$. Furthermore, it is well known that inference under nonstationarity is often non-conventional, and this issue is exacerbated in the presence of heavy-tailed data. The interaction of long memory and heavy tails significantly enlarges the nonstationary region---i.e., the covariate model space---where conventional inference methods typically fail. To address these challenges, we propose a new limit theory and methods that facilitate both workable asymptotics and conventional inference in parametric regressions involving stationary and nonstationary heavy-tailed covariate processes. Specifically, our approach develops a limit theory for three classes of heavy-tailed weakly nonstationary processes (hereafter, HT-WNPs), which lie on the threshold of nonstationarity (cf. Duffy and Kasparis, 2021, Annals of Statistics). We also develop limit theory for functionals of strongly nonstationary heavy-tailed fractional processes. We demonstrate that the proposed methods, particularly a weighted extension of IVX, facilitate conventional inference for a broad class of stationary and nonstationary heavy-tailed covariates. This class includes mildly and nearly integrated arrays, as well as nonstationary fractional processes with memory parameter $1-1/α<d<2-1/α$, where $α\in(1,2]$. A related weighted instrumental-variable estimator is also considered, primarily for estimation purposes.

items.title: Optimal power expansion planning under uncertainty in sub-Saharan Africa: A stochastic dual dynamic programming approach
items.summary: Universal electricity access and decarbonization are interlinked challenges for sub-Saharan Africa. Generation expansion planning methods used in the region rarely represent sequential and irreversible investment under demand and hydrological uncertainty. This paper develops a multistage stochastic generation expansion model solved with stochastic dual dynamic programming (SDDP) to address the problem. The model represents demand and country-specific Markov hydrological uncertainty, accounts for technology-specific construction lead times, and endogenous reliability. The model is applied to the Ethiopia and Zimbabwe power systems over 2025--2050. The results show that for Ethiopia, the least-cost pathway is hydropower, with wind and solar sources providing increasing diversification. The model reduces cumulative expected unserved energy by about 78 TWh relative to a lower-cost deterministic expected value investment plan. For Zimbabwe, the least-cost pathway expands solar, hydropower, and gas while retaining residual coal as inherited coal capacity retires. Additionally, carbon pricing reduces emissions and increases resource costs by about 3\% to 5\%, creating a gradual cost-emissions trade-off. Combining a carbon tax policy with concessional solar financing renders the lowest average annual emissions while keeping resource costs below the baseline, which solves the model without emission constraint. At approximately matched expected emissions, emission caps have higher net resource costs than the corresponding carbon tax scenarios. The overall results imply that adaptive investment model can reduce power shortage exposure, while carbon policy design and lower clean investment costs shape the cost of decarbonization in developing power systems.

items.title: Tracking the economy at high frequency
items.summary: This paper develops a high-frequency economic indicator using a Bayesian Dynamic Factor Model estimated with mixed-frequency data. The model incorporates weekly, monthly, and quarterly official indicators, and allows for dynamic heterogeneity and stochastic volatility. To ensure temporal consistency and avoid irregular aggregation artifacts, we introduce a pseudo-week structure that harmonizes the timing of observations. Our framework integrates dispersed and asynchronous official statistics into a unified High-Frequency Economic Index (HFEI), enabling real-time economic monitoring even in environments characterized by severe data limitations. We apply this framework to construct a high-frequency indicator for Ecuador, a country where official data are sparse and highly asynchronous, and compute pseudo-weekly recession probabilities using a time-varying mean regime-switching model fitted to the resulting index.

items.title: Large-Market Discipline in Combinatorial Double Auctions: No Recombination, Bundle Selection, and Complementarities
items.summary: Licences can forbid assembling bundles from several sellers or splitting them among buyers, a restriction we call No Recombination. We study its welfare cost in a double auction as the number of traders on each side of the market grows. We ask whether that cost vanishes as a share of welfare, as the gain from misreporting does with a single good. With two goods and Gaussian shocks, consider the prices that would prevail under free recombination. As the market grows, the loss as a share of optimal welfare vanishes if and only if expected demand for the two-good bundle equals expected supply of whole bundles at those prices. Otherwise the loss persists. In our market, sellers can never gain by misreporting. With two goods, buyers who commit to bidding their values plus fixed margins misreport in symmetric equilibria by amounts that vanish as the market grows. Under these conditions, in large markets No Recombination outweighs strategic bidding as a source of loss.

items.title: Robust Contracts with Exploration
items.summary: We study a moral hazard problem over an arbitrary finite horizon, with multiple agents whose action sets are unknown to the principal. The principal contracts with the agents sequentially and seeks to maximize the worst-case discounted sum of payoffs, where the worst case is over the possible action sets. The principal observes the action chosen by each agent, and then offers a new contract to the next agent based on the knowledge accumulated so far, thus having the opportunity to explore in every period before the final one. We introduce and compare three different notions of dynamic worst-case evaluation. Within each notion, we define a suitable rule of updating and characterize the principal's optimal payoff guarantee. We find that linear contracts are robustly optimal not only in static settings, but also in dynamic environments with exploration.

items.title: Delegation without Priors
items.summary: A principal makes decisions relying on the private information held by a biased agent. Lacking a prior over the circumstances that may arise, she seeks a delegation rule that minimizes worst-case regret relative to the complete-information benchmark. The optimal delegation mechanism governs two distinct margins: whether to depart from a common default action, and how much discretion to grant conditional on departure. This rule pairs the default action with an action gap, followed by a discretionary interval with randomized boundaries designed to balance regret across states. This structure is globally optimal within the class of all stochastic, incentive-compatible mechanisms.

items.title: Information Aggregation in Markets with Analysts, Experts, and Chatbots
items.summary: We study information aggregation when traders interpret public news, such as analyst reports, differently. This differential interpretation injects noise into equilibrium prices, compounding the informational bottleneck caused by noise traders. Next to analysts and experts, we consider the role of ``AI" chatbots, which (i) provide free financial advice and (ii) analyze traders' queries to learn about the asset's fundamental. Our model predicts that (i) chatbots aggregate information more efficiently than markets, (ii) increase trade volume, and (iii) enhance the informational content of prices. Ultimately, the AI platform extracts an absolute informational advantage over other market participants, highlighting a structural shift from information aggregation through market prices to ``AI" platforms.

items.title: Semiparametric Identification of the Discount Factor and Payoff Function in Dynamic Discrete Choice Models
items.summary: This paper studies the identification of the discount factor and payoff function in stationary infinite-horizon dynamic discrete choice models. In single-agent models, we show that nonparametric assumptions on per-period payoffs implied by economic theory, such as homogeneity, monotonicity, concavity, zero cross-differences, and complementarity, yield polynomial equalities and inequalities in the discount factor. These restrictions can identify the discount factor and the payoff function without normalizing the payoff of one action. Even when the payoff function is not point identified, they may still identify the discount factor. In dynamic games, we identify firm-specific discount factors by combining the irrelevance of other firms' lagged actions with restrictions such as exchangeability, even when the scrap value is unknown. We illustrate the approach with numerical examples and an empirical application to farmers' crop choices.

items.title: Information Divergence and Endogenous Evolution of Asymmetric Information
items.summary: Standard theories trace information asymmetry to privately held information, heterogeneous signals, or costly information acquisition. We identify a distinct mechanism: otherwise identical rational agents observing a common Markov state at asynchronous times can hold different predictive distributions because their information differs in age. When the transition kernel separates information ages, independent Bernoulli observation arrivals make such divergence recur infinitely often almost surely, even with identical arrival probabilities. When agents instead choose costly updating intensities, independent update realizations can regenerate heterogeneous information ages among ex ante identical agents. In a stationary Gaussian AR(1) environment, the consequences depend on common staleness as well as the age gap: holding the gap fixed, older information raises individual uncertainty while reducing expected squared forecast disagreement and the value of certifying relative freshness. This generates stale consensus: low disagreement despite high uncertainty. With multiple ordered ages, costly certification supports partial-unraveling equilibria in which fresher types certify and sufficiently stale types pool. Under geometric information ages, more frequent updating weakly lowers the smallest and largest equilibrium disclosure cutoffs wherever positive-certification equilibria exist. The framework has implications for credit, insurance, financial markets, and multi-agent AI.

items.title: Testing Conditional Moment Restrictions in Networks
items.summary: Parametric models of network formation, such as dyadic logit models, are increasingly popular, but few tools exist to test their specification. This paper develops a specification test for conditionally independent dyad (CID) models based on the probabilities that these models assign to subgraphs, the patterns of links among small groups of agents. Given the agents' characteristics, a parametric CID model determines not only the probability of each link but also the probability that a group of agents forms a triangle, a star, or any other subgraph. Under correct specification, the expected frequency of each subgraph among agents with given characteristics equals its model-implied probability. This forms the basis of the testable conditional moment restrictions. The test statistic is the weighted integrated squared distance between a nonparametric kernel estimate of these probabilities and the probabilities implied by the estimated parametric model. I derive its asymptotic distribution under the null hypothesis.

items.title: Fair Combinatorial Auctions
items.summary: An efficient and stable auction can leave the seller with no share of the surplus. We study how the gains from a combinatorial auction can be shared as equally as possible between the seller and buyers while respecting coalitional stability. We show that, when buyers are substitutes, the core is described by individual caps on the buyers' payoffs and contains a unique Lorenz-dominant payoff vector. Each buyer receives the seller's payoff capped at her marginal contribution. The seller consequently receives at least an equal share of the total surplus, without compromising efficiency or stability. We then construct a complete-information bargaining game in which the seller proposes a division of the surplus and rejecting buyers receive exit payments. Without discounting, the game fully implements the Lorenz-dominant vector in pure-strategy subgame-perfect equilibrium: an equilibrium exists, and every such equilibrium yields precisely this division.

items.title: Debiased Kernel Estimation of Spot Volatility in the Presence of Infinite Variation Jumps
items.summary: Volatility estimation is a central problem in financial econometrics, but becomes particularly challenging when jump activity is high, a phenomenon observed empirically in highly traded financial securities. In this paper, we revisit the problem of spot volatility estimation for an Itô semimartingale with jumps of unbounded variation. We construct truncated kernel-based estimators and debiased variants that extend rate-optimal spot volatility estimation to a wider range of jump activity indices, from the previously available bound $Y<4/3$ to $Y<20/11$. Rate-suboptimal CLTs are also established for $Y>20/11$. Compared with earlier work, our approach achieves smaller asymptotic variances through the use of more general kernels and an optimal choice for the bandwidth convergence rate, and also has broader applicability under more flexible model assumptions. A comprehensive simulation study confirms that our procedures outperform competing methods in finite samples.

items.title: The Effect of the U.S. Federal Production Tax Credit on Negative Energy Prices
items.summary: Negative prices frequently arise in electricity markets and production subsidies are commonly cited as a leading cause. Using data from the U.S. Eastern Interconnection wholesale electricity markets for the period 2000-2023, we document that at least 18 percent of the total hours with negative energy prices cannot solely be attributed to the federal production tax credit (PTC), a large, persistent production subsidy during the period of study. Next, we provide the first causal evidence that the PTC leads to negative energy prices. On average, increasing PTC-eligible wind generation by 1 percent increases the probability of a negative energy price by 3.4 percentage points. However, significant heterogeneity exists across electricity markets, and some markets show an effect that is an order of magnitude larger. Furthermore, the PTC explains only 10 percent of the observed negative prices that could potentially be attributable to it. Finally, we use the causal estimate to calculate a plausible value for the environmental benefits accrued from the PTC subsidy when energy prices are negative.

items.title: Welfare, Improvability, and Variance: A Principal-Agent Approach to Optimal Benchmark Item Aggregation
items.summary: AI benchmarks have well-documented limitations, with prior work examining contamination, saturation, and construct underspecification. Aggregation has received far less attention: benchmarks are typically summarized by uniformly averaging item-level scores, implicitly treating every test item as equally valuable. We model benchmarking as a multitask principal-agent game and show that the welfare loss from a benchmark is determined jointly by three item-level primitives: alignment with normative welfare priorities, marginal improvability, and performance variance. We translate the theory into an audit framework that ranks items along each of these three axes, and apply it to OLMES items using WORKBank for welfare, the EvoLM 4B suite for improvability, and the PolyPythias 410M panel for variance. The framework surfaces items that are Pareto-inferior within OLMES subject to a pro-worker welfare operationalization.
