Our findings suggest that the agenda power that management holds in corporate voting persists even without a formal hierarchy, and that ballot design and the visibility of proposers' preferences are governance choices rather than neutral implementation details.

items.title: Search and Verification for Strategyproof Facility Location on Metric Graphs
items.summary: We study automated design of strategyproof (SP) mechanisms for randomized facility location on continuous metric graphs, with the objective of minimizing total distance. We develop methods for computing upper and lower bounds on the optimal approximation ratio achievable by SP mechanisms for a given graph and number of agents. For the lower bound, we propose a cost-preserving reduction to a finite domain that yields lower bounds for unrestricted SP mechanisms through linear programming dual certificates. For the upper bound, we introduce finite representations of mechanisms, called piecewise-linear attributions (PL attributions), that mix piecewise-linear deterministic mechanisms using affine weights on a triangulation of the report space. We show that for mechanisms represented by PL attributions, checking SP and an approximation guarantee reduces to finitely many quadratic nonnegativity tests over compact polytopes. With exact arithmetic and comparisons, each verification certifies the proposed property or returns locations where it fails. In addition, we introduce a strengthening of the incentive notion called strong strategyproofness. We show that for fixed component mechanisms and regions of a PL attribution, the strong strategyproofness requirement can be expressed by a finite number of linear constraints on the attribution coefficients. Using these theoretical results, we propose a heuristic procedure for computing an upper bound on the approximation ratio. We compute certified upper and lower bounds on several metric graphs and numerically evaluate the proposed search procedure. Lastly, we show that deterministic SP onto mechanisms on graphs are strongly strategyproof and admit PL attributions. Thus restricting attention to strongly strategyproof mechanisms admitting PL attributions loses no deterministic SP onto mechanisms.

items.title: Open-ended innovation arm-race in zero-sum games
items.summary: We discuss zero-sum games with open-ended innovation, whereby each player may introduce new strategies. The innovation process is modeled as a draw of new strategies form a distribution. It is argued that, when the cost of innovation is vanishingly small, this setting can lead to an everlasting innovation arm-race. In particular, the introduction of new technologies of the advanced player increases the marginal utility for technological innovation of the backward one, whereas innovation of the backward player discourages the more advanced one to innovate.

items.title: Fair Division with Binary Valuations: Characterizations
items.summary: We consider the fair allocation of indivisible goods with binary valuations. In this setting, the maximum Nash welfare rule, the leximin rule, and all additive welfarist rules with a strictly concave function coincide. We show that for any number of agents, this rule is the only rule that satisfies envy-freeness up to one good, strategyproofness, neutrality, minimal completeness, and invariance under disapproving unassigned goods (IDU). Moreover, we present an alternative characterization for two agents, where we replace IDU with non-redundancy and resource-monotonicity. In both characterizations, all axioms are necessary.

items.title: Bankruptcy Rules for Strategic Agents
items.summary: Bankruptcy rules are rules for dividing an insufficient estate among people with different claims. Existing rules assume that the claims are publicly known. When this is not the case, claimants have a strong incentive to claim more than they are due, as bankruptcy rules give larger allocations to claimants with larger claims. A remedy often used by legal systems is to make over-reporting costly by requiring evidence and imposing penalties. But this remedy also increases the legal expenses of proving true claims, which might result in under-reporting. Encouraging true reporting requires fine-tuning of the legal costs. This paper incorporates the costs of supporting both true and false claims into the bankruptcy model. Claimants incur costs for the true and false parts of their claims, with false claims costing at least as much per unit as true claims. The goal is to set cost rates that induce claimants to report their true entitlements, neither more nor less. Whether this is possible depends on the allocation rule. The proportional and constrained equal awards rules cannot guarantee truthfulness at any positive true-claim cost rate; the same holds for constrained equal losses with at least three claimants. For $N\ge2$ claimants, the rule TAL-1/N from the parameterized Talmud family induces truthfulness exactly when the true-claim cost rate is at most 1/N and the false-claim cost rate is at least 1-1/N. This rule is optimal in the sense that its truthful cost region contains that of every piecewise smooth allocation rule: it gives the legal system the maximum possible flexibility in setting the legal costs. For two claimants, TAL-1/2 (aka Contested Garment rule) uniquely attains this optimal region.

items.title: The Costs and Benefits of Leveraged ETFs
items.summary: We study the costs and benefits of leveraged ETFs (LETFs), focusing on five determinants of performance: volatility drag, fees, financing costs, product launches, and market timing. Long broad-equity-index LETFs generated more than 100 billion US dollars in investor gains, including over 40 billion US dollars relative to counterfactual investments in the underlying assets, due to modest structural headwinds and rising markets. Single-stock LETFs, however, are launched on stocks near the top of the volatility and past-return distributions. This caters to retail demand for lottery-like payoffs, but it also creates larger volatility drag, higher financing costs, and greater exposure to losses from poor market timing.

items.title: Model Selection in High-Dimensional Linear Regression using Boosting with Multiple Testing
items.summary: This paper studies model selection in high dimensional regression settings. We propose a Boosting with Multiple Testing (BMT) approach designed to address proxy signal contamination in environments with strongly correlated regressors, including settings driven by latent common factors. At each stage, at most one regressor is selected conditional on those already included, using a multiple testing threshold for the remaining candidates. Under stated dependence, detectability and design conditions, BMT recovers the exact true model with probability approaching one. A separate extension permits growing signal counts under additional restrictions. For fixed numbers of signals and proxies, we also establish recovery of an approximating model containing all true signals and no noise variables under a separate set of conditions. Following exact selection, fixed dimensional least squares has the oracle asymptotic distribution under the stated moment conditions. A theoretical comparison identifies designs and tuning sequences for which BMT is consistent while the Lasso is not. In the main Monte Carlo comparison, BMT has the highest median Matthews correlation coefficient and exact recovery rate and the lowest median coefficient root mean squared error among the compared specifications. Applications to U.S. emissions and inflation show that BMT combines sparse specifications with favourable forecast performance, including the lowest emissions forecasting errors in the reported comparisons and the best one quarter ahead forecasts in the baseline inflation comparison.

items.title: Designing AI-Mediated Communication in Teams
items.summary: AI assistants increasingly participate in work that requires employees to exchange information and coordinate decisions. We study how a firm should design this communication when workers' interests conflict with each other's and the firm's. Two workers privately know local conditions and their preferred responses, while the assistant knows aggregate project conditions. The firm discloses project information before workers report and choose their own actions. Transparency improves adaptation but can undermine truthful preference reporting. When workers agree with the firm on the productive direction, coarsening project information under weak coordination can preserve useful preference reporting at a cost in forecast precision. Under strong coordination, the firm instead prefers full project disclosure and factual reports, because preference information induces costly accommodation of private objectives. Under weak coordination, a firm-optimal policy can leave workers worse off than direct exchange; requiring their acceptance can call for further coarsening. Releasing project context after reports can sustain factual communication that early release would prevent. With separate delivery decisions that cannot be revised jointly, endogenous forwarding weakly improves firm-preferred performance over unchanged forwarding and strictly improves it in some environments. Numerical comparisons show that full initial disclosure captures most gains in the aligned environments considered, while further design has greater value when workers can favor opposing directions. The results distinguish the credibility of employees' reports from their organizational value and show how disclosure timing affects both.

items.title: Auction Design with Private Priors and Costly Learning
items.summary: We study two-stage auctions in which bidders privately know their valuation priors and learning costs, while the seller jointly designs information acquisition, continuation allocation, and payments. Revenue maximization requires screening learning costs while satisfying cross-prior incentives, potentially distorting both experimentation and continuation allocation. We derive a revenue representation involving allocated posterior values, virtual learning costs, and prior-dependent rents, and characterize cross-prior incentives through difference inequalities. We establish existence of optimal mechanisms for finite experiment menus and arbitrary prior distributions. With finite prior support, bounded finite-category linear programs approximate optimal revenue at a linear rate while preserving exact dynamic incentive compatibility and interim individual rationality. Their dual yields joint optimality conditions for experimentation, allocation, and payments. A two-prior example demonstrates that efficient continuation can be revenue-suboptimal and that cost-contingent experimentation can strictly increase revenue.

items.title: The Verification Bottleneck
items.summary: This paper studies how generative AI, by lowering the cost of research production, affects scientific verification in a general-equilibrium model of peer review. Privately informed researchers choose observable output, an editor optimally assigns review depth, and reviewers supply time according to its expected scientific contribution. Costly output helps screen research quality, and cheaper production lets weaker researchers imitate stronger ones more readily. Beyond a technological threshold, reviewer capacity and verified knowledge weakly decline even under optimal editorial decisions, and strictly when a screening constraint has positive shadow value. Reviewer withdrawal can amplify the loss. With observable quality, the same progress weakly increases both.

items.title: Risk Sensitivity and Stationary Equilibrium in Incomplete Markets
items.summary: We study stationary equilibrium and comparative statics in an incomplete market economy with risk-sensitive preferences. We provide conditions under which a stationary equilibrium exists for every nonnegative degree of risk sensitivity. Under independent income, greater risk sensitivity strictly raises aggregate saving at fixed prices unless both economies have zero saving, and strictly lowers the smallest and the largest equilibrium interest rates. Under stochastically monotone Markov income, these comparisons hold whenever one of the two levels of risk sensitivity being compared is sufficiently low or sufficiently high. For pairs of intermediate values, however, greater risk sensitivity can strictly lower saving, contrary to an existing result in the literature, and can strictly raise the smallest and largest equilibrium rates. An exact decomposition identifies the forces driving these reversals.

items.title: From Individual Learning to Market Equilibrium: Correcting Structural and Parametric Biases in RL Simulations of Economic Models
items.summary: Applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) to economic modeling reveals a fundamental tension: standard RL agents do not behave as competitive price-takers. While macroeconomic models typically assume agents take aggregate conditions as given, a naive single-agent RL algorithm learns to internalize its impact on the environment, effectively exerting market power. We illustrate this divergence in a search-and-matching model with concave production, showing that a standard RL agent converges to a monopsonistic allocation rather than the competitive equilibrium. Furthermore, we show that RL's approach to time discounting distorts standard intertemporal economic trade-offs. To resolve these issues, we propose a Calibrated Mean-Field Reinforcement Learning framework that restricts the agent to optimize against an exogenous aggregate state to restore price-taking behavior, and recalibrates the RL reward structure to reflect true economic opportunity costs. By iteratively updating the aggregate state, our algorithm converges to a stationary fixed point that recovers the competitive equilibrium. This approach provides a method for embedding learning algorithms into dynamic general equilibrium models.

items.title: What Drives Energy Use? Prices, Policy, and Inefficiency
items.summary: Why is U.S. energy use so high, even among rich economies? Using a 2006--2022 panel of the 50 states and DC, an LMDI decomposition documents a 12.8% national decline alongside substantial cross-state heterogeneity. To explain differences in energy-use levels across states, we estimate a microfounded stochastic-frontier model and adapt the LMG relative-importance method to the frontier and inefficiency components. Our approach assigns 56.3% of variation to the frontier, 42.2% to inefficiency, and 1.5% to noise. Prices and efficiency-policy environments are the two leading observed contributors, jointly accounting for 31%: prices operate mainly through the benchmark, whereas policy contributes through both components. Their leading ranks are stable across 21 specifications. Persistent low prices, uneven efficiency-policy environments, structural demand, and a sizeable composite inefficiency component help explain high U.S. energy use. Policy should therefore combine durable price signals, coherent efficiency programs, structural investment, targeted measures addressing avoidable energy use, and targeted household support.

items.title: Designing Behavioral Profiles for Language Model Simulation of Out-of-Distribution Human Behavior
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but which descriptions of people improve prediction when experimental designs change remains unclear. We develop a framework that draws candidate behavioral features from the literature and constructs profiles from earlier human experiments. An LLM-based profile generator assigns feature values from observed actions, messages, and surveys; a separate LLM simulates behavior using these profiles. By comparing simulated and observed outcomes in the training data, we select profile contents through forward feature selection, adding features while they improve prediction. We then evaluate the selected contents without modification against outcomes from new participants under new designs. Across 616 public-goods games, 144 multi-party bargaining games, and 1,480 generalized 11--20 money-request designs, leading one-feature profiles predict human outcome distributions better than no profile or general-purpose personas. Profiles with more features provide no clear additional benefit, and features' relative predictive value largely persists across learning and validation. Using profiles from one game family to simulate another produces uneven gains and can make predictions less accurate than simulations without profiles. The framework makes the choice of behavioral information a testable part of simulation design, helping researchers assess which descriptions remain useful as experimental conditions change.

items.title: Sharp Identification for Regressions with Interval-Observed and Missing Covariates
items.summary: Researchers frequently estimate regressions when key variables are missing or observed only through intervals. Imputation or assumptions about the observation process can yield seemingly precise but misleading conclusions. We develop methods for identification and inference that remain robust to such incomplete data. For a broad class of conditional moment models, we characterize the sharp identified set, the set of all parameter values consistent with the observed data and maintained regression model, without restricting how incomplete observations arise. We establish Hausdorff-consistent estimation and uniformly valid confidence regions, and develop computationally tractable implementations for common regression models. In an application relating interval-elicited discount rates to on-time high-school graduation, conventional inference excludes zero, whereas our interval-data-robust confidence regions include it. Exploiting sharp identification nevertheless yields substantially tighter confidence regions than non-sharp alternatives.

items.title: When Listwise Deletion Works: Causal Diagrams and Complete-Case Regression
items.summary: Listwise deletion (LWD) appears more common than imputation: our review of leading journals finds that about 50% of articles state or imply LWD, versus 7% describing an imputation model. Assuming oracle regression with all required values observed consistently estimates the population average treatment effect, we ask when complete-case regression remains consistent. With constant effects, we offer two checks: whether covariates and the missing indicator satisfy the adjustment criterion in an augmented causal diagram (DAG), and whether the estimator pools valid within-covariate comparisons appropriately, potentially using inverse treatment-propensity weighting (IPW). For heterogeneous effects, assuming conditional effects carry over to the population, we reweight comparisons to the population covariate distribution. Simulations and empirical illustrations from American politics, comparative politics, and international relations demonstrate the framework's use and show why a missing-at-random (MAR) classification, although useful for assessing imputation, does not by itself establish whether complete-case regression consistently estimates the target population ATE. Thus, we recommend adding the missing indicator and its causes to causal models, then checking adjustment and weighting for LWD.

items.title: Ranking Experiments under Sequential Sampling
items.summary: We rank experiments when a decision maker samples sequentially and chooses when to stop. We define two orders: large-budget dominance compares values in every decision problem once the expected-sample budget exceeds a common threshold; small-cost dominance compares values net of sampling costs when the cost per observation is sufficiently small in each problem. Generically, the orders coincide and are characterized by directed Kullback--Leibler (KL) dominance: larger KL divergence for every ordered pair of states. We also characterize the cost per copy of producing a specified experiment at scale by sampling a fixed source experiment. With a full-support prior, these cost functions are precisely sums of statewise maxima of positively weighted directed KL divergences. These costs are additive with two states but exhibit economies of scope with three or more states. Both results rest on an exact reproduction theorem: any experiment generated by sequentially sampling one source can be reproduced exactly by sampling another, with sharp first-order KL conversion rates and a square-root remainder whose coefficient depends only on the two sources.

items.title: Agreements Have a Clock: Compute Growth and the Verification of AI Restraint
items.summary: Rival powers have agreed to limit nuclear arms, phase out ozone-depleting chemicals, and cut greenhouse gases, though each agreement was hard to reach. This paper asks what an agreement to pause frontier AI needs. A follower advances through own research and diffusion from the leader. Because diffusion fades as the gap closes, a paused leader stays ahead longer than its raw lead suggests. A solved agreement game adds voluntary entry, costly monitoring, secret advances, and credible responses. Cooperation is supportable when the monitoring needed to deter a breakout costs no more than either country gains from cooperating. As compute grows during a pause, a secret advance reaches the frozen frontier sooner, shrinking the response window: agreements have a clock. In an example with a fixed leader window, cooperation is supportable through month 18.9. Verified matched safety research extends this to month 25.5, and halving the monitoring cost to month 31.8.

items.title: Prizes, Shared Hazard, and the Speed of Frontier AI
items.summary: Frontier AI labs compete in a contest for commercial leadership while sharing the risk of catastrophe. Each lab gains from arriving earlier but bears only part of the hazard its speed adds, which this paper calls the hazard externality. In an illustrative calibrated takeoff model, three racing labs get through the takeoff period in 18 months, while a common rule on research shares would stretch it to 69 months. Neither force alone explains racing that fast. Removing the contest first closes over ninety percent of the gap in catastrophe probability between racing and a common rule when the catastrophe probability at full speed is 75 percent, and 69 percent when it is 25 percent; averaged over both orders of removal, the contest explains 65 and 44 percent. More labs make each lab race harder, when industry hazard at a common research share does not depend on the number of labs. Under open source in its ideal form, where every lab publishes its capability findings at once, labs slow to the coordinated pace, because no lab can get ahead and each bears all the hazard its research adds. One lab's restraint achieves much less than a common rule. The White House Accord on Super Intelligence of September 2026 audits safety but sets no limit on speed. In the model it does not slow the race, because each lab still gains as much from speeding up.

items.title: Optimal Subsidy Design for Productive Investment across Markets
items.summary: We study the optimal design of investment subsidies across heterogeneous monopolistic markets subject to a common expected discounted budget. Each producer faces a regular one-dimensional demand diffusion and chooses irreversible capacity expansion through a singular stochastic control problem. The regulator values weighted consumer surplus, producer profits, and an additional benefit from installed capacity, while accounting for the excess cost of raising public funds. We characterize producers' optimal investment responses through free boundaries and reformulate the regulator's stochastic optimization problem as a deterministic optimization over investment boundaries. An integral representation then recovers the optimal subsidy schedules that implement the resulting capacity policies. Under mild conditions on the diffusions, we establish existence of optimal schedules and uniqueness of the induced investment policies. Finally, we characterize the subsidy schedule and provide numerical illustrations.

items.title: Action Volatility in a Changing World
items.summary: We study how volatile agents' behavior is in a social learning environment with a changing state. We consider a simple sequential social learning model where rational agents arrive in order, each acting only once, and the underlying unknown state constantly evolves. Each agent receives a private signal, observes all past actions of others, and chooses an action to match the current state. Because the state changes over time, cascades cannot last forever, and actions also fluctuate. We show that actions change less often than private signals but, despite the presence of temporary information cascades, still more often than the underlying state in the long run.

items.title: Dynamic Pooling and Regional Participation in Deceased-Donor Organ Allocation
items.summary: Moving from geographically fragmented to pooled waiting lists in deceased-donor organ transplantation can improve efficiency, but it raises concerns about regional fairness and participation incentives. This paper studies Pareto gains from such transitions in a multi-class queueing model with impatient agents, perishable items, and a tractable homogeneous compatibility friction. In contrast to standard approaches that emphasize static match quality or overlook regional incentives in dynamic contexts, this analysis identifies dynamic risk pooling as the primary source of Pareto improvements for regions. Pooling reduces organ waste resulting from stochastic supply-demand fluctuations, temporal mismatches, and random compatibility outcomes. Although this dynamic surplus theoretically enables Pareto improvements, a purely utilitarian policy that treats all patients equally across regions often fails to achieve these improvements when regions are asymmetric. In these situations, utilitarian redistribution removes an excessive number of organs from high-supply regions and violates their participation constraints. To address this conflict, it is demonstrated that the set of achievable utilities can be represented by mixtures of static priority index policies. Building on this structure, the Constrained Pareto Frontier Search (CPFS) is proposed as a polynomial-time procedure that computes an approximately optimal allocation policy with arbitrarily small participation-constraint violations. The results indicate that, by adjusting priority indices to ensure redistribution remains within the gains from pooled supply, demand, and compatibility risk, policymakers can achieve global efficiency while maintaining local participation incentives.

items.title: Regression Discontinuity Approaches to Evaluate Threshold-Guided Interventions in Observational Studies
items.summary: This article provides an introduction to the Regression Discontinuity (RD) design, and its application to empirical research in the medical sciences. While the main focus of this article is on causal interpretation, key concepts of estimation and inference are also briefly mentioned. A running medical empirical example is provided.

items.title: Identification, estimation and inference in Panel Vector Autoregressions using external instruments
items.summary: This paper proposes an identification inspired by the SVAR-IV literature that uses external instruments to identify panel vector autoregressions (PVARs), and discusses associated issues of identification, estimation, and inference. I introduce a form of local average treatment effect, the $μ$-LATE, which arises when a continuous instrument targets a policy variable with linear effects, and which reduces to the local average treatment effect when the policy and the instrument are binary. Under standard assumptions of independence, exclusion, and monotonicity, I show that externally instrumented PVARs estimate the $μ$-LATE. I construct confidence sets for the impulse responses based on the Anderson-Rubin statistic and, with several instruments, on conditional likelihood ratio tests, which are robust to weak instruments and to common shocks across units. I apply the method to the effect of stock market wealth on local labor markets across US counties.

items.title: Revisiting Elliptic++ for Bitcoin Forensics: Feature Reconstruction and Leakage-Resistant Evaluation
items.summary: Elliptic and its address-level extension Elliptic++ are widely used benchmark datasets in Bitcoin forensics, cited by more than 1300 academic studies according to Google Scholar. We identify future information leakage in Elliptic++. Its positional data split does not respect temporal order, and the exact definitions of its address-level features remain undocumented. We revisit how the 55 Elliptic++ address-level features are computed and propose a leakage-resistant pipeline. First, the exact feature definitions are recovered by linking Elliptic transactions to public ledger data. Second, we compute the features with a temporal split based on each address's first appearance, using only information available at the time of prediction. Once temporal ordering is enforced, the random forest (RF)'s strong predictive performance largely disappears: its F1 score on the illicit class falls from $0.846$ under the original leaky evaluation to just $0.291$ under our leakage-resistant pipeline. Furthermore, RF no longer outperforms a simple logistic regression baseline. We provide the exact feature definitions and executable code to reproduce the leakage-resistant features, so that future Bitcoin forensic models can be evaluated based on genuine predictive capability rather than temporal data leakage.

items.title: Experimentally Validated Digital Twins: Evaluating Workforce Training Programs in the Age of Big Data
items.summary: Modern program evaluation prioritizes evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) because prior research found that observational estimates of program impacts often diverge substantially from experimental benchmarks. We revisit this finding --- which was based on small survey datasets --- in the era of large-scale administrative data. Using anonymized income tax records covering all American adults between 1999 and 2025, we estimate the effects of workforce training programs on earnings by using machine learning models to predict counterfactuals from rich data on prior work histories, demographics, and residential locations. Rather than testing whether our observational estimates are unbiased, we use 37 RCTs to estimate the distribution of their bias. We find that our machine learning estimates closely match the RCT estimates, with root mean squared error (RMSE) comparable to that of the RCTs themselves. Our method reduces RMSE by 60% relative to parametric estimators used in prior work because our larger samples and richer covariates permit more flexible, higher-dimensional models of the counterfactual. Applying our method to a broader set of sites and enrollment years beyond the experimental sample, we find that treatment effects on earnings vary substantially across locations and over time, even within a given program. Programs that place more participants into target-sector jobs generate the largest earnings gains, with impacts that persist even after participants leave their initial jobs. These findings provide guidance for improving job training programs and, more broadly, illustrate a scalable approach to program evaluation that uses observational data to construct experimentally validated ``digital twins.''

items.title: Heterogeneous Treatment Effects via Dynamic Panel Data Methods
items.summary: We study dynamic panel data methods in a causal framework where treatment effects are heterogeneous and history-dependent. Sequential exchangeability alone does not guarantee that a first-differenced instrumental-variable (IV) estimand is a convex average of current effects, even if those effects are constant. We characterize additional conditions that are sufficient and necessary for eliminating trend contamination and guaranteeing a convex representation uniformly over compatible distributions of potential outcomes and treatments. Next, for a model with autoregressive untreated potential outcomes, we propose a conditional first-differenced IV regression that identifies the average treatment effect on the first-time treated without sequential exchangeability. Finally, we compare sequential exchangeability and parallel trends under sequential randomization and forward-looking treatment choices with learning, and show that, when treatments depend on recent outcomes, equal pre-treatment trends can coexist with violations of parallel trends.

items.title: Refining the Notion of No Anticipation in Difference-in-Differences Studies
items.summary: We clarify the interpretation of identification strategies using difference-in-differences (DiD), which are widely applied in empirical research. In particular, DiD researchers often invoke an assumption commonly referred to as the "no-anticipation assumption". Taken literally, this assumption states that treatments in the future have no effect on outcomes in the past. Because standard causal models rely on a temporal structure in which causes precede effects, such an assumption seems to be inherently satisfied. However, most researchers attribute a different meaning to the assumption: they interpret the assumption as ensuring no effect of policy decision, e.g., immediate behavioral changes due to knowledge about the plan to implement the policy. We discuss the consequences of this mismatch, and give an alternative formulation of no anticipation that captures DiD researchers' concerns and clarifies identification arguments.

items.title: Unconfoundedness as an Information Constraint
items.summary: This paper provides an information-theoretic characterization of unconfoundedness within a general class of models allowing for endogenous selection. We impose a conditional mutual information (CMI) restriction requiring that the information about treatment contained in a potential outcome, conditional on covariates, does not exceed that contained in its latent heterogeneity. Under the maintained model conditions, this restriction is equivalent to a multiplicative factorization of treatment probabilities into separate functions of latent heterogeneity and covariates. Although the CMI restriction permits endogenous selection, sufficiently rich variation in treatment probabilities across covariate values makes it equivalent to unconfoundedness for the corresponding potential outcome. For binary treatments, any nonconstant propensity score suffices; for multiple treatments, a full-rank condition on the second-moment matrix of the propensity-score vector is sufficient. State-specific restrictions bound residual selection and imply exogeneity for individual treatment states under boundary-support conditions. Extensions cover continuous treatments and instrument exogeneity.

items.title: On inverse aggregate network assignment games
items.summary: To design platforms for multi-operator mobility markets coordinating their operations or infrastructure to support them, models are needed to understand the behavior of these operators and travelers in a shared network. Assignment games can prove useful, but operationalizing them requires adopting a more generalized aggregate assignment game framework that allows for identification and estimation. We extend such a framework to aggregate network assignment games, proposing a path-based formulation and a PURC-based formulation along with solution algorithms. An inverse optimization model is proposed for the link-based formulation. It is solved by a quadratic program that separates into a buyer block, which retains the node potentials and imposes every observed zero-flow cell, and a seller block. This estimator, introduced in the literature for uncapacitated route choice, is extended here to a capacitated two-sided market, with rationing prices supported on observed binding links and operator supply scales estimated by group. Computational tests with a toy network demonstrate the economic value of these models. A large-scale Long Island Rail Road network example (897 nodes, 671 census tracts, 123 LIRR stations, 8,320 directed links) is calibrated to 2026 fares, timetabled seat supply and National Transit Database operating costs. With 10-50% of links sampled, the misspecified inverse model fits oracle link flows with R^2>=96%. Held-out link error falls from 29% to 19%, correlations with the true rationing prices rise from 49% to 75%, and social optimal gross surplus is recovered within 6%. Deadweight loss is overestimated by 10-17%. Ablation tests show that ignoring the inactive cells more than doubles the held-out error and, at 30-50% sampling, roughly halves the correlation of the pricing wedge, while ignoring the rationing prices degrades every metric.

items.title: Information Intermediaries in Monopolistic Screening
items.summary: We investigate the relationship between product offerings, information dissemination, and consumer decision-making in a monopolistic screening environment in which consumers lack information about their valuation of quality-differentiated products. An intermediary, who is driven by the objective of maximizing consumer surplus but is also biased towards high-quality products, provides recommendations after the monopolist announces the menu of product choices. We characterize the monopolist's profit-maximizing finite-item menu. Our results show that as intermediaries place greater emphasis on consumer surplus over product quality, sellers are prompted to strategically expand their product range. Intriguingly, this augmented product variety decreases economic efficiency compared to scenarios where direct seller-to-consumer information provision is the norm. The role of information intermediaries proves pivotal in shaping consumer welfare, market profitability, and overarching economic efficiency. Our insights underscore the complexities introduced by these intermediaries that policymakers and market designers must consider when designing policies centered on consumer learning and market information transparency.

items.title: On the difficulty of characterizing top trading cycles with identical houses
items.summary: We study Shapley-Scarf housing markets (Shapley and Scarf, 1974) in which houses come in types and agents are indifferent between houses of the same type but rank the types strictly. On this domain of objective indifferences, top trading cycles (TTC) rules with fixed tie-breaking regain Pareto efficiency and group strategy-proofness (Sandholtz and Tai, 2026), properties that need not hold under general weak preferences. We ask whether the characterization of the TTC rule for strict preferences by Ma (1994) and the characterization of TTC rules with fixed tie-breaking for weak preferences by Ehlers (2014) extend to this domain. They do not. With five agents and two types of houses, we construct a rule that satisfies individual rationality, Pareto efficiency, group strategy-proofness, non-bossiness, and consistency, but whose restriction to the five-agent population is not welfare equivalent to any TTC rule with fixed tie-breaking. With two types, five agents are minimal for this fixed-population result. The same rule shows that several other characterizations of TTC for strict preferences do not extend either.

items.title: Do media narratives shape foreign ownership? Evidence from African regions
items.summary: Foreign investors rarely observe local business conditions directly, especially in developing economies where reliable subnational information is limited. In such contexts, media narratives may shape how investment locations are perceived by increasing their visibility and framing local risks and opportunities. This paper examines the relationship between media narratives and foreign ownership across African locations. We combine firm-level data from the World Bank Enterprise Surveys with a novel corpus of 167,746 English-language news articles on industrial investment in Africa published between 2014 and 2019. Using text mining and semantic network analysis, we construct investment-location measures of the semantic importance of business-related media themes through the Semantic Brand Score (SBS) and study their associations with firm-level foreign ownership. The results point to a significant association between how the media frames a location and the level of foreign presence there. This association varies across frames. It is predominantly positive, relates to both the intensive and extensive dimensions of foreign ownership depending on the theme, and may interact negatively with the investment climate. This paper contributes to research on the geography of foreign capital by identifying public narratives as a feature of the information environment associated with observed foreign-equity participation.

items.title: Inference under partial identification with minimax test statistics
items.summary: In partially identified models, specification and subvector tests often minimize a measure of sample violation over the parameter space. Such statistics have the minimax form $T_n=r_n\inf_{θ\inΘ}\sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}v_n(θ,t)$, which includes $r_n\inf_{θ\inΘ}ξ(m_n(θ))$ for a convex loss $ξ$ of Banach-space-valued moments $m_n$. We characterize their limiting distribution through familiar geometric objects. The limit is an upper bound in general and exact under convexity in $θ$, a standard polynomial minorant condition, or continuity of the contact set. It retains the loss directions that bind locally and cannot be absorbed by moving $θ$, which under convex loss are the subgradients of $ξ$ at $m(θ)$ that are nonnegative along every first-order movement of $θ$. A re-optimization bootstrap common to Hong and Li (2018) and Bugni, Canay and Shi (2017) re-solves the minimization after a random perturbation and needs no estimate of the identified set, the contact set, or any derivative. We show that it consistently estimates the limit under any of the three conditions for exactness. Under a standard uniform minorant condition, it is also uniformly valid for minimax criteria and for general convex losses on Banach-valued moments. Without a uniform minorant, the two properties can be incompatible. In simulations, the re-optimization bootstrap has close to nominal size and closely tracks the sampling distribution of the statistic.

items.title: From macro to micro: Economic complexity indicators for firm growth
items.summary: A rich theoretical and empirical literature has investigated the link between export diversification and firm performance. Prior theoretical works hinted at the key role of capability accumulation in shaping production activities and performance, without however producing product-level indicators able to forecast corporate growth. Building on economic complexity theory and the corporate growth literature, this paper examines which characteristics of a firm's export basket anticipate future performance. We analyze a unique longitudinal dataset that covers export and financial data for 57,586 Italian firms. We find that firms exporting products typically exported by wealthier countries -- a proxy for products characterized by a greater level of productivity and sophistication -- tend to experience higher growth and labour productivity. Crucially, where firms diversify matters: Across firms, only diversification outside of a firm's core export area is positively associated with future growth, whereas diversification within the core is negatively associated. This is revealed by introducing novel measures of in-block and out-of-block export diversification, based on algorithmically-detected blocks. Our findings suggest that growth is associated not just with how many products a firm exports, but also with where these products lie within the production ecosystem, at both local and global scales.

items.title: When Covariates Mask Pre-Trends
items.summary: Honest difference-in-differences methods judge how far parallel trends may fail after treatment by how far it failed before treatment, as shown by placebo estimates. When the design adjusts for covariates, the placebo estimates are adjusted too. We show that this benchmark is valid only if the covariates are measured before the earliest placebo window. A covariate measured later already reflects shocks to the outcome during the placebo period, so adjusting for it hides part of the pre-trend. The placebos then look flatter than the true trend and the resulting confidence sets are too narrow. When the covariate is also observed at an early date, the distortion can be estimated and tested. Of 90 recent published studies that adjust for time-varying covariates, 77 measure at least one covariate too late.

items.title: Sharp Fréchet--Hoeffding Bounds under Selectively Incomplete Observation
items.summary: Incomplete records can sharpen bounds on joint outcome probabilities even when no pair of outcomes is jointly observed. I derive sharp pointwise Fréchet--Hoeffding bounds combining known population marginals with selectively observed records, without restricting the observation mechanism. I establish an exact reduction of the identification problem to finite-dimensional optimization, yielding computable characterizations of both bounds. Illustrations involving income mobility, potential outcomes, and split questionnaires demonstrate how incomplete records can improve identification relative to the classical bounds.

items.title: The Price of Intelligence: A Quality-Adjusted Price Index for AI Services
items.summary: How fast AI inference prices have fallen depends on how an index holds quality constant. We build quality-adjusted price indices for text and code inference sold through APIs, joining 21,024 posted prices to a capability scale fitted to 4,605 benchmark scores. From January 2025 to July 2026, matched-model methods record an annual fall of 0.07 in log price per token. Our pre-specified hedonic index falls at 0.51 a year in logs (95% interval 0.11 to 0.89), entirely through the rising capability of the models on sale. Across three treatments of measurement error and two anchor sets it runs from 0.34 to 0.89. Excluding six anchors flagged for possible contamination leaves model rankings intact (rank correlation 0.998) yet lowers the rate by 0.40 to 0.51 under two treatments. Agreement on rankings therefore does not license claims about levels or increments. Per completed task, the data do not establish a quality-adjusted decline.

items.title: SAUSS: Stochastic Approximation with Unbiased Simulated Scores for Limited Dependent Variable Models
items.summary: Simulated maximum likelihood is widely used in latent-variable models where likelihood evaluation requires intractable integrals or probabilities. With a fixed number of simulation draws, its estimating equation is generally biased. We develop Stochastic Approximation with Unbiased Simulated Scores (SAUSS), combining score simulation with stochastic gradient descent. The Hajivassiliou--McFadden identity, an instance of Fisher's identity, expresses the likelihood score as the conditional expectation of the complete-data score given the observed data. Exact conditional draws yield an unbiased simulated score for any fixed number of draws. The estimator averages stochastic gradient iterates computed using mini-batches of fixed size regardless of sample size, avoiding repeated full-sample likelihood evaluations. Under local regularity and initialization conditions, we establish asymptotic normality and a functional central limit theorem for the partial-sum process of the iterates under multi-pass sampling from an observed sample. These results support plug-in and random-scaling confidence intervals that remain asymptotically valid when algorithmic uncertainty is non-negligible relative to sampling uncertainty. We develop multinomial probit as a leading application. In simulations and two applications, SAUSS returns estimates in every reported run, including cases where the simulated maximum likelihood implementation returns none. When both return estimates, SAUSS gives comparable estimates in less time.

items.title: Leverage Dynamics in Product-Market Networks
items.summary: We examine whether corporate leverage persistence reflects only firms' own adjustment frictions or also the past financing choices of economically connected firms. We combine annual firm fundamentals with time-varying text-based product-market networks and estimate a heterogeneous dynamic partial-adjustment model with interactive effects using defactored instrumental variables. The estimator accommodates time- varying network weights and spatial dependence in firm-specific coefficients. Network-weighted lagged leverage is positive and statistically significant, with a mean coefficient representing approximately 45% of the sum of the own and network lag coefficients for book leverage. Accounting for network dependence reduces the persistence attributed to firms' own financing histories and increases the implied own-firm speed of adjustment. Firm-specific estimates reveal significant product-market clustering in own-leverage persistence and in responses to several leverage determinants, showing that heterogeneity in financing behaviour is systematically related to product-market proximity. The evolution of product-market connections matters quantitatively for network dependence: holding the network fixed produces a substantially larger network coefficient and considerably larger indirect effects than using annual network weights. Network dependence is therefore an economically important component of leverage dynamics, while its measurement depends on both the specification of economic connections and heterogeneity in firm behaviour.

items.title: Labor Market Returns to Education and Intra-family Educational Inequality: Theory and Experimental Evidence
items.summary: How do labor market conditions shape educational inequality within- and between families? A growing body of evidence documents convex wage returns to education in labor markets across the world. We develop a theoretical model that demonstrates that earnings convexity can increase or decrease between-sibling differences in investments and outcomes depending on the parameter of parental inequality aversion. We recover the distribution of this structural parameter from a highly-incentivized lab-in-the-field experiment with 246 parents in San Luis Potosí, Mexico, in which token allocations determine children's access to an AI course. Parents make allocation decisions across six scenarios that vary convexity in the payoff function and endowment-investment substitutability. We identify three types of parents: Rawlsian parents display perfect inequality aversion (12.6%), interior parents that are moderately inequality tolerant (76.8%), and Utilitarian parents who maximize total payoffs (10.6%). While these three groups respond to earnings convexity in heterogeneous ways, on average, greater convexity increases the share allocated to the high-endowed child, thereby widening within-family inequality.

items.title: The Market for AI-Assisted Signaling
items.summary: This paper studies a market in which AI providers choose technologies and prices for assistance used to signal ability. Individual adoption is unobserved. Profitable assistance can lower welfare relative to signaling without AI, even when ability remains fully revealed. Easier imitation increases the output required to demonstrate ability, and the extra signaling can outweigh production savings. Providers can profit from improving assistance for lower-ability senders because this increases higher-ability senders' purchases. Such improvements can lower welfare relative to retaining existing tools. Competition among providers offering the same technology supports full information, but development costs can sustain monopoly provision that conceals ability. Greater verification capacity can also reduce information by changing which customers providers serve.

items.title: The inclusive Synthetic Control Method
items.summary: We introduce the inclusive synthetic control method (iSCM), an extension of the traditional synthetic control framework that allows units potentially affected by an intervention--either directly or through spillovers--to remain in the donor pool. Because synthetic control weights are estimated using only pre-intervention data, constructing a synthetic control for both the main treated unit and each potentially affected unit yields a linear system that links the contaminated estimates to the true effects of interest. Solving this system exactly removes the contamination without altering the underlying estimator. We illustrate the empirical relevance of our iSCM by re-estimating the effect of German reunification on GDP per capita, allowing for spillovers from West Germany to Austria.

items.title: Persuasion by Parts
items.summary: Classical Bayesian persuasion assumes that an information designer can condition signals on the entire state. We propose persuasion by parts. In this model, the receiver's payoff from acting is $X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ for independent coordinates $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ observed by separate sources. The designer commits in advance to a product experiment, in which each source $i$ can condition its signal only on $X_i$. Given the signals, the receiver computes her posterior mean $y$ of $X$ and acts with probability $g(y)$, where $g\colon \mathbb{R} \to [0,1]$ is a nondecreasing function. The designer aims to maximize the probability of action. Let $V_{\mathrm{prod}}(g)$ and $V_{\mathrm{joint}}(g)$ be the supremum probabilities of action under persuasion by parts and under joint persuasion, respectively. When the designer knows $g$, we show $$ V_{\mathrm{prod}}(g) \;\ge\; c\,V_{\mathrm{joint}}(g)^2 \qquad\text{for every nondecreasing } g\colon \mathbb{R} \to [0,1], $$ where $c > 0$ is an absolute constant independent of $n$ and the prior; the exponent $2$ is tight. When $g$ is unknown, we construct a product experiment $Π$ from the prior alone, whose probability of action $V_Π(g)$ satisfies $$ V_Π(g) \;\ge\; c_\varepsilon\,V_{\mathrm{joint}}(g)^{2 + \varepsilon} \qquad\text{for every } \varepsilon > 0 \text{ and every nondecreasing } g\colon \mathbb{R} \to [0,1], $$ where $c_\varepsilon > 0$ depends only on $\varepsilon$.

items.title: AI and the research assistant: Evidence from economics working papers
items.summary: Studies of AI in science observe isolated tasks or the authors on a byline. They do not observe the research assistants whose data cleaning, coding, literature search, and replication work language models now perform. Economics working papers record this junior labour in their acknowledgements, next to the full text. Using 24 working-paper series through October 2026, I compare papers by the same economist that do and do not disclose AI use, alongside a detector of AI-like prose. Disclosing papers credit 0.548 more named assistants than other papers by the same economist, two-thirds of the mean, and run longer, mostly in their appendices. Disclosures of operational use, such as coding and data work, carry the whole assistant difference; writing-only disclosures and AI-like prose show no consistent association with assistants or pages. The paper brings acknowledged junior labour and selective team disclosure into the study of scientific production. Within an economist's portfolio, operational AI accompanies wider, assistant-supported projects.

items.title: Conditional expectile-based value-at-risk: Semiparametric estimation and inference
items.summary: Conditional expectile-based value-at-risk (EVaR) has attracted increasing attention in financial risk management owing to its desirable theoretical properties. However, existing estimation methods for conditional EVaR either rely on potentially misspecified parametric models or suffer from the curse of dimensionality in nonparametric approaches. To this end, we study semiparametric estimation and inference for conditional EVaR in nonlinear time series models with unspecified error distribution. Specifically, we propose a two-step conditional EVaR estimator that achieves the parametric convergence rate. Furthermore, we derive a functional central limit theorem for conditional EVaR process, and then extend to investigate estimating both conditional expectile-based expected shortfall and conditional distribution. A residual bootstrap procedure is proposed for non-expert practitioners to conduct statistical inference. The asymptotic results and their applications are illustrated by numerical studies and an empirical application to S\&P 500 returns.

items.title: Quantitative Methods in Finance
items.summary: These lecture notes provide a comprehensive introduction to Quantitative Methods in Finance (QMF), designed for graduate students in finance and economics with heterogeneous programming backgrounds. The material develops a unified toolkit combining probability theory, statistics, numerical methods, and empirical modeling, with a strong emphasis on implementation in Python. Core topics include random variables and distributions, moments and dependence, simulation and Monte Carlo methods, numerical optimization, root-finding, and time-series models commonly used in finance and macro-finance. Particular attention is paid to translating theoretical concepts into reproducible code, emphasizing vectorization, numerical stability, and interpretation of outputs. The notes progressively bridge theory and practice through worked examples and exercises covering asset pricing intuition, risk measurement, forecasting, and empirical analysis. By focusing on clarity, minimal prerequisites, and hands-on computation, these lecture notes aim to serve both as a pedagogical entry point for non-programmers and as a practical reference for applied researchers seeking transparent and replicable quantitative methods in finance.

items.title: Joules-to-GDP: How Much Economic Value Do AI Systems Produce per Unit of Energy?
items.summary: AI systems are increasingly used to complete economically valuable tasks in various professions, such as software engineering and finance. This motivates the question: how much economic value does an AI system produce per unit of energy? To answer it, we introduce Joules-to-GDP, a framework that measures output dollar value minus AI execution cost per unit of energy, which we call Net Value per Joule (NVJ), and expert time saved per unit of energy, or Time Saving per Joule (TSJ). We then apply the framework to 220 GDPval tasks across 44 occupations. Four findings stand out. First, the most valuable work is not always the most efficient. For example, engineering work such as CAD design yields about 10% more net value per task than software development such as building websites, yet the latter yields about 27% more per joule. Second, defaulting to the most capable model can mean less total value from the same energy budget. Of the five tested models, GLM 5.2 delivers the most net value, $72.27 per task on average, using the energy of about four hours of active laptop use, while Gemma 4 31B achieves 56% of that with 23% of the energy, for 2.5x the NVJ and 2.8x the TSJ. Third, for the same model, NVJ and TSJ vary widely across different accelerators, and adding GPUs can raise energy use for modest gains: eight H100s use 3.2x the energy of one to cut completion time by only 22%, at similar net value. More capable models and more hardware must therefore earn their extra energy with enough gains in output value. Finally, the work of experts who use AI is harder for AI to match than that of experts working alone. Measured against it, GLM 5.2's NVJ falls by 70% and its TSJ by 65%. Taken together, these findings justify economic return per joule as an objective for selecting professional tasks and improving language models and accelerators, and as a basis for examining AI's effect on the economy

items.title: Robust Cauchy-Based Methods for Predictive Regressions
items.summary: This paper develops robust inference methods for predictive regressions that address key challenges posed by endogenously persistent or heavy-tailed regressors, as well as persistent volatility in errors. Building on the Cauchy estimation framework, we propose two novel tests: one based on $t$-statistic group inference and the other employing a hybrid approach that combines Cauchy and OLS estimation. These methods effectively mitigate size distortions that commonly arise in standard inference procedures under endogeneity, near nonstationarity, heavy tails, and persistent volatility. The proposed tests are simple to implement and applicable to both continuous- and discrete-time models. Extensive simulation experiments demonstrate favorable finite-sample performance across a range of realistic settings. An empirical application examines the predictability of excess stock returns using the dividend-price and earnings-price ratios as predictors. The results suggest that the dividend-price ratio possesses predictive power, whereas the earnings-price ratio does not significantly forecast returns.

items.title: Public salience mobilizes nationwide responses to violence against women
items.summary: Does public salience around femicides mobilize societal responses or trigger further harm through imitation? Using newly assembled case-level data on femicides in Italy from 2017 to 2024, we study the nationwide consequences of the most salient cases for help-seeking, police reporting, and lethal violence. We find that highly salient intimate partner femicides (IPFs) generate nationwide increases in help-seeking, and that an exceptionally salient IPF also leads to a marked rise in police reports of violence against women. Yet we find no evidence of an increase in femicides-a pattern inconsistent with copycat theories. Responses are strongest during periods of peak salience. No comparable mobilization follows a lower-salience IPF, a similarly salient femicide committed by family members, a highly salient killing of a woman not classified as a femicide, or a lower-salience falsification case. Together, these comparisons indicate that mobilization depends on salience intensity, the victim-perpetrator relationship, and the gendered nature of the violence, rather than reflecting a generic response to salient violent crime. These findings suggest that public salience can contribute to prevention strategies against gender-based violence without amplifying lethal violence.

items.title: The Market and the Jungle
items.summary: We study how different institutions governing property rights and economic transactions shape occupational choices and welfare. Individuals in our society choose occupations that determine their production and consumption opportunities, anticipating either anonymous, voluntary market exchange supported by public enforcement (the market), or allocations through a random coercive hierarchy (the jungle) without monetary compensation. We establish conditions for occupational equilibria to exist in the market and in the jungle, and compare their performance. At a common occupational profile, the market maximizes aggregate surplus, whereas allocations in the jungle are Pareto efficient with monetary holdings fixed but need not maximize surplus. Endogenous occupational choices introduce an additional source of institutional differences. We find that a market occupational equilibrium outperforms a jungle occupational equilibrium, in aggregate terms, under two conditions: (i) every occupation in the jungle is available in the market, and (ii) the market is perfectly competitive, in the sense that prices cannot be manipulated by unilateral changes in occupations. We also establish an individual welfare comparison without this price-invariance condition: among identical individuals, everyone weakly prefers an occupational equilibrium in the market to a symmetric occupational equilibrium in the jungle. Our analysis places the institutional foundations of exchange at the center of the welfare comparison and provides a framework for studying coercive institutions that survive alongside markets.

items.title: Ask More, Hear Less: How a Review Prompt Changes What Online Ratings Show
items.summary: Platforms ask customers for online reviews to reduce self-selection, but theory conflicts on whether review solicitation makes online ratings more or less informative. Selection theory implies that asking helps, voice theory that it dilutes the news, and research on rating inflation that compression destroys information. We reconcile these views with signal detection theory, which separates what a rating knows (its sensitivity) from what it shows (its criterion). We test the framework on Steam, a leading PC video game store, whose client began in October 2019 to prompt players for a review after about three hours of play. Using a difference-in-discontinuities design at that inferred threshold in 21.6 million Steam reviews of 315 games, we find that review counts just above the threshold become 4.25 times those just below, and the jump in the positive share grows by 6.6 percentage points. Agreement with critics changes little near launch and erodes later. The rating's movement changes far more: pass-through from reviews written in the first two hours falls from 0.73 to 0.18 just above the threshold, against 0.81 to 0.64 just below, and a fixed rating tier responds to 12% of downturns in those reviews above the threshold, down from 42%, against 41% and 47% below it. What the stream knows changes less. At equal review counts its sensitivity falls more above the threshold, because added reviews respond about half as much and scores near the ceiling are noisier per review, but at natural counts added volume offsets this loss, leaving a change of -0.03 relative to the stream below (95% CI -0.13 to 0.06). Failures that developers acknowledge, which run through complaints, still move the score after launch. Review prompts therefore mainly change how a rating must be read, and platforms that solicit reviews should recalibrate their rating labels.

items.title: Estimating Rail Commuter Preferences under Endogenous Crowding: A Population Game Approach to Train Choice in Tokyo
items.summary: We estimate commuters' preferences over schedule delay, travel time, and crowding from observed train choices on a commuter rail line in Tokyo. Because crowding is itself an outcome of these choices, we model train choice as a game in which train choices and crowding are jointly determined, and estimate the preferences by maximum likelihood using the closed-form stationary distribution of the game. Using individual-level data from Japan's 2015 Public Transport Survey for Metropolitan Areas matched with train timetables, we construct desired arrival times from reported work start times rather than inferring them from observed arrival times. We find that schedule delay costs are large relative to crowding costs. One minute of schedule delay early and late corresponds to 0.39 and 0.49 minutes of in-vehicle travel time, respectively, whereas one minute of travel at a crowding rate of 100% adds a cost equivalent to 0.04 minutes. The estimated crowding cost is, however, sensitive to the specification of desired arrival times. These results suggest that scheduling constraints are central to evaluating policies to reduce peak-hour crowding.

items.title: Comparing the Empirical Content of Economic Theories
items.summary: A fitted theory that predicts well may do so because of the structure it commits to or because it was fitted to the data it is evaluated on. We propose measures that separate the two by operationalising a theory as a functional form, a support restriction on behavior and a distribution over the parameters, with no parameter fitted to the evaluation sample. Probabilistic completeness is the share of the predictable variation that a rule drawn from the theory captures out of sample. Probabilistic restrictiveness is how much conceivable behavior such a rule excludes; it separates into what the functional form can reach and how the parameter distribution concentrates on it. The parameter distribution can be interpreted as uncertainty about a representative agent or as the distribution of parameters across heterogeneous agents, and the measures adapt to both interpretations through the choice of scoring rule, baseline and ceiling. A scope layer prices the domains a theory claims and compares theories across domains. We apply the measures to expected utility, cumulative prospect theory and disappointment aversion on certainty equivalents for binary lotteries. The functional forms exclude little conceivable behavior, while the literature's parameter distributions exclude most of what the forms leave open. A rule drawn from a literature-informed prior keeps two thirds of fitted prospect theory's completeness, most of expected utility's and none of disappointment aversion's. The flexibility-fit trade-off found for functional forms disappears once the theories are held with their literature priors. Read as populations, disappointment aversion and expected utility cannot produce the dispersion the subjects show, and the literature priors are less well placed for losses than for gains.

items.title: Local and Neighboring Food Retail Supply and Population across Japan's Municipalities
items.summary: This paper examines the relationship between food retail supply and resident population across Japanese municipalities. I develop a partial-equilibrium framework in which local food retail improves consumption convenience and population density supports retail entry. The framework allows positive local feedback and distinguishes local retail from neighboring consumption opportunities. Using Japan's 2010, 2015, and 2020 Population Censuses and the 2012, 2016, and 2021 Economic Censuses, I estimate municipality fixed-effects specifications with spatially lagged explanatory variables. Local and neighboring food and beverage retail supply (FRS) are positively associated with resident population. The corresponding coefficients are 0.0893 and 0.1364, respectively, and remain positive when prefecture-by-wave fixed effects are introduced. A common-sample comparison shows that the standardized local FRS association is stronger than that of food-service supply (FSS). The estimated local FRS relationship also varies across retail scale, although the magnitude of this nonlinearity and the negative slope at high establishment counts are sensitive to regional time effects and the estimation period.

items.title: Nought Venture, Nought Have: Risk Taking and Efficient Investment in Matching Markets
items.summary: We study a two-sided assortative matching market in which agents attract partners through costly investment and strategic risk taking. Each agent chooses an investment level and an arbitrary distribution of nonnegative quality that is a mean-preserving spread of investment. We allow for unequal populations and different investment costs across populations. Finite markets have a unique nontrivial semi-symmetric equilibrium, with investment below the Pareto frontier. We show that this inefficiency disappears as the economy grows with the population ratio held fixed and characterise its rate of convergence. The limit provides a foundation for the analysis of large matching markets, by selecting a unique efficient equilibrium from the continuum economy's infinitely many equilibria, which feature efficient investments but different risk-taking profiles.

items.title: Selective Randomization Inference for Interference
items.summary: Empirical researchers often use tests for interference as pretests or robustness checks. However, when the results guide the choice of models, parameters, or hypotheses, the resulting data-dependent selection can compromise the validity of subsequent inference. This paper develops a two-stage selective randomization inference framework for interference that explicitly conditions on the selection event to account for data-dependent selection. We first test the null hypothesis of no treatment spillover using a conditional randomization method. If this null is rejected, we test the null hypothesis of zero exposure contrast under a pre-specified exposure mapping that allows for spillover effects; otherwise, we test the null hypothesis of no direct effects under the assumption of no spillover. We prove that each second-stage test controls the selective Type I error rate in finite samples and evaluate the size and power of the proposed tests through Monte Carlo experiments.

items.title: Time-Varying Quantile VAR Models: Estimation and Inference
items.summary: We study time-varying quantile VAR models in which the conditional quantile does not propagate linearly through the recursion, and develop a toolkit for impulse response analysis, which to the best of our knowledge has not been established elsewhere. For example, we establish Bahadur representation for quantile VAR regression, infer model parameters via smoothed check function, and define and investigate the best linear projection of the time-varying tau-quantile impulse response via local projections. An application to U.S. industrial production growth and credit spreads from 1919-2025 uncovers structural shifts in tail relationships, demonstrating downside asymmetry diminishes at longer forecast horizons.

items.title: Owning What Can Quit
items.summary: Academic journals are part of the infrastructure of science, yet most journal titles are owned by commercial publishers while their standing rests on editors and boards who can leave. This paper asks what that separation means for the governance of science. Using a coded dataset of all 57 editorial mass resignations recorded by Retraction Watch from 2015 to 2026, data on editor tenure at 110 economics, finance and accounting journals, and journal-level publication and revenue data, I document three patterns. First, resignation does not reverse an owner's decision: in none of the 19 episodes involving an editor's replacement did the owner back down after the board resigned, so editorial communities have influence only before they leave. Second, whether a departing board can take a journal's standing with it depends on institutions outside the board: successor journals follow most often where a scholarly society backs the board and rarely in medicine, where non-profit hosts are scarce, while journal ranking lists, which rate titles rather than the people who edit them, keep reputation with the owner. Third, a stated limit on editor tenure was applied at the publisher's discretion; where it was applied, output grew almost fourfold, a short-run gain whose long-run effect on the journal's standing is not yet known. I draw implications for scholarly societies, funders, publishers, and the bodies that compile journal rankings.

items.title: Why Good Experience Can End Joint Activity
items.summary: Learning a partner's preferences through joint activity can make both partners worse off than receiving no feedback from the activity. We study a responder who values the partner's payoff but bears a cost when joining is attributed to personal interest. Both partners observe noisy evidence of whether the responder wanted the activity, available only after participation. Evidence of interest raises this cost, discouraging joining on unwanted days; joining only on wanted days would then be too revealing to sustain. With choices based on current payoffs, we derive a condition under which learning can end participation without ever making stopping beneficial to either partner. Feedback accuracy and preference persistence described by couples' diaries satisfy this condition at baseline payoffs. Once activity stops, no further evidence arrives and the belief that the responder generally wants the activity stays fixed, so waiting may never restore it; preference information available without participating can. A separate forward-looking model with highly persistent preferences shows why this remedy can also reduce joint welfare. When participation reveals preferences exactly, a responder may accept at a current loss to establish a lack of interest, making acceptance less revealing and so sustaining participation on wanted days. Free daily revelation outside the activity removes this incentive. At the model's baseline, it lowers the best joint value in monotone Markov equilibria with exact participation feedback, but raises it with feedback as weak as the diary's.

items.title: MOE-DGSCND: Multi-Objective Enterprise Green Supply Chain Network Design
items.summary: This paper introduces and studies the Multi-Objective Enterprise Doubly-Green Supply Chain Network Design (MOE-DGSCND) problem, an extension of Multi-Objective Supply Chain Network Design. The problem studied here is a three-objective combinatorial optimization problem that simultaneously minimizes total cost f1, carbon dioxide emissions f2 and customer dissatisfaction f3 over binary decisions regarding which distribution centers to open and how to assign customer zones to open facilities. The problem generalizes the capacitated facility location problem (CFLP) and is known to be NP-hard (Garey and Johnson, 1979). This paper formally specifies the decision variables, objective functions and constraints and investigates three solution approaches using a single numerical instance: (A) an exact weighted-sum integer linear programming (ILP) formulation solved with Python combinatorially and via PuLP, (B) three Fully Polynomial-Time Approximation Schemes (FPTAS) providing (1 + $ε$)-approximate solutions for $ε$ := 0.15 and (C) two baseline heuristics for comparison. On an instance with eight customers and five candidate distribution centers, the exact solver certifies the optimal (sampled) supported solutions across eight weight combinations, while the FPTAS-based approaches complete within milliseconds, compared to centiseconds for the exact ILP on this tiny non-stochastic instance.

items.title: Learning to Charge More: How Q-Learning Firms Lock In Supracompetitive Prices
items.summary: There is growing experimental evidence that $Q$-learning agents can learn to charge supracompetitive prices. We ask when such behavior persists, whether it emerges, and which strategies support it. In a repeated pricing game in which firms condition on the previous period's price profile, we give conditions on the learned action values under which supracompetitive prices become an absorbing state once experimentation ends. We then show that under softmax exploration these conditions are reached with positive and explicitly bounded probability, both from a random and from an all-zero initial $Q$-table. In the latter case firms lock in supracompetitive prices because they never learn that undercutting pays; the same mechanism can lock in the competitive price, so the long-run outcome is selected by the exploration path.
